en: *Compendium of the Essentials of the Principles of Calm Abiding and Insight*, Scroll One (with Preface).
The *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* is the sublime practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The *Principles of Calm Abiding and Insight* are the linchpins and spokes of that sublime practice.
If one transmits the Way of Calm Abiding and Insight without clarifying its principles, then the sublime practice will collapse. In the past...
Tiantai Zhiyi received this teaching at Mount Ling; he attained awakening at the Bodhimanda; he expounded it at Yuquan; and he entrusted it to Zhang’an.
From Zhang’an down to Jingxi, the master and disciple were in perfect accord through the Way, and their sublime teachings remained uncontradicted.

Later, however, Qingliang’s biased views arose, giving rise to polemical disputes that opposed our path; turning their backs on our Tiantai school, they allied themselves with the Xianshou tradition, thereby suppressing the fundamental [teachings].

Taking the pure and subtle as the gradual perfection, while elevating the branches of the final stage that incorporate the coarse as the "sudden-of-the-sudden," has brought disorder to the source of the teaching and greatly misled the multitude of students;
thus, the wondrous practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* has nearly become obscured. Alas! When the Way is not yet lost, it rests with the wise master.
For this reason, the Venerable Jingxi, lamenting this perversion and confusion, composed the *Fuxing Zhuanhong* (The Commentary on the *Fahua Wenju*) to propagate [the true meaning].
The texts on the *Jue* (Decisions) and the *Yili* (Exemplification of Principles), among others, dispel erroneous views and clarify sublime practice.

Thus, those lost at the ford of delusion recognize the ferry, and the Buddha-vehicle begins its journey. For this reason, the *Mohe zhiguan* was greatly revitalized in the world through Jingxi [Zhanran].
To this day, all people receive his bounty. Nevertheless, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Xiao zhiguan*) unravels its detailed points, while the *Yili* synthesizes its overarching principles.

Section. The intent is to lead students to infer these principles and regulations, to investigate the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice of Samādhi and Prajñā), to cultivate *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and to harmonize with the Wondrous Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*).
Thus, they shall drive the Great Chariot of the manifold jewels through the four quarters, proceeding directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Therefore, one should know that if the Way of transmitting *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is not clarified through its principles and examples, then the wondrous practice will collapse. I, [the author], in the third year of Yuánfēng...

In the year of Gengshen, he moved his residence to Baoji Jiaoyuan in Angu. The following year, as the summer retreat was about to conclude and he was preparing to begin his practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, his disciples requested:

"Master, the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* (The Diamond Scalpel) points out that the nature of sentient beings is all-pervasive, leaving nothing excluded—be it grass, wood, tiles, or stones—and clarifies that even insentient things possess this nature. Yet, the allegorical records have already explained ten [of these cases]."
The *Fumon* (Gate of Non-duality) subsumes the ten wonders of the *Lotus Sūtra*, revealing the essential purport of this single scripture and causing its wondrous principles to shine forth clearly;
yet, although it has already been explained in the *Enpūki*, there has been no record [of its study] in the *Shikan-girui*.

As for the *Shikan-girui*, it comprehensively organizes the texts of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, refining and clarifying the heart-seal of the transmitted tradition so that it is as bright as if before one’s eyes; yet, I have not heard that there exists a record of it.

Moreover, for several hundred years now, this literature has survived without being studied. Although one may wish to learn *śamatha-vipaśyanā* today, one still suffers from the fact that the essential points remain unpenetrated.
I venture to hope for your instruction in order to dispel my ignorance and stagnation. Upon hearing this request, I could not decline.

Thereupon, I carefully examined the flow of the text and produced a single outline. However, as my studies and lectures were so numerous and demanding, I had not yet found the leisure to provide a detailed exposition.

It was not until the day of the Upper Jisi (the third day of the third lunar month) in the late spring of the year Jiazi, the seventh year, that I finally had the opportunity to compile the essential passages of the *Zhi guan fu xing* (Subsidiary Practices for Stopping and Contemplation).
I arranged them according to their respective sections to clarify their meaning, completing the work by the last quarter of the Mid-Autumn month. Thereafter—

It is titled *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium). Furthermore, it has been uniformly arranged into six fascicles. Because my disciples requested instruction, I have extensively established the Way of this school;
those among the later students of our tradition must not regard it with levity.
Compiled by the Yongjia śramaṇa Shi Congyi.
This is an exposition on the *Zhiguan yili* (The Meaning and Examples of Stopping and Contemplation). The text is divided into two parts. First, the general title, which is further divided into two.

First, the title of the work as originally composed: in full, it should be called the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Although the current text mentions only "Stopping and Contemplation," it also implicitly includes "Mahā. Therefore...

The *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice) states: "The two characters 'Cessation' (*shi*) and 'Contemplation' (*guan*) are none other than *mahā*. They are precisely the cessation and contemplation of the single mind’s three cessations and three contemplations.
Thus, one should know that the entire treatise is subsumed under this primary title.

Therefore, from the 'General Meaning' at the beginning to the 'Ultimate Return' at the end, everything is nothing other than the cessation and contemplation of *mahā*. In this way, the title serves as the general [heading], while the ten chapters constitute the specific [sections]."

Regarding the discussion of "principles and categories" (*yili*): "principle" (*yi*) refers to the underlying reason for *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). "Category" (*li*) refers to analogy, classification, and systematic rule.

Therefore, if one wishes to clarify the reasons for the Buddha-vehicle within the *Mohe zhiguan*, it is necessary to understand the seven categories, which correspond to the seven principles listed below.
However, these seven principles each have their respective categories; they are not to be devised arbitrarily from one's own imagination.
If one fails to establish this, then should one be confused regarding the texts of the seven categories, how will one clarify the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*,
and how will one dispel heterodox and deviant schemes?
Next is the name of the compiler. "Tiantai" refers to the place where he resided. "Śramaṇa" is the title for one who has left the household life.
"Zhanran" is the name of the author. "Tiantai Śramaṇa Śākyamuni [Shi] Yì" is as usual. According to the *Stele of Jingxi* composed by Liang Su, it says:
"His courtesy name was Zhànrán; his surname was Qì. His ancestors lived in Jīngxī, Jìnling. People revered his teachings."
He took this as his title. Since he resided at Tiantai, he is now called the "Tiantai Śramaṇa.
As for the phrase "the Śramaṇa of Pilin" used by Fuxing, this is a name derived from his native commandery. "Shu" (述) means to compose or record; it also implies following.

One who creates [original teachings] is called a Sage (Śāstra-kāra), while one who records [them] is called an Illuminator (Vidyādhara). Now, Jingxi merely recorded the Way of the former Sages and did not...
I have composed this myself. It is just as Zhongni (Confucius) recounted [the past] rather than composing anew.
Next, the text is divided into two parts. First, the names of the seven examples are listed. "First" (*di*) means order; "one" (*yi*) is the beginning of numbers.
From "second" to "seventh," these are all merely successive increments of the preceding number.
Regarding the specific lineage of transmission: Tiantai transmitted the three types of *zhiguan* (calming and contemplation) from Nanyue: first, the gradual; second, the indeterminate;
and third, the perfect and sudden. This present work, the *Mohe zhiguan*, belongs specifically to the category of the perfect and sudden among these three.

Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practices) states: "Within each section, there is no lack of both the primary and the secondary. For example, while the *Cidian Chanmen* (The Gate of Successive Meditation) primarily clarifies the successive [stages], it also incidentally possesses both [the primary and secondary].
Although the text has not yet reached its conclusion, the underlying intent is already present. 'Neither outflowing nor non-outflowing' refers to the text on the sudden [approach].

The sixteen phrases concerning the differences between cultivation and realization refer to the indeterminate [approach]. (1. Outflowing: namely, the ten wholesome paths, the four dhyānas, and so forth; 2. Non-outflowing.)

First are those that are both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*), namely the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*), and so forth. Second are those that are neither with outflows nor without outflows, namely the *Dharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and so forth. Regarding the sixteen types of "arising" (*udbhava*) through cultivation: first, four types of cultivation are clarified according to the gate of calm abiding (*śamatha*);

second, four types of cultivation are clarified according to the gate of insight (*vipaśyanā*). These are: (1) phenomena (*dharma*), (2) principle (*tattva*), (3) both phenomenon and principle, and (4) neither phenomenon nor principle. Within each of these cultivations, there are four distinct ways in which the arising of dhyāna is indeterminate. Therefore, there are a total of sixteen types of indeterminate arising of dhyāna, and so forth.

In the Six Gates of Subtlety (*liumiaomen*), the indeterminate is primarily elucidated, while the other two are also present as secondary aspects. The Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) is simply the sudden.

The "mutual production" (xiangsheng) refers to the gradual approach (within the Six Wondrous Gates, it is expanded into ten gates; the second is called mutual production, and the ninth is called perfect contemplation). Now, this text on the Perfect and Sudden also encompasses the other two.
Although it incidentally includes the other two, it is currently explained according to the primary teaching of the Perfect and Sudden. Therefore, it is referred to as a distinct transmitted lineage.
Since it is said that Tiantai transmitted the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* to Nanyue, we know that the person is the capable agent.

The Transmission. The Dharma is that which is transmitted. That which is transmitted generally encompasses three [vehicles], but here it refers specifically to the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight).

Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states in its explanation of the "Separate Preface": "The lineages inherited by teachers and disciples differ across the three divisions. Because the 'Sudden' is distinguished from the other two, it is termed 'separate.

Thus we know that among the three, it is specifically the Perfect and Sudden that constitutes the distinct division of the transmitted Dharma. This is what is meant by the distinction of the divisions of the transmitted Dharma. As for the correct basis...

As for "teaching" (*śāsana*), it refers to practice without teaching, which is as obscure as wandering in the night. Therefore, sublime practice must rely upon the correct teaching; for the correct teaching serves to distinguish itself from false teachings.
Thus, the note beneath the title of the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "What does practice propagate? Without the various teachings, there would be no basis established.
Since they are called the 'correct teaching,' one should know that that which relies upon them is sublime practice. It relies [upon the teaching].

Regarding the "correct commentary" (*saṃvyākhyāna*): the subsequent text cites the title and states, "The meaning of the text should be understood. Here, "text and meaning" refers to the words and meanings of the authoritative scriptures (*saddharma*) upon which [this work] relies.
"Commenting" (*saṃ*) means "exhaustively"; "explaining" (*vyākhyāna*) means "to disperse," "to analyze," or "to interpret.

As the Preface to the *Zuozhuan* of the *Chunqiu* states: "Like the soaking of rivers and seas, like the moistening of fat and dew; it causes the ice to melt away and the principles to flow smoothly. Thus.

This refers to what is attained later. Regarding the general and specific sections of the Great Chapter (*Dazhang*): the formal exposition of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is divided into ten chapters, beginning with the "General Meaning" (*Dayi*) and ending with the "Return to the Essential" (*Zhigui*).
As the *Fuxing* states: "Within these ten chapters, the 'General Meaning' serves as the general [section], while the remaining eight are the specific [sections].

This relationship between the general and the specific also carries the sense of being broad and concise; thus, the *Zhi guan* says: "The 'General Meaning' is concise, while the eight chapters are broad. The "Return to the Essential" is...

The "Return" (Guī) is neither extensive nor abbreviated. Therefore, the *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 4 (Xianxing edition), states: "In the preceding 'Discrimination' [section], they were termed 'extensive and abbreviated,' and also termed 'general and specific.
These two sets of texts, general and specific, mutually illuminate one another. Thus, the preceding text says: 'The five brief [sections] give rise to and reveal the ten extensive [sections].
Therefore, in the following passage explaining the analogy of the general and specific within the Great Chapters, it simply mentions the 'extensive.'"

This is a brief summary; it is precisely this meaning. Regarding the "explanation of the doubt concerning mind and objects": the "mind" (citta) is established in contrast to form (rūpa), while the "object" (viṣaya) receives its name in relation to observation.
Since the mind itself is taken as the object of observation, it is called "mind and object. Furthermore, the designation "mind" is restrictive.

The term "object" (*viṣaya*) is used here in a general sense, because phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), are collectively designated as the objects of observation.
This section on "Resolving Doubts" (*śaṅkā-vinodana*) employs analytical questions and answers to eliminate stagnation and achieve clear insight.

Regarding the phrase "understanding and practice support each other," the subsequent text cites the title as "practice and understanding support each other. Although the phrasing is reversed, the meaning remains unchanged; it is merely a stylistic feature of the composition.
This is merely a matter of citing the preceding and following sections alternately. Thus, the *Zhi guan* says: "The previous six stages rely upon the *sūtras* to open up wondrous understanding;
now, based on that wondrous understanding, one establishes correct practice. Oil and light depend on each other; the eyes and feet mutually assist one another. The *Fuxing* commentary states:

"Oil is capable of continuing the light, which serves as a metaphor for contemplative practice (*guanxing*); light is able to illuminate the oil, which serves as a metaphor for contemplative understanding (*guanjie*); the eyes are able to guide the feet..."

The analogy of "stopping" (*śamatha*) illustrates that the feet are able to reach the eyes; this serves as an analogy for the practice of stopping (*śamatha-caryā*). Both analogies are presented together to illustrate these two dharmas.

Although the phrasing differs—using "mutual reliance" (*xiang*) and "furtherance" (*jing*), or "relying upon" (*lai*) and "providing support" (*zi*)—the underlying meaning must be the same. "Relying" (*lai*) means to depend upon; "supporting" (*zi*) means to augment.
Thus, one should know that if there were no wondrous understanding of the six chapters, practice could not be perfected. This section clarifies the correct view by resolving doubts.
The commentary explains the titles and metaphors: "delusion" refers to being confused; "to manifest" means to clearly show; and "to depart from the heterodox" means to be correct. The note states:
"Regarding the title 'Dispelling Delusion,' those who request a revision say that there was an original draft manuscript where the title of the seventh section read 'Dispelling Delusion.
It should be revised to read 'Metaphorizing Doubt to Manifest the Correct. Thus, one knows that this text is a revised and polished version."
This is the essence of the *Sè* (Color/Form).

Next, the meaning of the seven categories is explained. The text consists of seven parts. First, the explanation of the distinct categories of the transmitted teachings, which is divided into two sections: first, the citation of the names;

second, a general reference followed by the detailed explanation of their meanings, which is further divided into three parts. The first part generally clarifies that what is transmitted pertains exclusively to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantùn*) teaching.
"Section" (bu) refers to a fascicle. The term "Perfect and Sudden" (yuándùn) is named according to its original source. If one were to follow the third revised title, it should be called "Mahā.
Furthermore, although the third revised title says "Mahā," when listing the names of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it likewise only says "Perfect and Sudden.
Following this intention, it is here called "Perfect and Sudden."
Regarding the term "Buddha Vehicle" (*buddhayāna*), it refers to what the sutra says: "Each son is given a single great carriage;

these carriages are high and broad, adorned with various jewels," and so forth. Regarding the term "right practice," this Buddha Vehicle—the great white ox-cart—is called right practice to distinguish it from wrong practices, such as the donkey carts.
Regarding the term "great essence," it is like a grand framework; [it encompasses] the lateral...

Although it encompasses both [the gradual and the sudden], its true essence lies in the Perfect-Sudden (yuantun). How could Qingliang possibly dismiss it as "gradually perfect" (jianyuan), or arbitrarily establish a "sudden-of-the-sudden" (duntun) outside of the three [categories]?

Next, following the "General Meaning" (dayi), the doubts are resolved and the characteristics of the Perfect-Sudden are correctly demonstrated. Although its general framework and structural form are indeed Perfect-Sudden, [the text proceeds...]

Yet, those with biased interpretations still largely remain in confusion. Therefore, it is necessary to resolve their doubts and demonstrate the characteristics [of this teaching]. This section is divided into two parts.
First, the resolution of doubts, which is further divided into two. First, the direct resolution of doubts: there are those who raise the following doubt:

"If this entire treatise is designated as the Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle (*yuan-dun fo-cheng*), why is it that in several places at the beginning of the *Dà-yì* (Great Meaning), the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*san-zhi-guan*) are used as concluding summaries?"
Therefore, this commentary states: "This merely provides a general, incidental, and borrowed designation to establish the meaning;

it does not mean that [the text] refers to the three types of practice-forms (as the current text erroneously reads '作' instead of '為'). Thus, one should know that the primary intent lies solely in the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]."

The general meaning consists of five parts: first, generating the great mind; second, practicing the great conduct; third, realizing the great fruit; fourth, tearing asunder the great net; and fifth, returning to the great destination.
Within the initial section on generating the mind, there are three parts: first, the preliminary discourse; second, the exclusion of what is not [the path];

and third, the revelation of what is. Regarding the exclusion of what is not, it says: "Furthermore, the teachings of the Sages are manifold; they may be presented in sequential order or in non-sequential order, and may be presented in full detail."

Alternatively, it may not be explained in full; even when it says, "In this way, these various [elements] mutually establish and manifest one another," it concludes with the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, which can be understood by the reader's own reflection.
Furthermore, it concludes with a single *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, stating: "The arousal of the bodhicitta is *vipaśyanā*;
the cessation of deviant and perverse thoughts is *śamatha*. Since the subsequent text states, "Therefore, use the three and one to encompass and conclude," [the meaning is clear].
This is a summary; therefore, the text now cites the passage that concludes with "one *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Within this section on manifestation, there are three parts.
First, regarding the Four Noble Truths, it says: "Since what has been explained above is extensive, I shall now conclude it with three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Second, regarding the Four Great Vows, it concludes with one *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, saying: "If one understands this mind, one will spontaneously attain [realization]."
Regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā: the absence of arousal and the absence of obstruction are *vipaśyanā*; their nature of quiescent extinction is *śamatha*.

Later, within the context of the six stages of realization (*ṣat-vidha-yoga*), there is also a concluding passage on "one śamatha-vipaśyanā" (as will be analyzed below). Next, within the cultivation of the Great Practice (*mahā-caryā*), the four kinds of samādhi are clarified.
Within the fourth samādhi, there are four [sections]: first, concerning various sūtras; second, concerning various wholesome dharmas; third, concerning various...
[Regarding] evil. Fourth, concerning the various indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states: after the four sections of the text, he concludes with the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, stating:

"Furthermore, based solely on the final 'good' (the 'final good' refers to the mutual comparison of the general characteristics of good and evil, wherein only the Perfect [teaching] is good; as the Perfect occupies the final position, it is called the 'final good'] to clarify 'following one's own intention.
This is the meaning of the gradual [approach]. If both good and evil are clarified as following one's own intention, this is the meaning of the sudden [approach]. If, according to...

Regarding the excellence of the *zhédié* (folding and unfolding): [the excellence of the *zhédié* means that it is not included within the previous two [categories], nor does it emerge from the previous two; arising in emptiness belongs to emptiness, and arising in existence belongs to existence]. This clarifies the "following one's own intention" (*suì zìyì*).

This, then, is the indeterminate intention (*bùdìngyì*). There are five general meanings [to this]. What is now referred to as "at the beginning of the text" points specifically to the first [section]:

the arousal of the great mind (*fā dàxīn*), and the second: the practice of the great path (*xiū dàxíngwén*). As for the phrase "in several places," it refers to three locations, as cited previously by Zhòngní.

It says: "If I were granted several years to study the *Yi*, I could then avoid major transgressions. "Several years" refers to three years; thus, we know that the term "several" (*shu*) in this context signifies "three" (*san*).
The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "In passages concerning response and resonance, there must be a conclusion with 'three' [aspects].
If the textual meaning is narrow, one concludes with only 'one. As in the examples below—the Four Great Vows and the Six Identities—one may conclude simply with 'three,' as detailed therein."
The following text clarifies these four truths and the four samādhis (one should say "the fourth samādhi" at the end of the passage).

At times, three or one are abbreviated together, as in the three abbreviations below; at other times, all three or one are employed together, as in the present text. One is general (*sāmānya*), while the three are specific (*viśeṣa*).
The general refers to that which pervades all three, and the specific refers to each one individually. Failing to perceive this intent gives rise to many divergent views. Question:
Why must it be concluded with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? Answer: These three dharmas universally crown all [teachings]. Now, these five summaries have their texts pervasively apply [to all];

therefore, the texts in various places conclude with the triad of [the three trainings] and [the two gates of] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Furthermore, this section is collectively titled "Śamatha and Vipaśyanā";
every word and meaning therein is nothing other than *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. One must not, upon seeing this conclusion with the names of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, assume that they are merely...

This is the method of cultivation. Just as within the "Six Identities" (*liu ji*), both Principle (*li*) and Name-and-Word (*mingzi*) are concluded with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (one should further add Practice and Similarity, as will be distinguished below), and in the present text only the response to the call (*gan ying*) is concluded [with them], how could there be another separate judgment for the one outside the three?

Thus we know that Principle, Teaching, Practice, Fruit, the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), and the response to the call are none other than *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Furthermore, although this section...

This is the general name for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. From the section on "Explaining the Names" (*shiming*) onwards, the textual characteristics are distinguished; henceforth, the three [types of] texts are no longer used to conclude [the sections].

(Although it is said that the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are not used for the conclusion, there are instances where a single *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is used for the conclusion—for example, in the third fascicle, the five categories of the partial and the perfect use a single *śamatha-vipaśyanā* to conclude the provisional and the real.

Furthermore, at the end of the section on the "Wondrous Object," it also says: "Passing through all phenomena, they are none other than gradual, sudden, or indeterminate. The *Fuxing* commentary states: "In the previous 'General Meaning,' the characteristics of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* were concluded and demonstrated within a single sudden-perfect [teaching]; now, within the 'Wondrous Object,' the three *śamatha-vipaśyanās* are subsumed as being identical to the single sudden-perfect [teaching], etc.")

Furthermore, it is said: "Therefore, the concluding text merely establishes three forms of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*); how can it be explained by means of 'cultivation'? It is further said:

"Moreover, since the concluding text does not possess the characteristics of cultivation, there is no need to further obstruct [the argument] with the distinction between the Perfect and Gradual [teachings]. As for the term "in a general sense": [it refers to...]
"Pan" (汎) means floating. "Er" (爾) is a particle used for emphasis. This is because floating and drifting are pervasive and diffuse, lacking specific definition.
"Jie" (借) means to borrow or use temporarily. It does not mean that [this teaching] is identical to the three types of practice; rather, it is spoken of in contrast to those two combined practices.
In reality, it simply differs from the other two modes of practice, for the practice of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) is precisely the characteristic of this school.
Therefore [it is so]. Furthermore, the concluding text is not itself the practice-pattern (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*) of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*).

Why? Because the practice-pattern of the Perfect and Sudden must fully incorporate the twenty-five expedients (*upāya*), as well as the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) and the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*) of correct cultivation.
How could the concluding text alone be considered sufficient? Thus it is said that this does not mean it constitutes the three types of practice-patterns.

The section following "By means of the broad meaning" (dà yì) next clarifies the reason for this, which may be understood by reference to what precedes. Regarding the phrase "the text is concise" (wén lüè), it refers to the five concise summaries (wǔ lüè).

Here, it specifically points to the first two concise summaries: namely, the arousal of the bodhicitta and the practice of cultivation. Regarding the phrase "the meaning is extensive" (yì guǎng), the meaning encompasses the nine extensive expositions (jiǔ guǎng).

Therefore, the *Fǔxíng* states: "The five concise summaries are formed by extracting the nine extensive expositions from below; because they reveal the purport of the nine chapters, they are called 'broad' (dà)."
"Intention. Furthermore, because all nine chapters provide a general summary of that intention, they are called "General Intentions" (*dà-yì*).

Thus, these five summaries are all named with the character "Great" (*dà*). Therefore, the *Zhìguān* states: "The first explains the General Intention, which encompasses the beginning and end, and crowns the initial and subsequent [sections].

Consequently, the *Fǔxíng* says: "Where the text on resonance and response is extensive, it must be concluded with the three; where the textual meaning is narrow, it is concluded with only one. This is to grasp [the essence]."
The term "one who" refers to taking [the teaching] with one's own hands.

Next, regarding "one should know the following," this correctly demonstrates the characteristics of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]. The text is divided into two parts. First is the general demonstration: "Therefore, one should know."
Although the text employs both [the gradual and the sudden] as provisional names to establish its meaning, the primary intent of this section lies solely in the Perfect and Sudden.

Therefore, following the introduction below, the subsequent citations of scriptural evidence are divided into three parts. First, the citation of the introductory text is further divided into two; first, the direct citation of the text itself.

The statement "as it says in the Preface" is an error. This passage originally appears within the "Discrimination" (liao-jian) section of the "Exposition of Stopping and Contemplation" (Zhiguan zhengshuo).

Therefore, the question in the "Discrimination" section of the *Mohe Zhiguan* asks: "Briefly indicating the general meaning, how do the similarities and differences [between the various teachings] stand?

The answer states: "In a general sense, the names differ but the meaning is the same; in a specific sense, the brief indication points to three gates, while the general meaning lies in the single 'Sudden' teaching. Furthermore, since this discrimination...

This chapter is Zhiyan’s comparative analysis of the general meaning of the formal exposition against the distinctions made in the introduction; it provides a concise explanation of the three gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (stopping and contemplating) as a means of systematic discrimination.
Therefore, it may also be said to belong to the "Introduction. A detailed citation from the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) is provided in full below.

Following this, the broad [exposition] is headed by the concise [summary], and next it is clarified that the broad and the concise are not different: the "General Meaning" is the concise version, while the remaining eight [chapters] are the broad.

This refers to the "Extensive" [text]. Since the five summaries (*pañca-saṃkṣepa*) of the "Great Meaning" (*mahārtha*) are already contained within a single session, how could the summary and the extensive differ in their path?

"Crowning" (*guān*) refers to head ornamentation. This means that the "Great Meaning" is used to crown the beginning of the ten chapters. Thus, the *Zhìguān* says: "First, the Great Meaning is explained;
it encompasses the beginning and the end, and crowns the initial and the final. It further states: "The arising of the five summaries reveals the ten extensives. Therefore, the Great...
The five summaries of the *Yì* (Contemplation) and the ten detailed expositions of the *Xià* (Lower) both correctly clarify the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Next, regarding the passage cited from the "Indication of the Location": this text indicating the location is precisely the preface written by Zhǎng Ān.
Thus it is said that the *Cí dì chán mén* (Gradual Meditation Gate) comprised thirty fascicles; the present ten fascicles are the private compilation of Fǎshèn of Dà Zhuāngyán Temple.

Commentary: Regarding the "indeterminate texts," this refers to works such as the *Six Subtle Gates*, which employ an indeterminate method of contemplation to traverse the twelve dhyānas (the twelve dhyānas refer to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the four immeasurables, and so forth up to the six pāramitās).
This was the text requested by Mao Xi, the Grand Chancellor of the Chen dynasty, for Zhiyi to produce.
Regarding the "perfect and sudden texts," these are those cited here [in the present work]. As the *Fuxing* states: "Next, the three types of texts are shown according to their distinct categories."

The teachings transmitted do not go beyond these three. For anyone wishing to practice, they must rely upon a specific division; therefore, the distinct divisions and locations [of the teachings] should be indicated.
The "Text on the Perfect and Sudden" (Yuántùn wén) refers to the present text, which was personally recorded by Zhǐguān (Zhāng'ān).
Yùquán Monastery is located in Jīngzhōu; the color of its spring water is like jade, hence it was named accordingly.
The following text is divided into two parts. First, a general indication that all subsequent passages are intended to reveal the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Within the initial introduction, since the teaching already pertains to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*), from this point downward, throughout the various sections of the formal exposition, every text employs the sequential contemplation of the three teachings.

The discussion of "mutual dependence" (*xiāngdài*) serves to manifest the "perfectly sudden" (*yuántùn*) single reality that is free from dependence. Thus, both the introduction and the main exposition correctly clarify the perfectly sudden teaching.
Next, the specific citation of the passage on the "Great Vehicle" (*dàchē*) serves as textual evidence to establish the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight).

After the explanation of the ten stages of practice (*shíshèng*) regarding the realm of the aggregates (*yīnjìng*) is concluded, the *Lotus Sūtra*’s Great Vehicle is cited as a metaphor for these ten dharmas; therefore, it is said, "in the text concerning the Great Vehicle. This is because of [the contemplation of] thought...

Regarding the discussion on how [the perfections] wait upon one another as attendants, the *Zhiguan* states: "The counteractive aids to the path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) extensively encompass all dharmas" (the inclusion of these dharmas is cited below).

Thus it is said that there are many attendants who serve and protect [the Bodhisattva]. The *Wenju* states: "It is like the *upāya-pāramitā*, which can adapt and comply with others to provide service;
it causes all Māras, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and those of minor practices to follow."

This is the functional application of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All are my attendants. Regarding taking the wondrous principle of true reality (*bhūta-tathatā*) as the body of the chariot, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* says:
"Observing that every momentary thought is nothing other than the dharma-nature and true reality is called the 'Great Equal Chariot.'"
To penetrate the source of the three truths is called "high"; to encompass the ten dharma-realms is called "vast.

Regarding the use of "the white ox" for the untainted, sublime contemplation (*anāsrava-prajñā*): the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states, "The wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness destroys the blackness of the eight inversions; this is called 'yoking the white ox.
The *Wenju* states, "It is like how untainted *prajñā* can lead one through the truths, conditions, and perfections across all myriad practices."
"Reaching *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), one realizes that this form is fundamentally such; it is immediately conjoined with original purity and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

As for the statement that 'all other dharmas are ornaments,' the *Zhiguan* says: 'The immeasurable factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*) are called the various jewels and adornments. The *Wenju* says:"
This is like the adornment of the myriad practices, such as the surrounding railings and so forth; these are not cited in full here. Therefore, in the *Wenju*, Zhanran (Zhang’an) privately remarked:
"The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is precisely the body of the chariot; all the various jewels used for ornamentation are merely the decorative implements.
Furthermore, the *Wenju* first establishes the topical outline (*pīn-kē*), stating: "In the section describing the body of the chariot, first describe its height and breadth, and next clarify..."

The "white ox" follows, clarifying the retinue. The *Wenju ji* states: "In accordance with the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), one should divide the body of the vehicle into the primary and the auxiliary;

the white ox corresponds to the fulfillment [of the path]. This means that the meaning corresponds to the two natures of cultivation and the single nature of reality, wherein the one further possesses the three.

'High and broad' signifies non-duality. Furthermore, the *Fuxing yin yi* says: "The rational nature is the body of the vehicle, which fully possesses the degrees and the resources for completion; the white ox is contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*). It also says:
That carriage is the inconceivable realm (the body of the carriage). The canopy and awning are compassion. The interlacing of jeweled cords is the arousal of the bodhicitta.

The installation of the red pillow—of which there are two types, inner and outer—is as follows: if it is the pillow within the carriage, it is the resting of all practices, which is the settling of the mind (*samatha*).
If it is the pillow outside the carriage, whether moving or still, "movement" and "stillness" signify only the meanings of penetration and obstruction (*pratipakṣa*). This breaks [the cycle].

Obstruction exists within penetration; by means of obstruction itself, one penetrates. Its swiftness is like the wind. To immediately shatter ignorance is the meaning of "shattering everywhere" (pervasive shattering).

Beginning with the white ox and ending with the level and upright path refers to the meaning of the *mārga-aṅga* (factors of the path) [the white ox]. Furthermore, having many attendants refers to the primary and auxiliary practices [the attendants].
Wandering through the four directions refers to the successive stages. Patience and detachment from attachment occur at the beginning of these successive stages. Peaceful abiding...
Patience merely involves enduring the two types of conditions—contrary and favorable—of the five grades, thereby causing one to enter the six sense organs and become free from craving;

this specifically means becoming free from the "craving for similar dharmas" within the six sense organs. Furthermore, as for the successive stages, these are merely the rungs by which practice ascends.

Fearing that practitioners might fall into confusion, the text separately sets forth the five grades and the purity of the six sense organs within the sequence of stages to exhort and encourage the practitioner.

Being free from hindrances and free from craving, we know that the first seven [factors] primarily clarify the body of the vehicle as well as its equipment and provisions (also including the white ox), while the latter three are merely the paths traversed by the vehicle.
If there were no path to be traversed, the meaning of "transportation" would not be established. Therefore, these ten factors are collectively named the Mahāyāna.
Third, "Therefore, we know" and below concludes by indicating the specific category.

As illustrated by the preceding examples, we know that this category resides specifically within the wondrous practice of the Perfect and Sudden Buddha Vehicle among the three types of śamatha-vipaśyanā; beyond this, there is no other path of the "suddenest of the sudden."
"Direction" (趣) refers to the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*). This is because there is no other distinct "sudden-sudden" intent established apart from this.
The second section, concerning the authentic teachings (*saddharma*) that serve as the basis, is divided into two parts:
first, stating the names; second, explaining their meanings. This section is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying that the authentic teachings upon which one relies apply universally...
"One generation" (*ekādhikāra*): "scattered" (*san*) means divided, distributed, or pervasive; "comprehensive" (*gai*) means complete or inclusive; "generation" (*dai*) means a year or a change.
Although the definition established is that thirty years constitute one generation, here it simply refers to a period of change.
This refers to the preaching of the Dharma by Śākyamuni during his fifty-year career as a single generation, distinct from the Buddhas of the past and future. That is to say:
Now, this single work on *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) is distributed throughout [the canon], extensively citing various texts;

it fully encompasses the teachings of Śākyamuni’s one lifetime across the five periods spanning fifty years. Therefore, the note beneath the title of the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "What does the practice propagate?"
It is not established without the collective teachings.
Next, it clarifies that the purport of the text lies solely in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras. This section has two parts. First, the general clarification:

although citations are scattered throughout and encompass the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime of teaching, the structural framework and primary intent of the text ultimately converge upon these two sūtras. The first follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The two gates of the fundamental and the phenomenal reveal the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Thus, the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states:

"Both the fundamental and phenomenal gates ultimately return to the true reality" (here, the fundamental stage of long life is set aside for the moment). Second, based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it further upholds the precepts to assist in revealing the eternal nature.

This is because these two sutras, the *Lotus* and the *Nirvāṇa*, are judged to be of the same flavor; both equally reveal the truth, as there is nothing therein that is not the single flavor of *amṛta* (the finest essence).
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of the "meal of the great king," and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* speaks of the "taste of *amṛta* (clarified butter).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* reveals the provisional teachings of the three vehicles to manifest the reality of the One Vehicle; this is called the "meal of the great king. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa* points out that the three inferior and shallow practices are, in truth, supreme, eternal, blissful, and self;
this is called the "taste of *amṛta*. There is no difference between the meal of the king and the taste of *amṛta*; both reveal the reality and the superior practice.

At that time, there were no side-shadows; thus, the timing and the flavor (rasa) of the two sūtras are fundamentally the same. Although this is the general outline, a detailed analysis reveals it is not so. The *Wenju ji* states:
"While the judgment on the flavor is that they are simultaneous, the schools (nikāya) differ. Regarding their principles, though the names are distinct, they all converge upon the eternal."

In terms of the capacity of the audience, that [teaching] is called "gathering the gleanings. In terms of the Dharma, it preserves the three provisional means (*upāya*). Regarding the intent of the treatise, it carries the Vinaya discipline.

Regarding the scriptural evidence, it includes the fruits of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Regarding the benefit received, there is no extensive record. The length of time for its delivery is forever distinct.

When discussing the "permanent," the past and future are not the same. The treatise’s analogy is like the remnants of a great army. The manifestation of auspicious signs and their symbolic significance are each distinct. The difficulty or ease of breaking through attachments is likewise different.

Understanding [the teachings] reveals that the near and distant traces diverge; the expositions are established because the capacities of sentient beings are unequal; their applications differ because they treat birth and death differently; and the entrustments vary because there are those remaining in the lower realms.

Having obtained these sixteen points, the rest may be known by abbreviation. If one loses sight of these similarities and differences, it will be exceptionally difficult to lecture upon or transmit them.

Not only these two sutras, but others as well are not easily understood. Scholars should take note of the explanations regarding the similarities and differences of these sixteen [points], as they appear in full within the supplementary notes to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

The following section provides a detailed exposition. The text is divided into two parts. The first clarifies that from beginning to end, all practice is based upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the primary path. This section consists of five parts.
The first part addresses the names and essences of the partial and the universal, based on the names and essences of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

It is further divided into two. First, it clarifies the name based on the metaphor. The preceding text refers to "relying solely on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to reveal the reality through its fundamental and manifested traces. Its meaning is as follows: [End of excerpt]

Why? This is precisely to demonstrate the reason for this. Therefore, within the ten chapters of *Zhiguan*, the second chapter, "Explaining the Names of Stopping and Contemplation," is divided into four sections:
first, the relative; second, the absolute; third, reconciling differences; and fourth, penetrating the three virtues. Thus it is said:
"Explaining names involves discussing the relative and the absolute. This is the application of the practice of stopping and contemplation within the specific title of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

"Intermediate" refers to the two types of marvelous teachings: those that are "relative" (*dai*) and those that are "absolute" (*zetsu*). The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "It is judged that the present *Lotus Sūtra* alone possesses these two marvels, namely the relative and the absolute.
As for what is called 'relative,' there is only the relative to the coarse that constitutes the marvelous; there is nothing relative to the marvelous that constitutes the coarse.

If one considers the provisional traces in light of the fundamental reality, they may mutually define one another; however, if one considers one section in light of another section, it is invariably and exclusively marvelous. Here, we are discussing this in terms of the Dharma."

The traces of the Flower [Sūtra] and its underlying principle further establish their mutual forms. Thus, the profound text and the ultimate [truth] are both termed "wondrous" (miao) as they await one another.

Therefore, when comparing the teachings of the various sections, there are both horizontal and vertical dimensions. Looking back toward the previous four periods is called "vertical waiting"; looking toward the three vehicles from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching] is called "horizontal waiting.
Since this text follows the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the general outline of its explanations regarding names and so forth conforms to that sūtra. As for their characteristics...

Relative dependence (*pratītya*) is "coarse"; in meaning, it involves discussing the sublime by depending on the coarse. Absolute transcendence (*atyanta*) is "sublime"; in meaning, it involves opening up the coarse to discuss the sublime.

These two are also termed "discarding the coarse" and "opening up the coarse. Therefore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, only these two types of the sublime are discussed; there is no further category of that which is neither relative nor absolute.

Since that [text] is for the purpose of classifying the teachings (*śāsana-vibhāga*), both the relative and the absolute are equally designated as "sublime. Now, this [present discussion] concerns relative dependence.
This is then judged to be coarse. It clarifies only the ultimate transcendence (*atyanta-vyatireka*); since there is no category to be depended upon, there is no vertical dependence.

Since there is no teaching to be anticipated, it is called the absence of horizontal dependence. Therefore, only this single transcendence serves as the expressive designation (*vācaka*). Although dependence is established to manifest this ultimate non-dependence, [the latter remains absolute].
Since even "negation" (jue) does not exist, what reliance could there be upon it? It is for the purpose of explicating the Three Virtues that we provisionally name it "negation.

By borrowing the term "relative dependence" (xiangdai), it is judged to be within the realm of conceptual thought (sishi). Therefore, only that which is absolute and beyond dependence (juedai) can be called "wondrous" (miao).

For this reason, although the Buddha-realm is wondrous following the realm of conceptual thought, it remains at the end of the nine realms and is collectively termed "coarse"; thus, it is all judged as not being what is employed here. Next, [it is] given...
The meaning of "not sequential" is also like this. Therefore, the meaning of "sequential" refers only to the *vaipulya* (Mahāyāna) gate;

as for the "universal" and "particular," they are used in their universal and particular aspects, yet are described as "seemingly universal" and "seemingly particular. Although it is said that they are not employed [in the ultimate sense], this is precisely based on the contemplation of the conceivable to clarify the inconceivable.

By opening up that which is depended upon, one achieves the capacity for absolute transcendence; this is the meaning of the "wondrous contemplation" (*miaoguān*) in the present text. This applies to all subsequent meanings in the explanation of names and so forth.

Therefore, the *Shiming lun* (Treatise on Explaining Names) relies upon discourse, while the *Lun dai lun jue* (Treatise on Transcending Discourse) is beyond it. Regarding the essence and characteristics, there are only the discussions of sequence and non-sequence;

the same applies to the six meanings of subsuming phenomena and the five gates of the partial and the perfect. Although there are no distinct sections that can be contrasted, one still borrows the flavor of the teachings to manifest the perfect and subtle.

As for the ten contemplations applied to every object, they should be exclusively subtle; yet even these rely upon the horizontal and vertical arrangements to manifest that which is neither horizontal nor vertical.

Thus we know that the text of this single treatise collectively establishes the Perfect Vehicle (yuan-cheng) as the wondrous contemplation that reveals the provisional (kai-quan). How could one point to a single phrase and claim it alone to be sublime and profound?
If that were the case, what would it differ from [the critique of] "physically treading" [the path]? As for the phrase "up to the texts concerning the partial and the perfect," it refers to...
This is a brief summary of the categories of the essence and characteristics of the teachings. Within the single section on the partial and the perfect (*piānyuán*), it is further divided into five:
first, the Great and Small; second, the Half and Full; third, the Partial and Perfect; fourth, the Gradual and Sudden; and fifth, the Expedient and Real. Regarding the Expedient and Real, it is said:

"The Expedient refers to provisional strategies that are employed temporarily and then discarded; the Real refers to the authentic record, the ultimate goal. There are three intended meanings for establishing the Expedient as a provisional category: first, for...

1. The implementation of the provisional (shishi-quan). 2. The opening of the provisional to reveal the real (kaiquan-xianshi). 3. The abolition of the provisional to reveal the real (feiquan-xianshi). These correspond to the three analogies of the lotus in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great matter; they originally establish the three provisional forms of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* for the purpose of the perfect and sudden single reality (*ekayāna*) of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
The provisional is not their primary intent, nor does the intent lie outside the provisional. It is simply by opening the three provisional forms of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* that...
This reveals the perfect and sudden (yuantun) single reality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Having established the provisional for the sake of the real, the Real is now established;

having opened up the provisional to reveal the Real, the provisional is itself the Real, such that there is no longer any provisional to be discussed. Therefore, the provisional is discarded to reveal the Real; the provisional is abandoned while the Real remains.

To temporarily employ this [method] for explaining the names is appropriate in meaning. Thus it is said: "Citing the three parables of the Lotus Sutra to explain the names. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "Temporarily..."
The passage from the *Fahua* [Sūtra] concerning the explanation of names is brought here to explain the terms "provisional" (*upāya*) and "real" (*bhūtārtha*). Question:

Regarding the three metaphors of the lotus—opening, unfolding, and shedding—which correspond to the three dharmas of bestowing, opening, and discarding—are these of the same essence (*ekasvabhāva*) or of different essences (*nānāsvabhāva*)? If one says they are of different essences...
"Why is it that you do not use the coarse flower as a metaphor, yet claim that because they are of the same substance (*samatā*), there is no means by which to bestow or reveal [the truth]?

If you say they are of the same substance, why then do you say 'for the sake of the lotus there is the flower,' such that the flower conceals the fruit, and only upon opening does the coarse reveal the subtle?
Answer: "If one does not understand the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the capacities of sentient beings (*indriya*), then regarding these various texts, one will simply..."
If the transmission were obstructed and stagnant, how could the great purport of this single school be revealed? Now, let it be elucidated through the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*):
thus, the lotus is a metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Consequently, the stages of concealment, revelation, and so forth are all of one essence.

Furthermore, when distinguished according to the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, the Tathāgata manifests the provisional (*neyārtha*) within the real (*nītārtha*). Here, the flower conceals the fruit; once the flower opens, the lotus appears.

This reveals the coarse and manifest as the subtle and wondrous. Thus, while they appear to be distinct entities, this is merely due to the strong concealment of the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings.

If one considers that the Tathāgata’s skillful means are fundamentally one, how could they ever differ from reality? Therefore, the flower exists for the sake of the lotus; this is precisely the provisional [expedient] within the real.

When the flower opens, the lotus appears; this is precisely the reality within the provisional. Thus, what was bestowed in the past is now revealed; for the Buddha, there is nothing that is not within the essence of the body (*dharmakāya*).

For this reason, it is said that the provisional and the revealed are of the same substance (*ekasvabhāva*). However, because the mental capacities of those in the past were obscured and they longed for a proximate fruit, it was judged to be "outside the essence" (*bhinna-svabhāva*);

therefore, the bestowal of the provisional was described as being of a different substance. Nevertheless, when their capacities have matured, the provisional must be revealed, and thus that [provisional] is opened.
To be able to provide protection for that which is near is what is called "opening" (*kai*). What is it that is opened? It is precisely that which is capable of covering.

Therefore, it is said that opening reveals the coarse and manifests the subtle. Since the coarse is opened and revealed, it is termed "subtle. Thus, it is taught that "opening and manifesting" (*kaigen*) is also called "identical essence" (*dōtai*).

Bestowing provisional means (*shiken*), however, carries the sense of "different essence" (*itai*). Although this may be so from the perspective of the capacities of sentient beings (*ki*), it is not the case for the Buddha. For this reason...
The gift of opening [the topknot] is the single identity of the same essence; the meaning of the analogy of the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) loosening his hair-tuft can be understood from this.

Therefore, when the Buddha, as a Wheel-Turning King, beholds the great beings who should destroy the great delusions and attain the merit of great wisdom, he loosens and unties the skillful provisional topknot of the same essence upon the crown of the true jewel Dharma-realm, bestowing the prediction of the bright pearl of the true mark (lakṣaṇa). If one grasps this intent, then all texts [will become clear].
This can be understood. That he does not see this and falsely establishes [his own views] is truly pitiable.

Regarding "Manifesting the Essence" (*xiantti*) below: next, the function of the essence of the *dharmatā* (real mark) is clarified. This is the third chapter, "The Characteristics of the Essence," within the ten chapters of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Hence it is called "Manifesting the Essence. The text on that "Characteristics of the Essence" is itself divided into four sections; the first is the "Characteristics of the Teaching" (*jiaoxiang*).
Second, the wisdom of the two eyes; third, the objective realm; fourth, gain and loss. Next, the meaning of the chapter on "Application" (yòng) is clarified:

it states that the *Fahua shu* uses the "Fourfold One" (sì-yī) to clarify reality (*shí*). Now, the four categories used here to manifest the essence (*tǐ*) can be categorized as analogous to that. The *Fuxing yin yi* says:

"Since the previous explanation of 'Names' already employed the two subtleties of 'relative' (*dài*) and 'absolute' (*jué*) from the *Xuánwén*, we now employ the 'Fourfold One' from the *Shu* to manifest the essence and clarify reality once again."

In reality, it is not different from that; therefore, it is employed. These four "Ones" (sì-yī) originally originated from Guangzhai [Temple]. *The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra* states: "Formerly, they were called the 'Four Ones,' namely:
one fruit, one person, one teaching, and one cause. Now, our school follows the old tradition and also establishes the "Four Ones," though the numerical count is the same while the names differ;

they do not entirely agree with the old version. What the old version called "one fruit" (*guò yī*), we now call "one principle" (*lǐ yī*). If there were no seal of principle (*lǐ yìn*), it would be identical to the teachings of Māra. What the old version called "cause"...

First, regarding "the practice of oneness": if the terminology is identical, it is singular; "practice" (xing) applies to both cause and effect. As for the two aspects of "person" and "teaching," their oneness is no different from the traditional view.
Furthermore, the *Xuanyan wen* treats the ten wonders as eleven; for now, we shall follow the fourfold scheme to correspond with the four chapters.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "In order to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Taking that which is known and seen as the "oneness of principle" (li-yi), yet—
Teaching the Bodhisattvas is the oneness of person; constantly performing a single task is the oneness of practice; preaching for the sake of sentient beings is the oneness of teaching.

The commentary explains that the oneness of principle pertains to the capacity for knowing and seeing. Furthermore, it provides a fourfold explanation: namely, the four wisdoms, the four gates, the four stages, and the contemplation of the mind.
These four chapters are sufficient in their meaning through the correspondence between subject and object. Wisdom is the eye-wisdom; the gates are the characteristics of the teachings.
Contemplating the mind is simply receiving the teaching and realizing wisdom; the successive stages are merely those ascended by eye-wisdom to accord with principle (and so forth).
As for the current statement that it "fully employs the fourfold ones of Guangzhai," there are two intentions:

first, to contrast with the three metaphors of the lotus mentioned in the preceding text, and thus the present reference is made to the "fourfold ones of Guangzhai"; second, the term "fourfold ones" is fundamentally...
It emerged from the Guangzhai [Monastery]. For now, we shall follow the traditional terminology; thus, it is said that there are "four ones" at Guangzhai.
In reality, however, the "four ones" elucidated by our present school differ slightly from those of the old tradition.

One must understand that since people receive the teaching and practice it to accord with the principle, the oneness of the principle is itself the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). What is now called the "four ones" is merely a general enumeration of both the subject and the object. Its...
In reality, it is simply that taking the principle known and seen as the "one principle" constitutes the correct essence of practice. As for this correct essence, the preceding text states:

"Taking the wondrous principle of true reality (bhūtatathatā) as the body of the chariot. Because this body is high and vast, adorned with all manner of jewels, it differs from the heterodox emptiness;
thus, it is called the "correct essence. Therefore, it cannot be treated identically to the "great essence of correct practice" mentioned in the preceding text.

Below the section "Furthermore, regarding all objects," the text next presents the fruit and retribution of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). This is based on the passage concerning the "Great Chariot" from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and is divided into two parts.

First, it clarifies the ten modes of correct contemplation regarding all objects, using the Great Chariot as a metaphor. This is further divided into two sections: first, it explicitly clarifies that for all objects—such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth—each is elucidated through the ten modes of contemplation;

furthermore, each mode of contemplation is illustrated by the metaphor of the Great Chariot. These details are extensive, as found in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), and will not be elaborated upon here to avoid prolixity.
Record. This is roughly as cited above regarding the ten vehicles of the great carriage within the contemplation of the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*).

The nine subsequent realms may be understood by analogy; why then need they be cited in full? Therefore, following the introduction below, the next section cites evidence for their arising. Regarding the end of the text:

in the *Zhiguan*, the clear contemplation of the realms of the aggregates is divided into two parts: first, the teaching (*dharma*); second, the parable (the great carriage). The initial teaching consists of six sections.
First, ten dharmas are listed; second, their arising; third, the citation of analogies; fourth, the praise; fifth, the detailed explanation;
and sixth, the summary. This present section is the fourth, the praise; therefore, it is the "end" of the second section on the arising of the text.

It is called the "end" because it is separated from the third section, which contains the analogies. Regarding "arising," the *Zhiguan* says: "Having already personally realized the wondrous realm, one immediately..."
One gives rise to the vow of compassion for others. Next, one performs the practice of fulfilling that vow.

Once the skillful application of vows and practices has universally shattered all obstacles, one discerns with precision the points of penetration and obstruction within this universal shattering, causing the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) to progress. Furthermore, one employs these as aids to open the Way.

Within the stages of the Way, one recognizes both oneself and others, remaining patient amidst internal and external honor or disgrace. By not clinging to the "Dharma-love" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) of the Middle Way, one swiftly enters Bodhi.
The stage of Bodhisattva. Regarding the third illustration: it is like Viśvakarman constructing a magnificent hall, neither too sparse nor too dense (and so forth).
As for the general eulogy, it praises the ten vehicles in their entirety. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states:

"Since these ten dharmas are what is mounted upon in the *Lotus Sūtra*, they are praised using the very words of the *Lotus Sūtra*. If explained in terms of the traces (*ji*), this refers to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū."
Taking the time since the victory over the Buddha as accumulated kalpas, and taking the site of enlightenment (śītinā-vana) as the wondrous awakening.

If one refers to the "Original Gate" (honmon), it indicates that the time when I originally practiced the bodhisattva path constitutes the accumulated kalpas, and the time of my original attainment of Buddhahood constitutes the wondrous awakening.

These two gates—the Original and the Traced—merely represent the eternal awakening to these ten dharmas. As for Śāriputra and the others, at the site of tranquility, [the Buddha] was about to preach to sentient beings...

The capacity [of the audience] was not yet suitable; fearing they might fall into suffering, he further employed skillful means. For over forty years, he matured them through various methods. At the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, he briefly revealed the provisional [teachings].
Their attachments were shaken and doubts arose, so they earnestly requested three times. When five thousand [monks] rose and departed, the branches and leaves were finally removed.
He pointed out the "Fourfold One" and expounded the chapter on the Five Buddhas. This was for those of superior faculties and is called the "Teaching of the Dharma. [For those of] middling...
Those whose faculties have not yet been liberated still hope for parables; those of inferior capacity further await causes and conditions.

The Buddha’s intention is continuously focused upon these ten dharmas; therefore, at the conclusion of each of the ten dharmas, they are all likened to a great vehicle. The meaning relied upon in the present text is precisely this.

Those who are deluded have not yet seen this; they still point to the *Avataṃsaka*. They know only the name of the "perfect and sudden" (*yuantun*) in the *Avataṃsaka*, yet they remain ignorant of that school’s doctrine of "concurrent inclusion" (*jiandai*).
Consequently, they completely lose the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*’s "absolute non-reliance" (*juedai*) and disparage the marvelous teaching’s unique capacity for manifestation.
Examining the two texts that verify the fundamental traces and scrutinizing the teachings of the five periods, the ultimate perfection is unmistakable; why, then, should one harbor doubt?

Therefore, the conclusion states: "It is precisely here. Next, regarding the phrase "this is knowing" and below, it concludes by demonstrating that when practice is perfected, one attains the great fruit.

As for the words "this is knowing," it means "it is known by virtue of this. Although the ritual procedures of the four practices—such as constant sitting and so forth—differ, the *dharmatā* (real nature) upon which they rely is without distinction.

There is a distinction. This is because the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the object of focus that is the dharma of peace and bliss, while the four kinds of samādhi are the practices of focus that constitute the conduct of peace and bliss.
Thus, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "The four practices serve as conditions; the observing mind relies upon these conditions to become harmonized and upright.
Therefore, they are called the sublime practices of the four kinds of samādhi. When these are perfected, one realizes the true mark. Having realized the true mark, the...
Because one attains that which relies upon the name, it is called the "Great Fruit. Thus, the commentary on the title of the "Chapter on Peaceful and Joyful Practice" states:

"Now, 'peace and joy' is none other than Great Nirvāṇa; this is a name established from the perspective of the fruit. 'Practice' refers to the path to Nirvāṇa; this is a name derived from the perspective of the cause.

All coarse causes and coarse fruits, including even the seven preliminary expedients (*saptaprayoga*), are not the practice of peace and joy; only this wondrous cause and wondrous fruit [constitute it]."
This is called "Peaceful Conduct. Regarding the statement that what is obtained based on this practice is termed a "Great Fruit," this refers to the eighth chapter, "The Chapter on Retribution.
Although it was not explicitly explained at the end of summer due to a lack of conditions, it should be understood according to the five summaries: that one indeed attains the great fruit.
The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) says: "That which is called 'retribution' refers to the Land of True Reward (*shibao-tu*). It is named after its retributive fruit.
The Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction must necessarily lie beyond the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder; it is the dwelling place of the Dharma-body from the first stage (*chuzhu*) upward.

It is not even the dwelling of Bodhisattvas who have attained patience (*kṣānti*) while still in their birth-bodies during the first stage, so how could it be the dwelling of those in the stages prior to the first stage who are still in their birth-bodies?"

It is asked: "In what place do those at the seven stages of expedient means reside? From the first stage upward, the Dharma-body is the primary retribution (zhengbao), and the Land of True Reward (shibao-tu) is the secondary retribution (yibao).
Therefore, it is said that they obtain this secondary retribution.

The three instances of "arousing the teaching" do not go beyond causing others to open, realize, and enter [the Dharma]. The "arousing of the teaching" in the Great Chapters is precisely the "tearing of the great net" in the Five Brevities.

The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "To respond with eloquence for the benefit of beings is called 'arousing the teaching'; to cause others to eliminate their doubts is called 'tearing the net.

Since the purpose of arousing the teaching is fundamentally to remove the nets of doubt for others, they are identical. Therefore, the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) speaks of "tearing the net."
The text states: "If one wishes to benefit sentient beings externally by establishing teachings according to their capacities, one preaches in accordance with what each person is able to receive.

This continues until the time of attaining Buddhahood and transforming beings—whether acting as a Dharma King to preach gradual or sudden teachings, or even manifesting as the forms of the ten dharma realms to inspire and awaken them (and so forth).
This is the *Fuxing* commentary on the inconceivable realm of transforming others.

It says: "However, this [teaching] for others differs in meaning from the subsequent initiation of the teaching. The latter refers exclusively to the manifestation of the eight phases of the true reward body (*vipākaphala*) to benefit sentient beings, thereby initiating the provisional and the real, and the opening, the establishing, the abandoning, and so forth (etc.).

Since it is said that 'externally benefiting sentient beings by initiating the provisional and the real, and the opening, the establishing, the abandoning, and so forth,' one should know that this is solely for the purpose of causing sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge."

[The text] says: "If one speaks in terms of stages (*bhūmi*), then the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*) are respectively correlated with opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states: "It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

This does not refer exclusively to the Buddha’s own self-knowledge and self-vision. If one speaks only of the fruit of Buddhahood, one loses sight of sentient beings; if one speaks only of sentient beings, [one loses sight of the goal].
Because there is no Buddha-knowledge or Buddha-vision [in them], they must not be taken up in a partial manner.

Although the practitioners of the three preceding teachings are sentient beings, because they do not yet possess the Buddha-eye or Buddha-wisdom, they are unable to know and see the true reality (*dharmatā*). The four stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) are also sentient beings;

yet, as they have partially attained the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom, the status of being a "sentient being" is established, and the status of "knowing and seeing" is likewise established (and so forth).

The fourth section, "The Aim and Return," does not transcend the secret treasury of the three dharmas. The aim and return of this major chapter is precisely the five summaries returning to the great locus.

Regarding the term "aim and return" (*zhǐguī*): it refers to the destination toward which the meaning of the text proceeds. "Aim" (*zhǐ*) means that one directs oneself toward the three virtues (*triguṇa*). "Return" (*guī*) means leading others to enter together into the three virtues.
Furthermore, entering [the goal] oneself is called "return," while leading others to enter is called "aim. These are referred to as the three tracks (*trivartman*).
These—true nature (*dharmatā*), contemplative observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), and the provision for accomplishment (*niṣpatti*)—are these three nothing other than the single Mahāyāna Dharma.

As the Sūtra says: "If one seeks with utmost sincerity throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. This Single Buddha Vehicle is that which possesses the three tracks (*triyāna*).

These three are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*) and inconceivable; this is termed "wondrous" (*miao*). The wondrous is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the wondrous. Therefore, it is said:

It is the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma). The term "guideline" (kai) signifies a model or standard; it refers precisely to these three dharmas that serve as a model. This is the dharma in which the sublime stage resides.
Therefore, the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "You should know that this Sublime Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, the "Supernatural Powers" chapter states: "The treasury of all the Tathāgata’s secret essentials. Thus, one knows that the Sublime Dharma is indeed [this].

It is the treasury of the secret essentials. The *Shiqian* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) states: "Because it fully contains the three thousand [realms] and universally encompasses the three virtues, it is called a 'treasury' (*garbha*).
Prior to this stage, those who are not yet fit vessels are not granted these essentials. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Lamentation," asks:
"What is meant by the 'secret treasury'? It is like the three dots of the letter *i*; if they are aligned horizontally, they do not form an *i*, nor do they form one if they are placed vertically."
Just as the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara must come together to form the letter *i*, yet if the three dots were separate they would not form the *i*;
so it is with me. The dharma of liberation is not *nirvāṇa*; the body of the Tathāgata is not *nirvāṇa*;
the Mahāprajñā is not *nirvāṇa*. If these three dharmas were distinct from one another, they would not be *nirvāṇa*. I am now at peace...
Abiding in these three dharmas, one enters nirvana for the sake of sentient beings; it is like the letter *i* of the world. Zhiyi’s commentary explains:

"If we refer to the former teachings, it is called 'secret' (*mi*) because they are hidden, and 'treasury' (*zang*) because they are covered—meaning that impermanence and so forth cover permanence and so forth, causing permanence and so forth to remain hidden;
thus it is called the 'Secret Treasury. Now, this sutra opens and reveals them, like the moon situated in the sky, pure and manifest."

It is not as it was taught in the past. Rather, because the sublime Dharma is subtle, inconceivable, transcending names and free from marks, and because sentient beings do not understand it, it is called "secret" (*guhyaka*).
Because the *dharmadhātu* encompasses and contains all phenomena and its function is inexhaustible, it is called a "treasury" (*kośa*).
Now, the text of the *Guhyakośa* is explained in three parts: first, an analogy for the three dots; second, an analogy for the three eyes; third...
