What kind of good and evil do the icchantikas and the Tathāgata sever? Answer: The icchantika severs cultivated good, yet innate goodness remains;
the Tathāgata severs cultivated evil, yet innate evil remains. Question: Why are the innate virtues of good and evil not severed? Answer:
Because the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are merely the gateways of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, they cannot be severed; no one in all the worlds is able to destroy them.

For example, when Māra burns a sutra scroll, how could he cause the gateway of the nature-dharma to be exhausted? Even if he were to burn a record of evil, he could not cause the gateway of unwholesome phenomena to be exhausted. Question:
Since those with the icchantika-nature do not sever their innate goodness, they will eventually give rise to wholesome states once again. As for the Tathāgata...
Because inherent evil is not severed, one should eventually give rise to evil again. Answer:
Because icchantikas do not realize inherent evil, they later give rise to adventitious evil; because they do not understand inherent good, they are later defiled by adventitious good.

Therefore, by cultivating the good, the arising [of evil] is again prevented; one uses the cultivation of the good to remedy the cultivation of the evil, thereby ensuring that the cultivation of the evil cannot arise.
Although the Buddha does not sever inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*), he is able to fully comprehend inherent evil and attains mastery over unwholesome dharmas.
He is not defiled by the cultivation of evil, and for this reason, the cultivation of evil cannot arise. Thus, the Buddha is forever free from it.
Regarding the cultivation of evil, one exercises mastery over the dharma-gate of evil. If an icchantika can penetrate the cultivation of evil, they are no different from the Tathāgata.
Thus, we know that regarding both good and evil, one must thoroughly understand the nature of cultivation;

by illuminating the nature through cultivation and understanding cultivation through the nature, only those who can do so may be discussed in terms of the three causes of inherent virtue, saṃsāra, nirvāṇa, and afflictions.
Bodhi. The twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the three virtues. In this way, there is no principle among the infinite [teachings] that is not penetrated.

That text further asks: "If those with icchantika-nature have severed their roots of goodness and are entirely possessed by māra, such that all seeds are perfumed by internal and external factors, can they still give rise to goodness?
Furthermore, since this consciousness is indeterminate (avyākṛta), how does it differ from the True Suchness (tathatā)? Moreover, regarding these seeds..."
If you ask where the Son resides so that he is not perfumed [by afflictions] early on, one knows from this that provisional teachings are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

If someone were to say that the Buddha manifests supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to appear as evil in order to transform sentient beings, this would be a "volitional" power (*manasikāra-ṛddhi*), identical to the powers of those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*);
it would not be like a bright mirror that spontaneously reflects images. If the Great Sūtra says, "There is a buddha-nature even in icchantikas," [it is for the sake of leading them].
There is a Buddha-nature possessed by those with roots of goodness but not by others; the ancient masters called this the nature of the "evil realm.
There is a Buddha-nature possessed by those with roots of goodness but not by icchantikas; the ancient masters called this the nature of the "conditioning cause" (pratyaya-hetu).

There is a Buddha-nature possessed by both types of persons; the ancient masters called this the nature of the "direct cause" (hetu-hetu). There is a Buddha-nature that neither type of person possesses; the ancient masters called this—

It is also for the sake of being a cause. An interpretation such as this is the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*); it is not the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).

As for the definitive teaching, it is fully cited [in the section] previously clarifying the establishment of the Buddha-vehicle within insentient things (as explained in the section on the meaning of the Buddha-vehicle established in insentient objects).

Fourth, [the practitioner] merely knows that the evil inherent in nature universally manifests as the marks of the *sambhogakāya*, yet they do not understand that the principle-body of the fundamental emptiness—the basis upon which the nature possessing evil universally manifests—is utterly extinguished and vanishes.
Quiescence. This leads to what is discussed: that the "three thousand in a single thought" (yīniàn sāqiān) is identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

and that the three bodies, the four lands, principle and phenomena, and essence and function are all characterized by marks (*sanimitta*). I request that you examine carefully the Dharma-words of the various patriarchs before you can verify the errors of Siming. Question: The *Wenju ji* states:
"If one has not yet even heard the name of 'inherently evil nature' (*xing'e*), how can one believe in the existence of 'virtuous conduct of the inherent nature' (*xingde zhi xing*)? People...

There are many differing interpretations; what is the intended meaning here? Answer: If one understands that this present text does not sever inherent evil, then one will know that the practice of inherent virtue arises from hearing the name of inherent evil.
Why is this so? Although the medicinal herbs of skillful means and the parables are distinguished, there is no difference in their underlying principle of being provisional (*upāya*).
In the *Commentary*, in order to resolve the discrepancy between difference and non-difference, it clarifies the practice of inherent virtue.
One must hear the name of "inherently evil nature. Is this not the meaning of the provisional, wherein non-differentiation is itself differentiation? Furthermore, the preceding sentence says:
"In the face of this ultimate consummation, how could one fail to perceive the reality? Is this not the meaning of the real, wherein differentiation is itself non-differentiation?

Therefore, this is also a provisional manifestation of the practice of inherent virtue. This is because those who hear that nature is evil [do so] since, in various sutras, even those prior to the stages of the *bhūmis* still contravene principle and have not yet opened up the provisional.
In the present sutra, however, a mere snap of the fingers is shown to be nothing other than a cause for Buddhahood in order to reveal the ultimate reality.
Who would know that in the *Lotus Sutra*, the Buddha even designates evil conduct as "skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*)? Thus, King Āmrapālī, though possessed of false views—

Furthermore, as for those such as the rebellious Devadatta, who conceal their evil internally while manifesting it externally—there is none who is not likewise [an expression of] provisional skillful means arising from the fact that the nature inherently possesses unceasing evil.

Therefore, there exist these practices of the nature’s virtues. Thus, the nature’s virtues (*xingde*), the inherent possession of principle (*ligu*), and the evil of nature (*xing'e*) are essentially one and the same, differing only in name.
This is explained in detail in the "Substance and Virtues" section of the *Jinbi*.
It is said: however, one must understand the principle that within the emptiness of the true mark (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) there is no differentiation.

In reality, it inherently possesses the wondrous provisional (*prajñapti*) phenomena of the three thousand worlds (*tri-sahasra-loka*) with all their distinctions. Yet, because in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*) there is no inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of the nine realms (*navadhātu*) being originally present, both self and others are severed [from them].
Therefore, it is now clarified that in the nature of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun*), the nature inherently possesses the nine realms, and this nature is not severed.
Evil possesses the nature of virtuous conduct. To ensure that one's own practice is uninterrupted is the inherent principle;
to ensure that the transformation of others is uninterrupted is universal manifestation. Furthermore, these names are both provisional and real.

If it were not so, then one would merely be engaging in idle speculation, empty discourse, and superficial practice, vainly listing the name of the One Vehicle while ultimately lacking the essence of the One Vehicle. Since the teachers of the past have already... [text ends]
Having understood this, one employs the three contemplations and ten stages as the remedial medicine to eliminate the practices of inherent virtue;
the three obstructions and four demons are designated as the diseases to be eliminated by means of inherent evil.

It is for this reason that the "destruction of delusions of identical substance" is taught, which is also the meaning of severing inherent evil. To claim otherwise is merely to confuse virtues with faults and to misinterpret the teachings based on hearsay.

By what means can one understand the intent behind the teaching that the medicinal herbs of skillful means are without distinction, yet their differences are precisely what allow for transformation, and that this is a provisional (upāya) meaning?
The *Wenju* and the *Ji* clarify that delusions of the same substance must ultimately be forever destroyed so that ultimate purity is attained.

Just as a lamp produces light while extinguishing darkness—though there is no temporal sequence between them—darkness is definitively an obstruction. Since it is definitively an obstruction, it must also be definitively severed. How could it be appropriate to treat it as identical to that which is not severed?

The "intrinsic evil" (*xing-è*) of the wondrous provisional is also a skillful means (*upāya*). Therefore, one must not allow oneself to be deluded by [superficial] reasoning and thereby confuse it with intrinsic evil.

The clarification of the arousal of the bodhicitta is divided into two parts. First, the heading; second, the explanation, which consists of four sections. First, clarifying the objective realm upon which the mind relies. The mind does not arise in isolation;

it must necessarily arise in reliance upon an objective realm. Therefore, it is said: "First, contemplate the objective realm upon which one relies," such as the ten kinds of arousing the bodhicitta, and so forth.

This refers to the passage in the first fascicle, within the explanation of the five summaries, concerning the first [summary]: the generation of the great mind (*mahācitta*). Regarding the "ten kinds," they are: first, inferring through reasoning;
second, beholding the marks of a Buddha; third, witnessing supernatural powers; fourth, hearing the Dharma; fifth, traveling through lands;

sixth, seeing the assembly; seventh, seeing practice; eighth, seeing the extinction of the Dharma; ninth, seeing faults; and tenth, seeing the suffering of others. Each of these has four interpretations.
Regarding their differences: that is, each of the ten types of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*) gives rise to different understandings of the four teachings.

Because if one generates the mind while being biased or deviant, the myriad practices will be applied in vain; therefore, it is necessary to determine them through the fourfold understanding so that the Great and Small Vehicles are distinguished and the partial and the perfect do not become confused.
Thus, the *Fuxing* (Subsidiary Record) says: "Relying on objects to generate the mind, one generates it as one investigates; if one discusses its cultivation..."
The initial gateways of practice differ; thus, Zhan’an said: “Śrāvakas take the Truth of Suffering as primary; Pratyekabuddhas take the Truth of Origination as primary;
Bodhisattvas take the Truth of the Path as primary. This is explained according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

In the Shared Teaching, Bodhisattvas take the Cessation-Truth within the realm of desire as primary. In the Distinct Teaching, Bodhisattvas take the Path-Truth outside the realm of desire as primary. [In the Perfect Teaching...]
The teaching for Bodhisattvas takes the *nirodha-satya* (truth of cessation) outside the realms as its primary focus. Regarding the phrase "up to the point where the divisions and stages differ":

the four different interpretations explained above constitute the "divisions" (*dang-fen*). The first three involve generating the mind [of awakening] with the intention directed toward the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) single reality;

this constitutes "crossing the stages" (*kua-jie*). Therefore, the preceding passage concerning the analogy of the teachings of the Middle Way states: "Although following the teachings may be such that..."
Whether four or eight, the original intent was solely to reveal the One Buddha Vehicle. Furthermore, the precedent regarding the classification of sections previously transmitted states:
although there are four teachings and eight teachings in the subsequent text, both the relative and the absolute are intended to reveal the single reality of the Perfect and Sudden.

This is precisely that meaning. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) says: "Within its own section, it constitutes the aspect of the relative meaning of this sutra; transcending the sections, it constitutes [the absolute]."

Now, regarding the aspect of the provisional meaning (*upāya*) opened up in this sutra, it is further stated that these two meanings are no different from the two subtleties of the "provisional" and the "ultimate.

If one relies on the bestowal of the provisional, this refers to the meaning of "within their respective divisions" (for when the provisional has been bestowed, the provisional and the real are contrasted; thus, there are differences within the four teachings).

If one follows the Buddha’s intention, this refers to the meaning of "transcending the stages" (transcending the sequential order and not speaking of the distinctions between the four teachings, but clarifying only the single reality of the perfect and sudden). This "within their respective divisions" applies throughout the entire lifetime of the Buddha's teaching, and in the present context...

They are established in mutual dependence. This transcendence of the stages is found only in the present sutra. The Buddha’s intention was not merely for the present; (although the provisional means are employed, the fundamental intent lies in the Real;

since the Real is precisely what this present sutra reveals by opening up the coarse to manifest the subtle, the intent at the time of employing the provisional means already resides in this present sutra. Therefore, the Buddha’s intention was not limited to the present alone). Question:
Since this is now the second "arousing of the mind" among the ten vehicles, how can it be identified with the first "arousing of the mind" consisting of ten aspects within the fivefold summary?

[Question: They are not the same. [Answer: The previous [section] relied on the primary method of detailed commentary, while the examples investigated here concern the characteristics of the text (*vyañjana*).

Within the fifth example regarding "extensive" and "concise," or "existence" and "non-existence," it says: "For instance, in the section on generating the mind (*cittotpāda*), the enumeration of numbers is extensive while the textual characteristics are concise;

whereas in the subsequent ten dharmas, the textual characteristics are extensive while the enumeration of numbers is concise. It continues: "Although there is mutual omission, the meaning is complete within the mind; we now follow the comprehensive [perspective]."

Because it is explained as being complete, one may point back to the ten types [of practices] mentioned previously. Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states: "Moreover, these four great vows mutually support one another;
they are fully present in a single thought-moment without before or after, as detailed in the first section and the various passages below.

Therefore, here the first [vow] points back to the ten types, while the second points to the general and specific practices and vows mentioned below. Next, the complete fulfillment of the four great vows is clarified.

The statement that "every thought-moment is fully endowed with the Four Great Vows" reveals that, in each *kṣaṇa*, there is a continuous succession without interruption, never being separated from the Four Great Vows.

Therefore, the subsequent line says, "pervading many thoughts. As for how the general [principle] crowns the specific, such that each individual practice and vow is established from this, the eighth fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Zhiguan*), in the section on "Knowing the Successive Stages," states: "Because the two vehicles have exhausted [birth], they do not..."
One must make vows. When a Bodhisattva transforms sentient beings through successive births, they require both general and specific vows. The Four Great Vows (Sic-Vows) are the general vows.
Regarding the *Dharmakṣetra* and the *Avataṃsaka*, each virtuous practice and *dhāraṇī* has its own specific vow. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice of the Way) states:

"Because all vows are fully subsumed within the Four Great Vows, they are called 'general. As for the *Dharmakṣetra*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and so forth—these refer to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* and the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."
It further states: "Amitābha’s causal name was Dharmākara; he formulated forty-eight vows.

The fourteenth fascicle of the *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies the individual vows made during his successive practices. Thus, we know that whenever any bodhisattva encounters the various Buddhas, they invariably formulate both general and specific vows.
Now, the second stage within the Ten Vehicles—the arousal of the mind—already clarifies the generality of the Four Great Vows.
Therefore, it is necessary to use the general to head the specific. Thus, it is permissible in terms of meaning to point to what follows to understand the text concerning the successive stages.
Regarding "the four truths of non-action are but a single thought-moment," the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "The two truths of suffering and accumulation are both termed 'suffering.

In terms of their encompassing meaning, the ten realms are contained within a single thought-moment; hence it is said that 'one suffering is all sufferings. This does not clarify the wondrous object (*viṣaya*).
Regarding "the three thousand in a single thought-moment": how can one understand that the one encompasses all? The three thousand do not transcend the single thought-moment of ignorance;
therefore, there is only the cause of suffering and the fruit of suffering. Because one knows that ignorance is nothing other than the *dharmatā*, compassion arises.
The two truths of the Path and Cessation are both termed "bliss" (*sukha*). This encompasses the four teachings within a single thought-moment; thus it is said, "one bliss is all bliss.
If one does not speak of the wondrous realm of the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment, how can one understand that "one encompasses all"?

The three thousand realms do not transcend the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of a single thought-moment. Therefore, there is only the cause of bliss and the fruit of bliss, because one knows that the dharma-nature is nothing other than this.
Because this is ignorance, one gives rise to compassion. That which takes this as its object is the sublime object.

Therefore, in the Preface to *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it is explained regarding the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*): "The aggregates and sense bases are all suchness; there is no suffering to be abandoned. Ignorance and afflictions are themselves bodhi;
there is no origin to be severed. Extremes and deviance are all the Middle Way; there is no path to be cultivated. Birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa."
...Parinirvāṇa. There is no cessation to be realized. Because there is neither suffering nor its origin, there is no mundane world.

Because there is neither the Path nor cessation, there is no supramundane world. It is the single, uniform reality (*dharmatā*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (or *Catuḥsmṛty-upadeśa*) as saying:

"The single thought-moment possessing the suffering of the ten realms is called the Truth of Suffering (the three lands and two deaths). Possessing the delusions of the ten realms is called the Truth of Origination (the five abodes and three delusions). Suffering itself is Nirvana."

This is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Delusion itself is Bodhi; this is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). The *Miaoxuan* states: Because there is no agent, delusion is subtle within the midst of confusion, and thus it receives its name from the Principle (*li*).

Because one is deluded regarding the Principle, Bodhi is named after afflictions as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), and Nirvana is named after birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Because one is able to resolve [delusion], afflictions themselves are Bodhi, which is named the Truth of the Path. Birth-and-death...

That which is called *nirvāṇa* is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). It is the very reality of things as they are (*tathatā*), free from thought and recollection, and devoid of any agent—by "who" is meant "I," thus it is the absence of self (*anātman*)—and because it is not produced by volitional activity, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

for the sake of skillful means in accordance with sentient beings, it is taught that there are two truths. Those who have transcended the world know it to be the ultimate truth. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) says:

The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is precisely suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is precisely the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).

Because one wishes to cause sentient beings to perceive the path and cessation within suffering and its origin, it is said that they are "identical" (*yuan-ji*). In reality, however, there is no such mutual identity between these two dharmas.

Therefore, the summary concludes that the Four Noble Truths within the [Lotus] Sūtra are but a single reality (*eka-tattva*). This single reality is nothing other than the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) or four virtues (*catur-guṇa*). Thus, although there are four [truths], [they are ultimately one].
Name. [In reality] there are not four; since even one does not exist, how could there be four? The *Fahua wenju* states:
"All liberation is the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) Truth of Cessation; the Unsurpassed Way is the unconditioned Truth of the Path.

By means of these three truths, one destroys the unconditioned [conceptions of] the Truths of Suffering and Accumulation" (Regarding this, scholars of the Four Ming [Zhejiang] tradition all claim that the unconditioned aspects of Suffering and Accumulation are not destroyed; this is clearly in violation of the Patriarchs' teachings). Formerly, I wished to explain this, but sentient beings—

It is unbearable. Since the obstacles have already been removed, he speaks of this again. However, the name "unconditioned" (*avijñapti*) is established according to principle, whereas the term "Four Truths" (*catvāri satyāni*) is discussed in terms of phenomena.
Thus, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The four are formed through the causes and conditions of delusion and awakening."
Is it not that, from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), the Path and Cessation are identical to Suffering and Origination, and Suffering and Origination are identical to the Path and Cessation?

Thus, the four truths would no longer be four. Is it not that, from the perspective of principle (*li*), the *Śuqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fmen*) says: "Delusion and awakening reside in the person; their essence is eternally mutually identical. This mutual identity is the principle; delusion and awakening are the phenomena.

Furthermore, the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) are both principle and phenomenon. As for "phenomena being identical [to principle]," the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*) says: "It is called 'non-..."

The Four Noble Truths constitute the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). Furthermore, from the perspective of principle (*li*), these correspond to the Land of Tranquil Light (*jigguang*) within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* through the lens of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "On the side of retribution, one must speak of suffering and its origin;

because suffering and its origin exist, the Four Noble Truths must be complete. Within the land of retribution, the Land of Tranquil Light is discussed separately; since it must be explained from the standpoint of principle, it is solely the One True [Dharma-realm]."

The meaning is also that one should preach the Dharma within the *śāntaprabhāsvara* (the realm of tranquil light). [The *Sūtra Commentary* states: "To preach the single Truth of Reality (*ekasatyam*) is precisely the *nitya-śāntaprabhāsvara*"].

The *Fuxing* asks: "Since the *śāntaprabhāsvara* is the ultimate, why is it necessary to employ the teachings? Both the horizontal and vertical pairings employ the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). (This is because, within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the employment of the teachings in relation to the lands has both horizontal and vertical aspects.)

Therefore, in both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, the *sukhāvatī* (寂光) is paired with the *anabhisaṃskṛta* (無作). Answer: The teaching is intended for those of middling and inferior capacities, not for those who have reached the ultimate.

From the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward is termed the "lower *sukhāvatī*"; *samantabhadra* (等覺) is termed the "middling"; and *tathāgata* (妙覺) is termed the "upper. This is from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*.

Thus, when the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* explains the *nitya-sukhāvatī* (常寂光) in terms of the fruit and retribution, it is discussing the *sukhāvatī* in its divided sense. Within this divided discussion, there is furthermore... [text fragment].

The fourfold [Noble] Truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) belong to the land of retributive fruition (*vipākabhūmi*), whereas the Single Truth of Reality (*ekasatyatattva*) is the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhā-bhūmi*).

Thus, one should know that these are explained from the perspective of phenomenal retribution. It is necessarily by means of the Path and Cessation that Suffering and Origination are destroyed; how could one exclusively cling to the idea that suffering and origination are inherently complete (*prakṛti-pariniṣpanna*) and thereby claim that the non-action of suffering and origination is not destroyed?
Furthermore, the *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary) states: "If one contemplates only the inherent completeness of principle (*lī*), both [the defilements and the phenomena] are simultaneously destroyed."
Established together, both are the Dharma-realm. Thus, within the body of birth and death across the hundred realms, one realizes the principle of eternal abiding.

If the stinginess of the mind is broken, this constitutes the universal relinquishment of the single thought-moment of the ten realms and the hundred realms of the environment and its inhabitants (etc.).

Third, taking the wondrous realm of the subject and object of the single mind as the object of one's great vows, one takes it as the object of contemplation. Because the pain of self and others is shared by all, for this reason—
These are termed "subject and object," "self and other. The Four Great Vows do not transcend seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.

Within one's own single mind, both subject and object are fully present. Since this is so, it is likewise for the single mind of another in its seeking of enlightenment above and transformation of beings below.

This is why it is said that the principle of the Buddha-mind arising from a single thought of another is equal [to one's own]. To say the principle is equal means that this principle is no different from my own.
Therefore, when it says "thus the Bodhisattva relies on this to give rise to the vow," it is a summary indication. "This" (*si*) means "this very thing.

This refers to the Buddha produced by oneself and others, as well as the objective and subjective aspects. Regarding the fourfold clarification of universal establishment and universal refutation, the *First Part of Śamatha-vipaśyanā* quotes the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, which states:
"To destroy all [conventional] productions is called the production of the bodhicitta; one constantly produces [the mind] in accordance with the characteristics of bodhi."
The bodhicitta. Furthermore, it is to set forth without setting forth, and to follow without following. Moreover, it transcends all refutations and transcends all followings;
to simultaneously illuminate both refutation and following is called "setting forth the bodhicitta. These three aspects are neither identical nor different.

Because they accord with principle and accord with phenomena, yet do not accord with non-principle and do not accord with non-phenomena, they are called "suchness. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) says: The Sūtra records that the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
The characteristic of bodhi transcends the triple world. It transcends all names; the path of speech is cut off.

It transcends all arousal [of thought], for it extinguishes all arousal. This is called the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta. Therefore, the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of all arousal is the arousal of the bodhicitta.
He dwells in unobstructed arousal, an arousal like the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Non-arousal is arousal; he does not cling to anything.
It does not destroy the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); it does not shift, increase, differ, or unify. It is like a reflection in a mirror. Under each and every phrase, it is said:
"This is the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta. This "dwelling" is that which is relied upon. The first phrase establishes [the state] by means of destruction.

From the perspective of the dharma-nature (dharmatā), one engages in refutation and establishment by means of neither refuting nor establishing; thus, all such instances are termed "arousing the mind based on the object.

Therefore, it is said that arousing the bodhicitta and abiding in establishment is precisely to accord with the dharma-nature, which is both the simultaneous negation of both and the simultaneous illumination of both.

The present text merely attaches itself to the meaning of that sutra; because it combines the literal text with an explanation of its significance, there are slight differences. For example, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"That which is called bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be attained by means of the mind. After first extensively refuting [all positions], it subsequently establishes [its own view], saying: "Quiescence is bodhi," and so forth.
Furthermore, following [the conventional] is the provisional (*prajñapti*), while refuting [extremes] is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Both negations and both affirmations are [ultimately] non-dual.
Illumination is itself the Middle Way; this refers to the arousal of the mind based on the unconditional great compassion (*anālambana-mahāmaitrī*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, regarding the refutation of [extremes] such as following emptiness or the provisional through the lens of phenomena and principle, these points should all be understood accordingly.

Thus, one knows that the "perfect arousal" mentioned in the present text still requires the universal refutation and universal establishment of all things; this is precisely the arousal of the mind based on the unconditional [compassion] of the Dharma-realm.

The three knowledges (vidyā) settle the mind into two categories. First is the heading; second is the explanation, which consists of four parts. First, it clarifies that there are many iterations of the modes of practice (*ākāra*). Regarding the "sixty-four":

within the two practices of faith (*śraddhā*) and Dharma (*dharma*), there are eight iterations each, totaling sixteen. These eight iterations exist because both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* each possess the four *siddhāntas*.
Furthermore, the practice of faith transforms into the practice of Dharma, and the practice of Dharma transforms into the practice of faith.
Each of these also has eight variations, making sixteen in total; together with the preceding ones, there are thirty-two variations.

Since it is thus for transforming others, it is likewise for one’s own practice; therefore, there are sixty-four variations. Furthermore, these constitute the sixty-four variations of those whose faculties are exclusively of the "root-nature" (mūla-gotra);

additionally, there are another sixty-four variations of those whose faculties consist of the "mutual support" of faith and dharma (śraddhā-dharmanusārin). Thus, they form [one hundred and twenty-eight].

One hundred and twenty-eight variations. Furthermore, if one explains it in terms of three successive stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (these three stages refer to the sequential three contemplations;

that is, by means of the sequential, the non-sequential is revealed), there are three hundred and eighty-four variations. Additionally, there are sixty-four variations for the single-mind (*ekacitta*) *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which together total five hundred and twelve variations.
For this reason, one does not establish such a multitude of variations to accommodate the various capacities of sentient beings. This is the Dharma.

The gate is thus incomplete. Next, we clarify the relationship between the subject and object, both collectively and individually. Samādhi and prajñā, or śamatha and vipaśyanā, are termed the "subject" (the means).
The realm of the unconditioned truth (*anabhisaṃskṛta-dharma*) is termed the "object. Only when the subject and object correspond can one achieve "settling the mind" (*anxin*).

Therefore, within settling the mind, there is both the collective and the individual. Collectively, one uses stillness-illumination (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) as the means of settling, and the wondrous realm of *dharmatā* as the object.

"An" (Peace/Rest). Taken separately, it opens into various distinctions such as the *dharmas* and so forth. One should know that the "total" (*zong*) is the totality of these separate categories, while the "separate" (*bie*) is the particularity within the totality.

Therefore, it is called "departing from the total to produce the separate. Each separate category possesses its own totality; though they differ, they are the same, and though they are the same, they differ.
Thus, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) says: "Therefore, one knows that herein [the 'total'] is separate yet not separate. The following text is the separate [category]."

Within the Middle Way, there is no distinction yet there is distinction; both the general and the specific rely upon the wondrous object. Because they accord with people, the general and the specific differ.

Since delusions are heavy while contemplation is subtle, one must necessarily follow the particular circumstances. Thus, the modes of practice—whether through faith or through the Dharma—revolve according to the four *siddhāntas*.
When people do not perceive this, they settle upon the specific and give rise to divergent views, thereby losing the Great Master’s principle of adapting to what is appropriate.
It is possible. The mutual identity of the three insights (*trividyā*) and the quiescent marks (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*) can be seen from the text itself.

Therefore, in the *Preface to the Mohe Zhiguan*, it is stated that the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is such that "the beginning and the end are non-dual, like a practitioner flying through the air. The *Fuxing* commentary explains: "The space near the ground and the space at ten thousand fathoms share the same substance;

hence they are called non-dual. Here, "practitioner" (*xingren*) is a metaphor for the person on the path; "flying" (*teng*) is a metaphor for practicing the contemplation of principle; and "space" is a metaphor for the sudden [attainment].
The principle is non-dual. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two, etc. This is the teaching that the beginning and the end are non-dual.
Regarding the fourth point, Master Fansi’s *Zhiguan* says: "Having already explained the sharpness or dullness of the practitioner's faculties, how does one settle the mind?
The teacher should ask: 'Regarding concentration and wisdom, what do you aspire to? Therefore, it is said..."
One must question them regarding their capacity; it is not clear what their spiritual disposition (indriya) may be.

There are those for whom faith and the characteristics of the Dharma mutually support one another, turning toward the signs of the four *siddhārtha* methods of settling the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. However, if one employs a single method universally to accommodate all capacities without providing benefit to others, it is said that "though the same stage is established, the locus of benefit is not yet seen.
Thus, the *Mohe Zhiguan* says: "It is like nurturing life: whether by drinking or eating, one must suit [the individual]."
To sustain one's life, one relies on food; likewise, to nourish the Dharma-body, one does so through cessation (*śamatha*) as the drink and insight (*vipaśyanā*) as the food.
The medicinal methods are also twofold—either pills or powders—to eliminate cold and heat and treat the disease of ignorance. Here, cessation is the pill and insight is the powder.
It is like the principle of yin and yang: yang consists of wind and sun; yin consists of clouds and rain. Excessive rain causes rotting; excessive sun causes scorching.
Yin is like meditative concentration (*samādhi*); yang is like wisdom (*prajñā*). Those who are biased toward either wisdom or concentration do not perceive the Buddha-nature. It continues:

"If one were to interpret [the teachings] in a single-minded way, why would the Buddha have taught in such various ways? Heaven does not remain perpetually clear, and a physician does not prescribe only dispersing medicines. Food...
"One does not eat constantly. This is true even in the mundane world; how much more so in that which transcends the world?

As for the claim that "even those who dabble in various strange and divergent practices," these are merely words used to disparage others. Regarding why those of the same school have diverged into different branches, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states in its explanation of the Constant Sitting Samādhi:
"Therefore, Master Xìn originally used this sūtra" (this sūtra refers to both the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*).

He took this as the essential core of the mind. However, because people inherited and applied it with differing perspectives and attachments, the Chan school became divided between the regions south of the Yangtze and the capital region north of the Yellow River.

This was much like how Master Xianshou (Fazang) established his lineage and categorized the teachings, yet when it came to the characteristics of practicing Chan meditation, he pointed entirely to the *Tiantai Zhiguan* for clarification.
Furthermore, while Qingliang (Zongmi) followed Xianshou as his doctrinal authority, he employed the practical methods of Tiantai. Up to this point...
Furthermore, Guifeng himself claimed that he had encountered the Southern School of Chan and met with the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) teachings;

yet, he simultaneously disparaged the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (stopping and seeing) taught by the Tiantai school. How tragic it is that master and disciple were thus so contradictory and diametrically opposed! Regarding this term "contradiction," the *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) states:
In the state of Chu, there was a man who sold both spears (*máo*) and shields (*dùn*). A customer came to buy a spear and said to the seller: "This..."
A spear destroys a thousand shields. When someone comes to buy a shield, the seller says to the buyer, "This shield destroys a thousand spears.
While the buyer of the spear is still there, another buyer of a shield arrives. The buyer of the spear says to the seller, "Give me back your spear and let it destroy your shield;
how many shields will you get for that? The seller has no answer, because his own words are self-contradictory. "Spear" (矛) refers to a *ge-mao* (a type of halberd or spear).
The *Shuowen* says: *qiú* (pronounced as in *jíliú*) is a spear. It is mounted on a war chariot and is twenty feet long; it represents its form.
As for *dùn*, it belongs to the category of *yǔ* (pronounced as in *lánggǔ*; the *Shuowen* says it is a large shield). The *Shuowen* says: it is a *fá* (pronounced as in *fúfā*).

It is used to protect the body and shield the eyes; it represents its form. *Zī* means "much. Now, in the *Jiaben* (the character *biàn* is an error; it should be *biàn*), the masters first distinguish [the characters].
Regarding the phrase "ordinary persons and sages alike," the *Zhiguan* states: "Teaching others is of two kinds: first, the sage teacher; second, the ordinary person teacher.

The *Fuxing* commentary explains: "If discussed generally, those in the six faculties and the five grades all belong to the category of ordinary person teachers, as they have not yet broken through ignorance and thus remain bound by all fetters."

If discussed separately, this refers to the five stages of practice (*pañca-varga*). Because the six sense faculties are purified, one is freed from the two fetters (namely, those of *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vāsanā-kleśa*).

Thus, they are "similar sages" (*pratirūpa-ārya*). (Since the *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-pratipatti-sūtra* places these five stages within the ten stages of faith, it is known that Chih-i also designates them as "similar sages," as fully explained in the *Dafu bufa* [Supplementary Dharma Section] of the *Mohe zhiguan*).

According to the analytical discussion in the first fascicle, the six faculties are generally taken to constitute the "ordinary masters. The previous reference to "sages" pertained to the initial stage.

Because they remain [in the world], even the six sense-faculties are still referred to as "illness" by the Teacher; how much more so for a *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattva, who has not yet severed all [afflictions]. Question:
The teaching established by others relies on the "remedial prescriptions for illness," which is a general presentation of the characteristics of both the Dharma and its metaphors.

One should employ the four *siddhāntas* according to what is appropriate and convenient for each case. Since the two practices of faith and Dharma mutually benefit one another, why must one stubbornly cling to them, guarding the stump all day long?
As stated in the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), it criticizes others by saying: "One type of Chan master does not permit contemplation (*guan*), but exclusively employs stillness (*zhi*).
He cites a verse: 'To think and think is but vain thinking; to think and think is but vain suffering. To cease thinking is itself the Way; where there is thinking, one never beholds it.
Furthermore, another Chan master does not permit stillness, but focuses exclusively on contemplation. He cites a verse: 'Stillness...'"
Cessation merely brings cessation; in the darkness, there is no basis for it. Cessation upon cessation is itself the Way; contemplation upon contemplation leads to the realization of principle.
These two masters each entered through a single gate and used their own realization to benefit others, yet students failed to perceive their underlying intent.

It is difficult even to obtain milk gruel by following such a path, let alone the clarified butter (*sarpis*). Regarding the phrase "one who guards the stump," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "In the Song dynasty, there was..."

There was once a plowman who, while working in the fields, saw a rabbit strike a tree stump and die. Thereafter, he abandoned his plowing and remained constantly by that stump, hoping another rabbit would come along.
Although those nearby tried to reason with him, he refused to stop. Thus, it has been passed down in common parlance that one who persists in delusion is called a "stump-watcher."

The fourth section, "Clarifying the Pervasive Penetration," is divided into two parts. First, the heading; second, the explanation, which is further divided into four sections. The first clarifies the intent of the Gate of Non-arising (*anutpāda-mukha*).
Regarding the phrase "Although the non-arising mind pervades horizontally and vertically": the non-arising mind is precisely the Gate of Non-arising. Thus, the *Zhi guan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan) states:
"First, the Gate of Non-arising—from beginning to end, exhausting its very source and bottom—vertically penetrates all phenomena. The *Fu xing* (Sub-commentary) explains: "Exhausting the source..."

Therefore, it is "transversely pervasive" (heng-zhou) because it exhausts the bottom; it is "vertically exhaustive" (shu-qiong) because it probes the meaning within the chapters by addressing the central points. Thus, it is said that it "exhausts its source and bottom.
That is to say, the three delusions each pervading [all phenomena] is called "transverse pervasion," while their universal extension to the ultimate reality (shixiang) is called "vertical profundity.
Furthermore, the horizontal inclusion of all things is called "transverse pervasion," and the fact that each reaches the ultimate limit is called "vertical depth. Moreover...
Regarding the statement that "the six [aspects] in the subsequent stages must vertically exhaust [all realms]":

because the initial non-arising (anutpāda) horizontally and vertically breaks through all-pervasiveness, this stage is located in the first abode (*prathama-bhūmi*) at the stage of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); therefore, it is called the "mind of the patience of non-arising.

Since this is the case for the first abode, the subsequent stages from the second abode up to the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) can be understood accordingly; thus, it is said that one must further require the subsequent stages, additionally including those prior to the [first] abode.

Because there are six stages—namely, the six identities such as "identity with the Buddha-nature" and so forth—it is called "six identities. These six positions, from beginning to end, are termed "vertically exhaustive.
This classification into six positions is made based on the differences in phenomena (*dharma*); however, if one considers them in terms of the identity of principle (*li*), this is not the case.

Therefore, it is said that whether horizontal or vertical, everything is none other than the principle itself. Being the principle itself means being neither horizontal nor vertical; horizontal and vertical are non-dual.
This is stated with reference to the vertical discourse on the single gate of non-arising, which inherently possesses both the horizontal and that which is neither horizontal nor vertical;

therefore, this explanation is given. If one discusses the horizontal gates, it is likewise so. This is why it is called a "horizontal gate": each and every one of them is without exception endowed with the vertical, as well as that which is neither horizontal nor vertical.
Thus, one should know that within the vertical there is fully present the horizontal and the non-dual. The remaining two categories are to be understood by analogy.
The remaining two are the horizontal and the single mind. Thus, the *Zhiguan* says: "Second, traversing all dharma-gates:
from beginning to end within each gate, one exhausts their source and bottom, horizontally breaking through the dharmas universally. Third, the non-duality of the horizontal and vertical:

from beginning to end, exhausting their source and bottom, neither horizontal nor vertical, one breaks through the dharmas universally. Now, I shall first clarify the horizontal and the vertical; the single mind follows below.

This is clarified in the following passage: "Furthermore, a single thought-moment encompasses both gates," and so forth. The *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) further states: "The single gate of non-arising is vertical;
when the immeasurable various gates are viewed in relation to the gate of non-arising, the remaining gates are horizontal.
As for the horizontal gates, as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says: 'Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, neither coming...'"

It does not depart. Next, it clarifies that the principles and so forth of other gates are non-arising. When one gate is considered in relation to the remaining gates, non-arising constitutes its own nature, while the remaining gates are termed "other.
Although self and other differ, their ultimate destination is no different; therefore, they are called the "principles and so forth of other gates.
Third, it clarifies entering other gates by means of the [non-arising] gate. This refers to taking the ten objects and ten vehicles within the gate of non-arising and transforming them.
One transcends and enters the gates of non-extinction, as well as the immeasurable gateways of neither permanence nor annihilation, neither identity nor difference, neither coming nor going.
These gateways all possess ten objects and ten vehicles; therefore, it is said that one "transcends and enters the gates of others.
All dharmas are without distinction. If one employs a single gateway such that all other gateways are integrated within it, this is precisely to follow the application of that single gateway.

This refers to the mutual integration of all gates. Because there is no gate that does not immediately coincide with principle, they can be harmoniously subsumed without any distinction of superiority or inferiority.

Thus, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) says: "Furthermore, the vertical gates now fully embody the meaning of the three truths; by entering the horizontal gates, each and every gate possesses the three truths.

Consequently, within the horizontal gates, there is nothing horizontal that is not vertical, and from the perspective of the vertical toward the horizontal, there is nothing vertical that is not horizontal. From the beginning...
Because all [phenomena] ultimately possess the nature of being transitory. Just as when one is unborn, all are unborn, so it is even unto non-emergence (which is to say, non-departure).

To subsume these horizontal and vertical dimensions, they are all contained within the single mind, as explained in detail below. Since these eight cases are thus, the same principle applies to all other categories.
Therefore, the present text enters into these various categories, just as the first two chapters of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* enter into the six [categories]. This is so.

Therefore, in the present text, all dharmas are first shown to enter into non-arising (*anutpāda*). The remaining seven [perfections] then successively and mutually enter one another, and this principle applies to everything else as well.
For this reason, we first clarify the entry into non-arising; how much more so regarding the explanation of the meaning of *nirvāṇa* and so forth. As stated in the *Zhi guan*:
"The teaching of non-arising vertically encompasses cause and fruit, its significance already manifest; it also horizontally encompasses [all phenomena]."
The meaning shall now be explained. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one hears the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one understands all meanings.

The initial letter *A* encompasses the forty-one letters, and the forty-one letters encompass the initial letter *A*; the same applies to the intermediate letters. This meaning is difficult to perceive;
therefore, I shall further cite the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* to demonstrate its characteristics, then cite the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* to explain its significance, and finally discuss the gate of non-arising.

Regarding the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*pó fǎ biàn*): the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states that when the kalpa-ending fires arise, a Bodhisattva can extinguish them with a single spittle and form a world with a single breath.

This is not a process where destruction occurs first and formation follows later; rather, within that single act of spitting, there is simultaneous extinction and formation. That sūtra clarifies that external function corresponds to internal union:
the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda-mukha*) is both the pervasive destruction and the pervasive establishment. Destruction and establishment do not require two moments of thought. If...
If there is no such virtue within, there will be no great function without. That the external manifests the internal by way of reliance is of such a nature.

Regarding the interpretation of the meaning of *nirvāṇa*: the single phrase "not hearing what is heard" has various meanings. The first says: "the non-arising of arising; the non-arising of non-arising."
"Arising, non-arising, arising of arising"—according to these four phrases, the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is explained.

It encompasses all phenomena, such as the causes and effects of one's own practice and the capacity to transform others, both subject and object, pervading them all (and so forth). Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"From the night I attained the Way until the night of my parinirvāṇa, I have not spoken a single word. The Buddha made this statement based on two factors: namely, the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the primordially abiding dharma (*paurāṇasthiti*).

Dharma. The Dharma itself is the realization of the true nature of the noble truths. The "primordially abiding Dharma" refers to the path of the ancient sages, the eternally abiding realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).
This meaning is identical to the intent of the "four things that cannot be expressed" in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (and so forth).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* contains four types of maturation: namely, the śrāvaka lineage, the pratyekabuddha lineage, the buddha lineage, and the bodhisattva lineage.
Without these four natures, there would be no maturation in the happy realms. The Buddha-nature is the universal capacity; the Bodhisattva-nature is the specific capacity.

The Śrāvaka-nature possesses distinct roots of goodness and refers to the capacity for the Tripiṭaka. The nature that regresses from the Great Vehicle to take up the Small Vehicle refers to the general capacity.
Those four types of maturation correspond precisely to these four kinds of capacities and conditions; therefore, it is said now:
Regarding the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, which accords with the teachings and enters various gates in accordance with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*):
if one is within the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*), all such meanings conform to non-arising; if one enters the various gates, these same meanings are likewise termed non-extinction (*anirodha*).

It is neither permanent nor discontinuous; neither one nor different; neither coming nor going, and so forth. Furthermore, to encompass both gates within a single thought-moment is precisely the third [gate]:
the non-duality of the horizontal and vertical. The single mind of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is neither horizontal nor vertical.

Furthermore, it fully encompasses both the horizontal and the vertical; thus it is said that it "covers both gates. The text of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* has already been cited above. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:

"Within the 'Gate of Non-duality,' the inclusion of all horizontal aspects is called 'horizontal pervasiveness' (*heng-zhou*), and the fact that nothing is not perfectly consummate is called 'vertical depth' (*shu-shen*).
This is precisely that meaning. Regarding the "high, broad, and great chariot moving without shifting," this refers to *śamatha*.
The *Avatamsaka Sūtra* states: "That vehicle is high and broad, and its horizontal and vertical dimensions are non-dual; thus it is neither horizontal nor vertical.
Therefore, it is said that "this Dharma is equal, with no high or low. Because this is the function of the essence, it is said that "it moves without moving," and so forth.

The Fourth Clarification distinguishes [the stages] according to their positions. Within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, after explaining the universal destruction of dharmas by entering from emptiness into the provisional, it says:
"Second, clarifying the benefits of entering the provisional: the Bodhisattva does not originally value emptiness when practicing emptiness;

he practices emptiness solely for the sake of sentient beings. Because he does not value emptiness, he does not abide in it; because he seeks to benefit sentient beings, he must emerge [from it]. Therefore, there is the arising from the true."
One should accord with the Dharma-eye to suit the capacities [of beings]. If they are to be delivered by means of a Buddha-body, one manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma;
this extends even to the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:

"To clarify that the true benefit of emerging into the provisional [world] must reside in the first stage (*bhūmi*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Distinct and Perfect [Teachings], this is the fourth demonstration of the subtle purport of the text" (the six demonstrations of the subtle have already been cited in full previously). Thus, it is known that the clarification of the benefits is precisely [this].
To clarify the meaning of the text: the text speaks of the "True" (zhēn) and then again of the "Dharma-eye" (fǎyǎn).

Therefore, this Dharma-eye is certainly not the stage prior to the [ten] stages (dìqián); rather, it is the inconceivable provisional [reality] that constitutes the Dharma-eye. By this we can verify that this benefit definitely resides in the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

(In the *Zhǐguān*, it further clarifies that during the ten stages of faith, the six sense organs are purified, such that one universally sees and hears the phenomena of the ten dharma-realms. If one had entered emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there would not even be a single thing; since it says the six organs function interchangeably, this refers to the stage of entering the provisional [reality]. This corresponds to what is said in the "Section on Non-duality" regarding the aspect of illumination.)

The ten realms each possess [the three thousand] with absolute clarity; their underlying principle is one and the same. Regarding the recent tradition of the students of Siming, I request that you examine carefully the texts of *Zhi Guan* (Stopping and Contemplation). Cease further erroneous claims that the three thousand exist inherently within emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If you do not believe this, why does the *Zhi Guan* say: "Entering emptiness, there is not a single thing; entering the provisional (*prajñapti*), the six sense faculties function interdependently"? Is it not the case that the Great Master did not understand the wondrous subtlety [of the Perfect Teaching], but merely engaged in analytical distinctions? Based on this, the three thousand worlds are definitively the wondrous provisional.

If not even a single dharma can be established within emptiness, what else remains to cause confusion? Therefore, it is called "pervasion upon entering" (*ru-zhu-ying-bian*); only when it is pervasive upon entering can it be called pervasion of the provisional. — *Fahua Wenju Ermen* (The Two Gates of the Lotus Sutra Commentary)

It says: "The manifestation of partial truth throughout the ten realms is likewise due to this. Furthermore, regarding "the pervasiveness of the true," this refers to the passage on the pervasiveness of the refutation of dharmas within the third [chapter] of the *Zhongguan* (Mādhyamaka).
Therefore, the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) clarifies that there are five intentions for practicing Mādhyamaka. Regarding the fourth intention, it states:
"The four studies as great skillful means" refer to the Tathāgata’s effortless skillful expedients (*upāya-kauśalya*) and his boundless great functioning.
Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they manifest various inconceivable powers of skillful means. It continues until it says:
"In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one destroys a portion of ignorance. This is an abbreviated expression, which may also be termed "immeasurable categories.

At this stage, one is able to perform Buddha-activities throughout the entire Dharma-realm in an immeasurable way, as explained in detail within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Therefore, this is a provisional [designation].

"Universal" (*biàn*) and "true universal" (*zhēn biàn*) differ in wording but are identical in meaning. This is because only by internally realizing the reality of the Middle Way can one externally respond so as to be universal throughout the Dharma-realm.
Such true universality is the manifestation of the universality of the inherent nature (*xingjù*) prior to the first stage (*chūzhù*).

Therefore, it is said thus. The preceding [stages of] contemplative practice (*guānxíng*) and semblance [realization] (*xiāngsì*), in terms of their positions, still pertain to both the conventional and the real. — *Zhǐguān* (Stopping and Contemplation)
It is said: For example, when the six sense organs of a person at the stage of semblance-attainment (*sādharmya-bhūmi*) are purified, they have not yet given rise to true vision of the Middle Way.

Although they contemplate the three truths, this is explained according to their specific stage; they merely destroy the four abidings (*catur-vāsana*) and the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust. Since they have realized the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), these are merely subsumed under the two truths.

However, upon entering the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), one destroys ignorance (*avidyā*) and perceives the Buddha-nature; only then does the simultaneous illumination of the two truths truly constitute [the realization of the Middle Way].

Wisdom (*jñāna*) likewise possesses the three truths, yet they are consolidated into the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). When emotion and wisdom are discussed together, this refers to speech that accords with the intentions of both oneself and others.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "As in the section 'Similarity' and below," it is judged according to stages (*avasthā*).

Therefore, the division of the conventional and ultimate truths is attributed to emotion; these stages reside within the six sense faculties. The Middle Way is yielded to and attributed to wisdom; these stages reside at the beginning.

Regarding the stages of abiding: those prior to the seventh stage of faith are subsumed under the True (the *zhenshi*), as the *Zhi guan* says, "Upon entering emptiness, there is not even a single thing.

Those from the eighth stage of faith onward are subsumed under the Conventional (the *shisu*), as the *Zhi guan* says, "The mutual functioning of the six sense organs is the stage of entry into the provisional. Thus, from the first stage upward, there is also the identity of the true and the conventional;
and within the purity of the six sense organs, there is also a semblance of the Middle Way. Therefore, in the following chapter, Zhanran provides both an affirmation and a negation.
Commentary: This means that the six sense faculties are stripped of their "semblance" Middle Way and granted their "semblance" True and Conventional [Truths].

As for the statement that "one must still sever attachment stage by stage even while abiding in the subsequent [state]," this does not refer to severing attachment to the semblance-dharma; rather, it refers to severing attachment to the dharma within the true stage (*bhūmi*).
Once attachment to the dharma is severed, ignorance is purified and the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) become manifest; only then does one ascend to the [higher] stages.
The stage reaches ultimate perfection. Regarding the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyā*), there are two parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation, which is divided into four sections. The first clarifies the sequential examination at each stage;

this is the passage concerning the penetration and obstruction of the single mind. Within *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* employs the analogy of "there being a single guide who is skillful... [the text continues].

One must know what is permeable and what is obstructed; therefore, one must still understand the opening of the provisional. All phenomena have nothing external to them and exist solely within the single mind. Examine this point by point:
there is no contemplation that performs the examination, nor is there a mind capable of attachment. When subject and object are both stilled, this is called "permeability.
Next, it is clarified that there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm. The *Zhi guan* says: "Truly, because the single mind is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle."
Wherever there are obstructions to touch, all are permeated without hindrance; one can pass through five hundred *yojanas* to reach the place of jewels.

This is called "penetration" (*abhijñā*). Penetration is fundamentally contrasted with obstruction. Since the locus of touch is like empty space, there are no further obstructions. Where there is no obstruction, there is no penetration.

If, within this absence of obstruction and penetration, one gives rise to the afflictions of suffering and its origin, obscured by ignorance, these are all immediately the emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Being endowed with the truths, conditions, and the perfections (pāramitās) is called "simultaneously illuminating both penetration and obstruction" without being either obstructed or unobstructed. The *Fuxing* (Explanatory Notes) says:

"If one does not accord with this single mind regarding its horizontal and vertical aspects of penetration and obstruction, then within this single mind, one will again give rise to obstruction and attachment, thereby producing the suffering, accumulation, ignorance, and obscurations.
One must examine the penetration and obstruction of this single mind; one must know that suffering, accumulation, ignorance, and obscurations are themselves this [single mind]."
The blockages of the mind—there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm—are perfected as the unconditioned truths, the factors of enlightenment, the perfections, and so forth;

this is precisely the penetration of the single mind. The three clarities and six stages serve to distinguish [this process]. Therefore, after explaining the penetration and blockages of the single mind within the *Zhiguan*, it concludes with the judgment:
"This is for the beginner; having passed five hundred *yojanas*, one should clarify the meaning of the six stages. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "This is..."

This serves as a concluding summary for what follows. To explain it in this manner—wherein the five hundred [aspects] of the rational nature (*dharmatā*) of all sentient beings extend even to the ultimate five hundred [aspects] of the Buddhas—is unlike the old interpretations that cause ordinary people to recoil in awe.
Thus, it is established that even the slightest virtue becomes a cause for attaining Buddhahood;
as the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) states: "Within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, nothing is excluded—not even grasses and trees, which share the four subtle elements with the earth."
What is the difference? Every step taken upon the long journey leads toward the Isle of Jewels; every snap of the fingers and every joining of palms serves as a cause for attaining Buddhahood.

Granting one [opportunity] and allowing three [paths] does not contradict the original intention. This meaning is fully explained in the *Yuyan ji* (Record of Parables); students should seek it there.

Regarding the four [elements], Ming-neng states that they become the "object" (*suǒ*). The *Zhìguān* says: "If one is like the non-Buddhists who are attached to the wisdom of contemplating emptiness, one should employ the four..."

The four propositions of "pervasive obstruction" (quàn-sè) are capable of refuting [the opponent] just as they are refuted [by the object]. This causes the multitude to abandon their obstructions and attain penetration. If one does not cling to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, then the refutation will not conform to the refuted;
it will merely break through the obstruction so that penetration remains, like removing the film to nurture a pearl, or destroying bandits to protect a general.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Regarding the attachment that arises in the subject of refutation, this is the same as the non-Buddhists. One should employ the four propositions of pervasive obstruction and penetration to perform a universal refutation."
Therefore, we know that in the previous refutation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), one used only the refuting agent (*bādhaka*) to refute the object of refutation (*bādhyam*).

For those who have not yet awakened to this, their minds will inevitably become obstructed and attached to the categories of agent and object. If they become attached to the agent, then even though their contemplation of phenomena may be correct, their attached mind is as mistaken as any error;

thus, it must be refuted. Therefore, it is said: "One is attached to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness. For this reason, one must use the three provisional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) and the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) to refute the agent.

One should cause the mind that clings to have no place to stand; one destroys the clinging wisdom just as one destroys the delusions to which it clings. Therefore, it is said that "the destroyer is like that which is destroyed.
Although one does not cling to the contemplation that acts as the destroyer, one may still cling to the delusions that are destroyed. Therefore, it is said:
"If one does not love [the destroyer], or if the wisdom contemplating emptiness is such that it can destroy [delusions] as they are destroyed, then one merely employs the destroyer."
It universally destroys delusions. Next, regarding the analogies presented, first, the analogy of removing the film and nurturing the pearl serves merely as a partial metaphor (*fen-yu*).

However, if one destroys the enemy and protects the general, it becomes a universal metaphor (*pian-yu*). (These partial and universal metaphors are two types of analogies among the eight great metaphors of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, as cited in detail in the *Shiqian*).

Why is this? Once the film has been removed and the pearl nurtured, the pearl cannot become covered by film again; therefore, the analogy of destroying the enemy and protecting the general is used once more. If the general were...
The thief breaks this thief; if the thief serves as a general, that general also protects [the thief].

Thus, in turn, all generals become thieves, and one breaks them down limb by limb. Therefore, it is said now: "One must understand that the subject who can break becomes the object that is broken. This refers to the case where the thief acts as the general;
this analogy is clear. This constitutes becoming a *caṇḍāla* among Bodhisattvas; regarding the meditative states of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this is based on the causal stage.
In the *Cenming Shicheng Guancha Fa* (The Tenfold Contemplative Method for Clarifying Dhyāna), it is stated in the section on "Knowing the Successive Stages":

"If a person does not understand the various stages mentioned above, they will erroneously give rise to grasping and attachment, thereby becoming an arrogant one (*adhimāna*)—that is, a *pāṇḍaka* (outcaste) among bodhisattvas. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) explains:

"Regarding the phrase 'If a person' and below, which concludes by denouncing the *pāṇḍaka* among bodhisattvas: *pāṇḍaka* is translated here as 'slayer. [Such a person] arbitrarily conflates themselves with the higher stages."
This kills the life that is eternally abiding. If one speaks of it to others, one harms their wisdom-life. By this reasoning, those who fall into such distress are numerous.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "One must not hear that 'the contemplation of the mind is itself [Buddha]' and immediately become confused and indiscriminate, giving rise to overweening pride and acting as a *caṇḍāla* among Bodhisattvas.
If one does not accept these words, then one lacks faith in the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the various Mahāyāna sūtras."

[This] explanation (the commentary clarifies the six stages of realization in detail in the preceding section, hence these words are used). Since the current text has already clarified "skillfully knowing the open and the obstructed," it likewise employs this same intent to conclude by criticizing those who do not see [the truth].

Those who preach the contemplation themselves fail to perceive the various meanings of the open and the obstructed; they falsely give rise to attachments and erroneously explain the practice of contemplation to teach others.

Regarding the phrase "yet some may exceed [the mark]," "yet" (*ran*) means "indeed" (*shi*). Indeed... (Note: The character *ran* is used here as a particle of affirmation, equivalent to "indeed" or "it is so.")
"Accomplishment" refers to the accomplishment of contemplation. Alternatively, "transgression" refers to the arising of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Whether practicing for oneself or teaching others, both cases harm the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom. Therefore, such individuals become *caṇḍāla* Bodhisattvas.
Sixth, the elucidation of the *mārga-varga* (Chapter on the Path) is divided into two parts. First, the heading; second, the explanation, which is further divided into four sections.

The first clarifies that both the Great and Small Vehicles employ [the path] together. Regarding the terms "hearing" (*śruta*) and "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*): "hearing" refers to hearing the teachings, and "contemplation" refers to the practice of meditative observation. As for the necessity of both the Great and Small Vehicles:

within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, four types of *mārga-varga* are explained: first, the distinct categories (*pratyeka-bhāga*); second, mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*); third, according to stages (*avasthā*); and fourth, sequential generation (*anuloma*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "This..."

The *Situolun* (Treatise on the Fourfold Penetration) encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. To distinguish them specifically: the third [penetration] pertains exclusively to the Hīnayāna, while the remaining three pertain to the Mahāyāna.
Although there are four textual sections, they nonetheless contain only two meanings; this is because the first three serve to establish the fourth.

As for the lecturer who explains them solely by way of the Hīnayāna stages, this is a critique. It merely correlates the stages of the Hīnayāna with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). This, however, is simply...
This refers merely to the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) according to their stages. Therefore, it is rejected by saying:

"If one has already lost even the mutual arising and mutual inclusion of the factors of the path in the Hīnayāna, how much less could one attain the factors of the path in the other three teachings of the Mahāyāna gate? As for "Mahāyāna and so forth," this refers to those who study the contemplations of the Mahāyāna in a superficial or confused manner.
They then claim that the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are practices of the Hīnayāna and not the Dharma of the Mahāyāna; thus, they discard both the Great and the Small Vehicles.
What then shall serve as the standard for their practice? The Tathāgata bequeathed his final instructions, commanding them to follow the foundations of mindfulness in their cultivation of the Path.

Since they do not comply with this, they are left without any standard for their practice. Next, the various categories [of practitioners] are explained in order to harmonize and reconcile these differences.

This refers to the fourth [aspect], the "arising in succession" (*anuloma*) of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and their "harmonious adaptation" (*samāropa*). Thus, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"Just as the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) can give rise to right effort (*samyakpradhāna*), right effort gives rise to the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The bases of power give rise to the five faculties (*indriya*), the five faculties give rise to the five powers (*bala*), the five powers give rise to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the seven factors of enlightenment enter into the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). This is what is meant by "arising in succession" and also by "harmonious adaptation."

This is because various schools speak of it in conjunction with those who practice it. To say "only the foundations of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) is to employ only one among the seven categories [of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment].
Furthermore, what hindrance do the latter six categories and thirty-three items present that they should not be employed?
Regarding the section following the "Chapter on the Three Clarities" (Samvid-pada), which clarifies the three gates of emptiness following the "Chapter on the Perfect Path" (Paripūrṇa-mārga-pada):

within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, after explaining that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ) are accomplished through the single mind and the three contemplations (ekacitta-trivipaśyanā), it states:

"Furthermore, when practicing the thirty-seven factors of the path and approaching the city of the untainted (anāsrava), there are three gates to this city. If one enters these gates, one immediately attains [liberation]."
