Having concluded by citing scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to corroborate the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, he then concludes: "Having cited these proofs in this manner, how could one not believe them?

Thus, this constitutes the citation of various sūtras to increase faith. For example, the citations of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Mādhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* likewise constitute such citations.
Various treatises serve to assist in its completion. Regarding the section "Contemplating the Mind" (*guānxīn*) below, that which was transmitted by Siming is forever distinct from others.
The *Preface to the Mohe Zhiguan* states: "The clarity and stillness of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* were unheard of in previous generations. It further states:

"This *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is the Dharma-gate practiced within my own mind, as taught by Tiantai Zhiyi. Furthermore, within the "Essential Nature and Characteristics of *Śamatha-Vipaśyanā*" (*zhíguǎntǐxiàng*), it says: "Such an interpretation is based upon..."
Contemplating the mind is truly not a matter of reading the scriptures and arranging them in sequence. Rather, it is to avoid the suspicions of others and to increase their faith;
since it fortunately accords with the *Sūtras*, I have cited them as proof. The *Miaoxuan* states: "The *sūtra* (the warp) provides the underlying meaning.

It is like the silk *sūtra* (warp) of the world, which, when woven with the weft, forms patterns of dragons and phoenixes (the 'weft' refers to the horizontal threads; the 'warp' refers to the vertical threads). The Buddha, by means of the world..."
The *siddhānta* explains that for a bodhisattva, because the world is woven together by warp and woof, the patterns of the noble ones (*ārya*) are formed.

Furthermore, regarding warp and woof in terms of practice: wisdom-practice is the warp and conduct-practice is the woof; because warp and woof are joined, the pattern of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is formed.

Moreover, regarding warp and woof in terms of theory: that which elucidates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the warp, and that which elucidates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the woof; because warp and woof...
Through their union, the patterns of the Two Truths are formed. It continues, saying: "The object of contemplation is the warp;
the wisdom of contemplation is the woof. Through observation and turning, they are woven together to form all literary patterns.

Now, this *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) is the Tiantai Master Zhiyi’s method of taking the contemplation of the mind as the warp and all phenomena (referring to all phenomena within the holy teachings of the One Vehicle) as the woof, weaving them into fascicles (the correct term is *zhì*; also written as *zhì* or *zhí*; meaning a volume for books).
[This refers to] a case-binding (also called a book-cloth). It is not of the same category as the practices of other schools; thus, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*) states:

"From antiquity, no one has surpassed him in the gate of contemplation. Since even from antiquity no one could surpass him in the gate of contemplation, for Guifeng to have summarily disparaged him was like a person from the banks of the Bin River attempting to block the Mengjin Ford with a handful of earth.
(Meng is the name of a place north of Luoyang, where all major roads converged; it has served as a ford since ancient times; today it is the Heyang Ford.)
This is so. It is simply that they do not know its measure.

[The following is] the "Twentyfold Examination of the Great Master’s Oral Instructions on the Gate of Chan" (the extant printed edition contains six pages), titled "The Essential Heart-Method for Treating Illness.

The text consists of two parts. The first part, the question, is easily understood. The second part, the answer, consists of two sections. The first clarifies that all [methods] treat illness. At the beginning of that text, it clarifies...
In the *Ānāpāna-shouyi*, the characteristics of illness are clarified only in the subsequent passage; it differs from the present text which claims that all [practices] treat illness.
For now, I shall answer according to that subsequent passage. That text clarifies that there are many kinds of illness: first, illness produced by the body;
second, illness produced by spirits; third, illness produced by Māra; fourth, illness resulting from unregulated breath; and fifth, illness caused by karmic obstructions. [These are] treated...

These various illnesses are as described in detail therein. For example, regarding the treatment of the first type of bodily illness, it is said: "When sitting, one may lean against a wall or a garment;

or one may lie down before the assembly has departed. This is mental indolence. Mara seizes this opportunity to enter the body and produce illness, causing the person’s back and spinal bones to ache with pain.
This is called the 'Infectious Illness' (*nirveśa*), which is difficult to cure. The practitioner must be cautious."
As for the method of treatment: use the breath to cause the circulating qi to flow from the head toward the spine, passing along the sides of the bone joints and descending downward.
One must apply the mind with great care before a cure can be achieved. Following this, there is a clarification of a single verse of the essential heart-essence.

This text consists of two parts: first, the citation of the verse. This verse is precisely the initial passage clarifying the onset of illness in the subsequent text; therefore, that text says: "Sit..."

A practitioner asked about various illnesses. The Master admonished him, saying, "Simply bind the mind to its object and do not allow other conditions to intervene; the illness will naturally subside.

Those who applied this method found that even after three days, there were none whose illnesses did not improve. Question: When the mind is distracted, one sees things erroneously. Answer: One can recover by gathering the mindfulness. Question:
When the four elements are increased or diminished, how can one recover? Answer: The movement of the mind is like the turning of a fan.
There is wind; it abides according to the principles of natural order. However, when the Master’s instructions and admonitions constantly cite the full text of a verse, it is precisely as it is now.
"True mind" refers to the perfect mind; "true realm" refers to the wondrous realm. Regarding "binding," as stated in the *Zhiguan*:

"Binding the conditions to the dharma-realm" means the single thought-moment of the dharma-realm. Binding the conditions is *śamatha* (calm); the single thought-moment is *vipaśyanā* (insight). The *Fuxing* commentary states: "Although one binds..."
Although mindfulness does not go beyond the *dharmadhātu*, although there is cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), stillness and illumination are simultaneous.
"Alternately" (*di*) means to exchange or to alternate. "To focus" (*zhù*) means to record, to concentrate, and is also like the pouring of water.
The commentary below next explains why the mind focuses on the object and the object focuses on the mind; this should be understood by applying the fourfold analysis from the preceding text here.

Apply this principle. Furthermore, you should expand upon this by means of the general purport of various texts, so that the meaning of the mutual resonance between mind and object may be clearly understood.
Reflect on this deeply, reflect on it again; I shall not provide a detailed exposition here.

The sixth section, the illustrative text on the mutual support of the characteristics of practice and understanding (*caryā-pratipatti-lakṣaṇa-saṃsarga*), is divided into two parts: first, the citation of the names; second, the explanation of their meanings. The latter is further divided into two parts. First, the judgment regarding the sequence of practice and understanding, which is itself divided into two.

First, the formal judgment regarding practice and understanding based on the preceding seven [sections]. Regarding the phrase "as in the *Vibhaṅga*," the ten meanings are also termed the ten gates (*daśamukha*).
Therefore, in the first section of *Zhiguan*, ten meanings are distinguished across ten chapters, beginning with the True and the Conventional and ending with the Horizontal and the Vertical.

Among these, the sixth meaning concerns the self and others; the first eight chapters are termed "Self-Cultivation" (*zixing*), while the chapter on "Arousing the Teaching" is termed "Transforming Others" (*huata*).
The ultimate aim (*zhiguī*), however, is neither self nor other; thus it is said: "Within this, for the time being, we shall rely upon self-cultivation."

This refers to the transformation of others and so forth. As for the statement that "retribution is the fruit, but it is not the primary intent here," this is because practice and understanding support one another primarily at the stage of the cause;
only when the cause is perfected does one finally achieve the great fruit. Therefore, retribution is not the primary intent here.
That the first five [perfections] produce understanding while the latter two constitute practice is evident from the subsequent text.

Next is the section "Discriminating the Lower [Levels]," which explains away doubts. The text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of doubts; second, clarifying that the understanding of one’s own practice consists only of the first five chapters. Regarding the "explanation of doubts":
the ten meanings of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) are distributed across the ten chapters. Among these, the seventh meaning corresponds to both the eyes and the feet.

From the "General Meaning" up to the "Arousing of the Teaching" constitutes the eyes; from the "Expedient Means" up to the "Fruit and Retribution" constitutes the feet. The "Ultimate Return" is neither eye nor foot.

[The commentary] concludes. Master Fuxing states: "Regarding the statement that 'the general meaning up to the section on the Arising of the Teaching' refers to the 'head,' this follows the convenience of the phrasing. According to principle, it should rather say:

'The first five chapters and the section on the Arising of the Teaching constitute the head. The 'head' is a metaphor for understanding; the preceding five chapters are precisely the head of self-cultivation."

The first chapter on "Arousing the Teaching" causes others to gain insight. Regarding the statement that "the means (upāya) up to the stage of fruition (phala-vipāka) constitute the 'feet'": the feet are a metaphor for practice (*caryā*).

The means consist of correct contemplation with effortful application (*sābhoga-prayoga-caryā*), while the stage of fruition refers to the positions from the first *bhūmi* upward, where practice occurs spontaneously through effortless mental engagement (*anābhoga-manasikāra*).
Although these differ slightly, they both belong to the category of practice. If one follows the fifth fascicle [of the *Xianxing Yinben*], the text states: [text continues].

Fourth) Regarding the initial statement: "The preceding six stages belong to understanding" (Fuxing says: "In relation to the five [subsequent stages], the *upāya* (expedient means) somewhat resembles the beginning of practice; however, in relation to the correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), it has not yet been discussed as practice at all.

Therefore, the preceding six all belong to understanding"). Thus, *upāya* is also subsumed under understanding. Now, since *upāya* can serve as the beginning of practice, it is provisionally judged to belong to practice.
As for the current text stating, "Transcending the sequence to take up the text because it also involves transforming others," this refers to the first five chapters and...

The subsequent section on "arousing the teaching" (qǐjiào) is analogous to the eyes; this is because it transcends the intermediate sequence of the three chapters concerning skillful means, correct contemplation, and the fruit of retribution.
Since arousing the teaching constitutes the understanding for transforming others, the understanding for one's own practice consists solely of the preceding five chapters.
Therefore, fearing that people might suspect that since the eyes are used as a metaphor for understanding, [the subsequent sections] must then begin from the general meaning and proceed until...

The establishment of the teachings is nothing other than interpretation (*vyākhyā*). Why, then, has it been judged heretofore that only the first five of the seven [categories] belong to interpretation?

Therefore, this commentary states: "Although they are equal within the text concerning discrimination (*vikalpa*). Thus, one must understand that interpretation possesses both a self-referential and an other-referential dimension.
Since we are now discussing the interpretation of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), there is no need for the interpretation directed toward others (*parārtha*) to pose an obstacle.

Next, following the "General Meaning" (Dàyì), the text clarifies doubts by explaining that the fruits of the five abbreviated practices (*lǜxíng*) do not constitute the characteristics of formal cultivation (*zhèngxū*). The text is divided into two parts. First, the direct clarification and the resolution of doubts.

As the *Fǔxíng* (Supplementary Practice) states: Question: Among the preceding five abbreviated practices, there are both practice (*xíng*) and understanding (*jiě*), as well as cause (*yīn*) and fruit (*guǒ*).
Why then does it say only that the six layers are understanding? Answer: It says "General Meaning" because this term serves as a heading for both practice and understanding.

Since the causes and effects of self and others are difficult to manifest through mere intention, one instead provides explanations such as the causes and effects of practice and understanding (*pratipatti* and *adhigama*). This does not mean that one already possesses the fruits of practice and so forth;

rather, the general meaning constitutes the whole, while the remaining eight constitute the particulars. These particulars are specific explanations of the causes and effects of practice and understanding.
Furthermore, if there is someone who, relying on the five preceding summaries, practices and realizes the fruit, thereby being able to benefit others, this constitutes a separate [category].

In the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*), within the section explaining the meaning of the "Constant Sitting Samādhi" (*changzuo sanmei*) and its associated "Mindfulness and Contemplation" (*yi zhi guan*), it says: "From this point up to 'neither walking nor sitting,' these are all roughly based on the original text’s brief indications of the gates of contemplation.

Even though there may be aspects resembling those of the Ten Contemplations (*shigan*), the wording is concise and abbreviated; thus, they cannot be used to discern the beginning and end of the contemplative methods. This is also true for the initial arousal of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) and the three subsequent summaries. Therefore, these five summaries are merely called 'General Meanings' (*dàyì*).

If one wishes to provide a detailed commentary, one must first be proficient in the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*shicheng guanfǎ*) found in the lower text before one can avoid error. If the intent of the treatise belongs solely to the category of "explanation" (*jie*), there is a fear that within such explanation, the understanding will not be comprehensive.

Therefore, it is necessary to thoroughly clarify the names, essences, and characteristics such as the inclusion of dharmas (*saṃgraha-dharma*), before one is capable of establishing the ten objects and ten vehicles that follow.

For instance, although the *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states that there are ten different types of generating the bodhicitta and distinctions between the four samādhis and the clear practices (*vidyā-caryā*), [it does not suffice without this prior clarification].
However, merely listing the headings to distinguish their characteristics is insufficient. Therefore, [this text] has not yet touched upon the ten objects (daśaviṣaya) or the ten vehicles (daśayāna).

Thus, it is now termed the "General Meaning" (mahātman). Although it mentions practice (caryā), retributive results (vipāka), and so forth—even stating that these do not mean they are identical to the characteristics of actual cultivation—[it remains a preliminary overview].
Next, what is meant by "inferior"? This is raised to verify it through the correct cultivation of the expedient means (*upāya*). The text is divided into two parts. First, the formal presentation:
How is it known that within the preceding five brief stages there is not yet the characteristic of correct cultivation?
It is because the characteristics of practice must both employ the twenty-five dharmas as expedient means and take the ten objects and ten vehicles as correct cultivation; yet these five...

Since this point was not clarified within the *Lüzhōng* (略中), it can be verified that it merely explains the beginning and the end; it does not yet constitute the characteristics of actual practice (*xiūxíng*).

The following section [“次所以下”] provides the underlying intent. However, this only explains the reason for "correct cultivation" (*zhèngxū*), hence it says, "if there were no ten objects" (*shíjìng*) and so forth.
It still lacks an explanation of the reason for "preparatory means" (*fāngbiàn*). Therefore, one should say: "If..."

Without skillful means, correct practice cannot be established. If the ten objects (daśaviṣaya) are absent, there is no essence (*tattva*). This "essence" refers to the essence of the very substance itself.
If one considers the essence as that which is relied upon, it is simply the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states:

"Furthermore, these ten objects are precisely the essence revealed in the preceding text. The previous section established the name 'essence' based on the capacity of what is revealed to encompass [all things]."

Now, because they are established as objects (*viṣaya*) in relation to the observing subject, they are designated by that name. Furthermore, while previously they were explained from the perspective of principle (*li*), their essence was one;
now, from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), there are ten objects. Since phenomena are identical to principle, each and every object is inconceivable;

since principle is identical to phenomena, each and every object has distinct and differing characteristics. Thus we know that if the ten objects to be observed did not exist, [the practice would be impossible].

There is no one capable of observing the essence of the ten vehicles. Because, according to principle, there is nothing that exists [independently], yet it is omnipresent within phenomena, one must manifest principle precisely through phenomena;
only then does the essence of the Great Vehicle of the Ten Vehicles come to exist. The *Fahua Wenju Ermen* (The Two Gates of the Lotus Sutra) states:

"Therefore, to extract the ten wonders as the great body of the contemplative method refers to the essence of that which is relied upon. If viewed from the perspective of the contemplating subject, then...
The ten wonders (daśa-māyā) further constitute the very essence of the objects of the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth.

Although the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is the principle and the Perfect and Sudden teaching is the reality, and although the origin is remote, when viewed from the perspective of contemplation, it belongs to the phenomenal (vastu). This is because the phenomenon is precisely the very essence of the object itself.

Therefore, one should know that the statement here—“if there are no ten objects, there is no vehicle, and thus no essence”—refers to this very essence of the object itself. As for the preceding text...

It says: "Taking the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena as the body of the vehicle" refers to the foundational substance (*āśraya*). Although the two paths are distinguished, their principle is not of different tracks;
therefore, the foundation in its entirety constitutes the actual entity (*tattva*), while one must still realize that this actual entity is itself the foundation.

"Principle is identical with phenomena, and phenomena are identical with principle—is this not so? Question: "If the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) are taken as the substance of the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*), then the ten objects do not transcend the afflictions of the burning house (*āgnyagāra*).
Yet, the *Śūxing qiàn* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) states: 'Taking the burning house as a jeweled island [is like] being certain to be consumed by fire;
taking afflictions as the vehicle itself means it must be overturned. This contradicts the present position. How should this be reconciled?"
[The questioner] asks: "Now, you take the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) as the substance of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*). These are merely the bodies of the chariots;

yet, if these chariot-bodies lack the adornments of various jewels, the white oxen that pull them, and the attendants who guard them, how can the practice-conditions (*prayoga-pratyaya*) and the realization-conditions (*pariniṣpatti-pratyaya*) of the ten vehicles be manifested?"
However, this is merely a "bald vehicle" (túchéng); it will certainly overturn and be consumed by fire. Therefore, the second line says:

"If one lacks the ten dharmas, it is called a ruined donkey-cart. This is precisely for this reason. Regarding the statement that lacking the ten dharmas constitutes a ruined donkey-cart, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Brahmacarya Chapter," states:
"Riding a ruined donkey-cart, he travels due south. Zhan’an’s commentary explains: "Riding a ruined donkey-cart..."

This is like the spontaneous movement of unwholesome dharmas. There are three interpretations regarding the phrase "traveling directly south. First, it says that the south represents the *li* hexagram (the mountain) and the north represents the *kan* hexagram (the water).
To leave the water and approach the mountain is a metaphor for losing the wholesome and giving rise to the unwholesome. Second, it says this is explained in reference to all directions.

The north is the upper direction. This is like a person who has severed their roots of goodness falling from above. Thirdly, it is said that the Son of Heaven faces south, possessing sovereign power over life and death;
this person of false views likewise judges that cause and effect do not exist, and their mind is similarly sovereign.

Therefore, at the conclusion of the text on the ten vehicles for clearly contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*) in the *Zhi guan*, it says: "People nowadays merely believe that abandoning evil and grasping at emptiness is the Great [Vehicle]."
This emptiness still does not exempt one from the evils of the sixty-two views, whether taken individually or in combination. How could it be moved or issued forth as a vehicle (*yāna*)?
Even if it were borrowed as a vehicle, it would be merely a "shaven-headed vehicle," lacking the dharma-gates and the complete means of deliverance (*pāramitā*).

Within the Great City of the True Dharma and the Vajra Treasury, everything is fully present and without deficiency; what is there that is absent? How could it be permitted to remain as mere bald emptiness? If it were only thus, it would not be a vehicle.
"To enter dangerous and evil paths by means of false views is merely a ruined donkey-cart. (The *Fuxing* [Commentary on the Meaning of the Text] says:
"The phrase 'People of today' below criticizes the heterodox; 'The True Dharma' below reveals the orthodox. How could such a wondrous vehicle be the same as an evil emptiness?

Speaking in terms of inclusion, it possesses only the body of the cart but lacks the various implements and degrees; therefore, it is called 'bald. Speaking in terms of exclusion, both its substance and function are non-existent."
It is called "bald. Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* cites the example of riding a broken donkey cart;

it is not only lacking white oxen, but since Prajñā is being ridden by a donkey, it proceeds spontaneously rather than correctly, and thus is neither lofty nor expansive. Furthermore, it is said to be "broken" and entirely devoid of adornment;
how much more so when one gives rise to views and enters the three evil realms!
Next, "Therefore we know" and below clarifies mutual assistance. The text is divided into three parts. First, it clarifies that wondrous understanding guides the commencement of expedient practice.
This section has two parts. First, it clarifies that understanding has both extensive and concise aspects, as discussed above.

Therefore, one must know that it is essential to first generate the inconceivable understanding of self-cultivation through the preceding five chapters. Within the generation of this understanding, the general meaning is as follows:

Regarding the brief explanation of the beginning and end, as well as the causes and effects for oneself and others, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "The general meaning constitutes the whole, while the remaining eight [sections] constitute the particulars.
Both the general and the particular include the causes and effects of one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*) as well as the capacity to transform others (*parārtha*) and its objects.

Why is this? Within the general explanation, "arousing the mind" and "practicing" constitute the cause of one's own practice; "subsequently attaining the great fruit" constitutes the fruit of one's own practice; and "subsequently tearing the great net" constitutes the transformation of others.

It is indeed so. Since there is that which is capable of transformation, there must necessarily be that which is transformed. The text briefly cites the capacity [of the means] to encompass that which is transformed;
once the matters of the capacity and its object are concluded, they both enter the ultimate goal. Furthermore, it says: "The beginning of practice is the cause; the end of practice is the fruit.

Is this not precisely the beginning and end of one's own practice? In the subsequent detailed explanation, from the interpretation of the name up to right contemplation, these constitute the causes of one's own practice.
Next is the Chapter on Retribution (*vipāka*), which concerns the fruit of one’s own practice (*sva-caryā*). The Chapter on Initiating the Teaching concerns the ability to transform others;

the meaning of "that which is acted upon" corresponds to the sphere of transforming others (*para-caryā*). Although the texts for the final three major chapters are missing, their meaning is identical to the general intent.

Regarding the brief discussion of the beginning and end in the final three [chapters], this refers to the respective beginnings and ends of both self and others. The beginning of one's own practice is the cause (*hetu*).
The end of self-cultivation is the fruit; the beginning of transforming others is the capacity; the end of transforming others is the object.

This is, for example, the meaning of the beginning and end of the Ten Profound Subtleties (and so forth). Regarding "the text is concise while the meaning is expansive," this refers to what was previously stated:

that the text is brief while the general meaning is broad. As for "the next four [profundities] focus exclusively on name and substance," the term "four" refers to the collective enumeration of the four.

This refers to the chapters. Regarding "the names and the essence," this specifically cites the first two chapters; although the first two are cited separately, they also encompass the latter two. Thus, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says:

"As in the 'Explanation of Names,' there is first the 'relative' (*dai*) and then the 'absolute' (*jue*). The absolute is simply the opening-up [of the relative]. The various distinct virtues come together to constitute the meaning of the absolute.
This clarifies that in the four sections on the essence, each proceeds from the partial to the perfect as the relative and the absolute. The essence is the object.
Regarding "Explanation": Once the names have been revealed and manifested, the essence follows the names. The essence thus revealed universally encompasses all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Since the characteristics of these phenomena are difficult to clarify, they are further divided into six meanings that pervade both fact and principle, cause and effect, and self and other. These six meanings, in turn, mutually subsume one another.

Furthermore, by means of five gates, the phenomena so subsumed are judged; only then does one understand how the contents within the essence are mutually integrated, and subsequently realize this integration.
The provisional is not confused with the real within the middle [truth]. Furthermore, these four chapters on the provisional and the real are mutually illuminating.

Therefore, by citing only the two chapters on name and essence, one can understand how the inclusion of phenomena—whether partial or perfect—is thereby made known. As for the "extensiveness of principle and text":

since the four chapters have been opened, is it not the case that the text is the means of expression (*vyañjana*) and the principle is the object expressed (*artha*), such that the principle is likewise extensive?

Therefore, what follows next clarifies that the "thorough understanding" (*pravicaya*) guides the beginning of practice. The reason it simply says "thorough understanding" is merely for the sake of literary convenience;
in reality, one must say that the "wondrous understanding" (*miao-jie*) of the five chapters guides the beginning of practice. Thus, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says:

"When the wondrous understanding is somewhat sharp, one further uses this understanding to guide the preparatory practices (*upāya*). It also says: "Furthermore, one passes through the twenty-five dharmas to generate understanding based on phenomena (*vastu*). Only then...
This alone is capable of serving as the skillful means (*upāya*) for correct cultivation. The term "skillful means" applies to both the partial and the perfect [teachings]. Therefore, it is said:
"The twenty-five dharmas are distinguished according to the teachings. Only through bestowing, opening, abolishing, and synthesizing can they be named the foremost of sublime practices (*sucarita*).
This can be seen by reflecting upon it.

Therefore, next, it is explained that wondrous understanding serves as the support for the practice of correct cultivation. The text is divided into two parts; the first provides the direct explanation.

Regarding the term "the doctrine" (*zong*): this refers to the three chapters on the skillful means, correct contemplation, and the fruit of retribution. Within the fivefold profound meaning (*wuchong xuanyi*), these constitute the doctrine.

Therefore, the ten dharmas now being correctly cultivated are designated as the "Essential Doctrine" (*zong*). Regarding the "sequence," it refers to the orderly arising [of the stages] without confusion.
Regarding "being self-sufficient in principle," this is because these matters have already been fully and clearly elucidated within the preceding section on "Exquisite Understanding.

As for the phrase "while the characteristics in the current text are still extensive," this means that the characteristics of the contemplative methods within the section on "Correct Cultivation" are vast and comprehensive.

This is intended for those of dull faculties. As for those of sharp faculties, having already attained the essential meaning of the preceding sublime understanding, they need only have the names and sequence of the ten dharmas explained within the current section on formal practice; their underlying principle will then be naturally complete.

Now, fearing that those of dull faculties may not understand the sequence of the ten modes of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-vidarśanā*), I shall specifically cite the excellent explanations from the preceding text and discuss their characteristics in detail within the context of entering correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Why is this?

For instance, among the ten dharmas practiced in right cultivation, is the "single-minded *śamatha-vipaśyanā*" not precisely the "absolute (*atyanta*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*" explained in the preceding section on the interpretation of names? Dharma...
Is the wondrous principle of *xing* (nature) not precisely the essence and characteristics of the preceding discussion on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?

Are the delusions to be destroyed by these practices of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* not precisely the phenomena subsumed within the preceding discussion? Are the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles, the provisional and the real, and the coarse and the subtle not clearly manifest as the characteristics of the partial and the perfect in the preceding discussion?
Thus we know that the characteristics of the ten dharmas for formal cultivation are actually an extension of the preceding wondrous [teachings].

This is merely a detailed discussion for the purpose of understanding the entry into contemplation. If it were otherwise, then understanding would not be the practice of one who practices, and practice would not be the conduct of one who understands;

how then could they mutually support one another to accord with the principle? Nevertheless, in the midst of the formal cultivation of the ten objects such as the aggregates and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is necessary to provide a detailed exposition of the sublime practices of the ten dharmas.
However, fearing that the text might become overly prolix, I have instead fully elucidated these ten [practices] specifically within the context of the aggregate objects.

Regarding the ten vehicles of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna*): the nine subsequent objects can be understood by analogy with the ten vehicles of contemplation applied to the object of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Thus, the preceding text states: "The ten dharmas constitute the contemplation; however, one must thoroughly understand the underlying causes and conditions regarding the aggregates and sense bases (*āyatana*), whereas for the other nine objects, contemplation may be established only once they have arisen.
Therefore, within these nine objects, only the objects themselves are distinguished; the ten contemplations applied to each object are not discussed in detail. However—
The illumination that follows along with objects is not related to the extensive exposition; therefore, it is not the case that the various texts lack both secondary and primary aspects.
This has two meanings. First, when speaking in terms of understanding and practice, the first five chapters take wondrous understanding as primary and wondrous practice as secondary.
Thus, although practice and fruition appear within the five summaries, they do not refer to the actual characteristics of cultivation; rather, they concern correct cultivation—
Although the preceding detailed treatise on entering contemplation through understanding is cited therein, it cannot be said that this merely clarifies "wondrous understanding.

Therefore, within the stage of formal cultivation, "wondrous practice" is primary and "wondrous understanding" is secondary. Second, while the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*) incidentally clarifies the characteristics of the objects, it correctly demonstrates the ten vehicles;

thus, the ten vehicles are most detailed within the realm of the aggregates. In the nine subsequent realms, the characteristics of the objects are correctly demonstrated, while the ten vehicles are treated incidentally.

Because it is a vehicle (*yāna*), among the nine objects (*viṣaya*), one distinguishes only the object itself. The ten contemplations (*daśa-vipaśyanā*) following the object will not be discussed in detail;
although the text is tangential, the primary meaning is necessarily complete.

Furthermore, as follows: next, the practice of correct cultivation that accomplishes the Dharma-body at the Bodhi-tree is explained. The text is divided into two parts; first, the Path (*mārga*) is explained.
The tree [of the text] consists of three parts. First, the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is clarified. Thus, in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Zhi guan), Zhiyi’s disciple Zhang’an privately remarked:

"For example, the great earth is one, yet it can produce various kinds of sprouts. The *Fuxing* (Fuzheng xuanyi) says: "Dharmatā is like the earth; the seeds are like the objects (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"However, all aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), both within and outside the realms, arise from the mind. This is the root of delusion; the mind encompasses them all."
"All. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice) states: "If one reveals the essence of the objects of contemplation, contemplating the mind alone is sufficient.

This is because the mind is all-pervasive and subsumes all other phenomena. Therefore, it is said here that, for instance, the ten objects of contemplation are merely the ground where a single thought-moment functions.
Because the essence of the mind universally subsumes everything, it can be metaphorically compared to the earth. Thus, the *Fuxing* says: "The Dharma-nature is like..."
"Ground" (*bhūmi*). Since this mind is the object of contemplation, it is called the "ground of practice.
To display each of these objects distinctly means that the ten objects, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), are differentiated and do not become confused.
Regarding "the seed of practice," the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "The seed is like the object; 'seed' has the meaning of 'to produce. This seed produces..."

At that time, cultivation (śikṣā) transforms entirely into the nature of cultivation (śikṣātva). Since this cultivation arises from the great earth of the dharma-nature (dharmatā), the nature of cultivation and the nature of reality are both identical within the one suchness (tathatā);
there is no separate essence that comes from without. If the ten objects (daśaviṣaya) do not serve as the vehicle, there is no essence.
This is the meaning. Question: If this is so, how are "seed" (bīja) and "nature" (prakṛti) distinguished? Answer: That which is capable of producing...
It is the seed. That which is unchanging is called "nature" (*dhātu*). Please allow me to clarify this through a metaphor: because grain produces grain, it is called a "seed";
because the grain-seed does not change, it is called "nature. From the mind of a single thought, the ground of the Dharma-nature arises;

therefore, it is like a seed. From beginningless time until now, that seed has remained unchanged; for this reason, it is called "nature. Although the seed and the nature are distinct, their essence is fundamentally non-dual. This is from the perspective of function.
The distinction between the two meanings is perfectly clear, as detailed in the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* (*Jìngmíng shū*).

Regarding the phrase "each and every one arises below," the next section correctly explains the Bodhi tree. This text is divided into two parts: first, the correct explanation; [the *Fǔxíng* merely states: [End of excerpt]

Contemplative practice (*guanxing*) is like rain; its emergence is like the sprouting of shoots. Although the trunk, medicinal herbs, flowers, and fruit are omitted for brevity, one gives rise to the tenfold contemplations (*shicheng guan*) within the ground of the Dharma-nature (*faxingdi*), moistening the seeds of the objective realms (*jingzhong*) so that they may germinate; therefore, it is likened to rain. The character "ya" (牙) is an error;
it should be "ya" (芽), meaning a sprout. The ten objective realms, such as the aggregates (*yin*), are caused to grow by being nourished through the rain of contemplative practice.
Birth transforms into a wondrous realm, just as a seed sprouts and sends forth its shoots. "Trunk" (gàn) refers to the main stem;

because one seeks the goal by exerting the mind, it is likened to the trunk rising upward. Since there are sixty-four methods for settling the mind (*anxin*), it is therefore likened to the great abundance of branches and leaves.
From the "universal destruction" up to the "antidotes," these constitute both the primary and auxiliary practices.

Practice begins with the cause; therefore, it is likened to a flower. Furthermore, practice culminates in the fruit; thus, it is said that one proceeds through the successive stages until reaching the fruit of practice, which is the departure from craving.
Once one has departed from attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), one enters the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), which is called the "partial fruit" (*aṃśaphala*).
This is explained in terms of departing from "semblance-craving" (*pratibimba-tṛṣṇā*). If one departs from "true-craving" (*tattva-tṛṣṇā*), one must further discuss the ultimate fulfillment.

The result is the granting of the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) and wandering to the ultimate limit; this is precisely the meaning [of the preceding]. Next, "If there were no... and below is the summary.

If there were no rain of the first practice of contemplation, up to and including the fruit of the sixth stage, which is the departure from craving, then the Tree of the Path (*mārga-vṛkṣa*) could not be made majestic.
Therefore, the Tree of the Path is only perfected through these six matters. This is because the tree is used as a metaphor for the path of cause and effect. Thus it is said.

It is said that [the path] is like a tree. However, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), it states: "The *Vibhāṣā* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* both use the metaphor of a tree for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and thus call it the 'Path-tree' (Dàoshù), and so forth."

The third section below clarifies that although the sequence of the three faculties differs, one must proceed through the aforementioned six matters until one reaches detachment from craving before finally accomplishing the fruit.
This is explained according to the sequential order of the ten dharmas of contemplative practice.

However, if speaking in terms of individuals, the case is not so. Why? Because individuals possess three types of faculties; those of superior faculty [attain it] directly within the seeds of the mental ground.
One gives rise to the fruit through subtle and wondrous contemplation (*sūkṣma-pratyavekṣā*).

It is not necessary to proceed through the stages sequentially until reaching the tenth stage, where one has abandoned attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), before entering the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) and proceeding to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*tathāgata-bodhi*). Thus, the text says: "Therefore, regarding the state of illness...

This refers to what is stated in the passage on the "wondrous object" (*miao-jing*) within the first contemplation of the Ten Vehicles. Therefore, after the *Mohe Zhiguan* explains that contemplating illness is the wondrous object, it cites the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

The "Chapter on Removing Illness through Radiance" states: "Upon merely hearing these words, the illness is immediately cured. This refers to the meaning of the initial contemplation. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says:
"Merely upon hearing these words, that which was afflicted is immediately removed; this is analogous to hearing of the wondrous realm and attaining entry into the First Abode (*prathamavihāra*).

It further states that "initial contemplation" refers specifically to the initial contemplation of the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*). Regarding those of middling and inferior capacities, the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) also...
It says: "Furthermore, there are those who are deeply afflicted and difficult to cure; they must go to an elder to have various medicines compounded before the illness can be cured.
This refers to the meaning of the subsequent nine contemplations. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "This is like contemplating the wondrous object while ignorance has not yet been eliminated.
Thus, from the arousal of the bodhicitta up to the departure from craving, it is called 'various medicines. By employing such contemplation, one may also enter the first stage (*bhūmi*)."
This refers to the stages (*bhūmi*). Even if one has not yet entered the stages, attaining entry into the five grades is called "minor elimination of differences.
Therefore, one should know that it is only upon reaching the transcendence of craving that it is designated as the "fruit"; this is explained in reference to those of middling and inferior faculties.

As for those of superior faculties, they immediately contemplate the seeds of the objects and achieve the inconceivable, thereby ascending directly to the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) and proceeding to the state of *miao-jue* (wonderful enlightenment). Thus, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) says: "The ten vehicles..."

There are ten aspects of the text and ten meanings. Regarding the faculties, there are three types; regarding the mind, there are two, distinguished by their proximity or distance. The near refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*), while the distant reaches the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, the *Dàyì* states: "Those of superior faculty have only one dharma; those of middling faculty have two or seven; only those of inferior faculty possess all ten.

(According to the Goryeo edition of the *Four Teachings*, those from the arousal of the mind up to the sixth stage of the path-factors are called middling faculty; from the stage of counteraction up to the detachment from attachment to dharmas are called inferior faculty.)
Next, below that, the Dharmakāya is elucidated. The text is divided into two parts. The first part provides a specific explanation, which is further divided into two sections.

The first section correctly explains the Dharmakāya by way of sublime practice (*sucarita*). To begin with, regarding the four matters as observed through the sublime object (*viṣaya*) according to the Initial Vehicle (*ādikarmika-yāna*):

first, one contemplates that the mind is the inconceivable object. Does not the single character "contemplation" (*guan*) refer to the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of tranquil illumination? Furthermore, it says: "Since [the practitioner] themselves..."
Upon attaining the wondrous realm, one immediately gives rise to compassion; is this not "arising"? As cited from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"The mind is like a painter who creates the five aggregates," etc.; is this not "citing an example"?

Furthermore, [the text] refutes the common people's judgment that the first five "Thusnesses" belong to the provisional and the mundane, while the latter five "Thusnesses" belong to the real and the sagely; is this not "refuting the ancients"? Again, it asks: "When the mind arises, it must..."
"Entrusting to conditions" and so forth—is this not a question-and-answer explanation for resolving doubts? Since it is thus with the first vehicle, the remaining nine may be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, the subsequent explanation below also relies on the wondrous understanding to clarify the Dharma-body; it is spoken from the perspective of an extensive interpretation, hence it mentions "explaining the names" and the other four aspects.
The text is that which manifests [the meaning], and thus belongs to the skin; the meaning is that which is manifested, and thus belongs to the flesh. The intent lies in...
The intentional resolve (*cetanā*) of correct cultivation is the bone. The ultimate goal of correct cultivation is the extinction of phenomena and the realization of the true nature (*dharmatā*);

that which the intentional resolve reaches is called the marrow. The passage beginning with "Next, if there were no... is a general interrogation, which serves as a summary of the four aspects each of practice and understanding, thereby accomplishing the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
One must know that the Dharma-body is both whole and fragmentary; the various provisional teachings are termed "fragmentary," whereas the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is...
Truly, this is called "wholeness. Therefore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* clarifies that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has seventeen names;

its twelfth name is "The Solid Relics of All Buddhas. Since this present *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* is the wondrous interpretation and wondrous practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one should know that it is indeed the wholeness of the Dharma-body.
Thus, the *Wonderful Sutra* says: "Wherever this sutra volume resides, all..."
One should erect a stūpa made of the seven precious substances; it is unnecessary to further enshrine relics (referring here only to bodily relics). Why is this?
Because the entire body of the Tathāgata is already present herein. This is the intended meaning.

Third, "Therefore, below," [the text] refutes what is incorrect to reveal what is correct. The passage is divided into two parts. First, it refutes the scholars of that time who read the text while remaining ignorant of its intent.

This section entirely serves as a summary refutation of Qingliang’s erroneous interpretation, which takes one or two biased phrases to establish a "sudden-sudden" [teaching], thereby rendering the ten vehicles of wondrous practice of the present *Zhiguan* incomplete. The details are as explained in the preceding and following sections of the text.

[The commentary] says (and so forth). Next, regarding "the subsequent practice" and below, the text correctly reveals that what is transmitted exhausts the profound depths. The text is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies that understanding and practice are perfected and together return to the wondrous principle.
As for the term "collected understanding" (*jijie*), the character "collected" (*ji*) is likely an error; it should be the character "cultivated" (*xi*).
Now, below this, the ten chapters are concluded in succession to encompass all dharmas exhaustively.

The phrase "the meaning is only thus" refers to the preceding passages concerning the cultivation of practice, the coming [of the teaching], and so forth. Therefore, the preceding passages on the practice of understanding and skillful means (*upāya*) are precisely the ten great chapters of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Thus, one should know that there is nothing not subsumed within these ten chapters. Even as I establish these precedents and expound upon the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), I still fear...

Not having clarified the essential meaning of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, how could one expect that a search for essentials through overly concise explanations could serve as a gateway for universal practice?
This was clearly the work of those who were ignorant in previous generations, who falsely invoked the name of Jingxi to give rise to reckless views;

they arbitrarily engaged in acceptance and rejection, causing immense harm. A brief discussion of this may be found in the *Supplementary Notes to the Great Commentary* (as explained at length therein).
The seventh section, which clarifies the correct teaching by addressing doubts through an analogy, consists of two parts.

First, the citation of the title serves to clarify the confusion of the Master Qingliang (Zhiyi) regarding the contemplation of stillness and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), thereby elucidating the correct practice of the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* he transmitted. Question: How is it known that this refers to the Master Qingliang?

Answer: The *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* states: "In the tenth year of the Dali era, Master Qingliang Guanding followed Dharma Master Zhanran of Jingxi to study the Tiantai *Zhi Guan* (Stilling and Contemplation) as well as the commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and others... (and so forth).

I have also perused Master Qingliang’s sub-commentary (*Chao*) on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, wherein I observed his stubborn adherence to the provisional passages of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, [claiming that] tiles and stones are not...
Regarding the nature [of the teachings], there are further erroneous establishments of "gradual and sudden" and "sudden-sudden.

From this, one can know that the composition of the *Jinbi* (The Golden Needle) and the emergence of the *Yili* (Exemplary Meanings) were both intended to instruct Master Qingliang Guanding. This is likewise true of all that is refuted in various texts such as the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) and the *Fuxingji* (Record of Aiding Practice).
Thus, the second of the ten intentions regarding the origins described in the *Fuxing* states: "Formerly, I received the lineage from..."

This is because they abandon the root and follow the branches of their views; it is truly for this reason. Furthermore, the various masters of recent times have not deeply investigated their own fundamental school nor have they studied its texts extensively;
consequently, they often deviate from the tenets of their own school and adhere instead to the biased views of others.
How tragic, how tragic! This has been exhaustively refuted as erroneous in the *Yuyan ji* (Record of Parables) regarding the "Golden Scalpel"; scholars should seek that out.
Following this, the explanation of the meaning of the text below is divided into three parts. First, clarifying the origins:

regarding the phrase "the doctrine studied by this school," etc., it refers to the doctrine studied by this particular lineage from the time of Zhizhe Dashi (Zhang'an) down to Jingxi Zhiyi, which they all collectively follow and uphold.
Tiantai has but one master: Zhiyi alone. Thus, the *Jinbi* states: "The Great Master Tiantai personally received [the teaching] at Vulture Peak and attained wondrous awakening at Mount Dasu;
he is my teacher. The *Mohe zhiguan* is the Dharma he inherited.

Therefore, the method of the *Zhiguan* has been passed down through successive generations with its principles and texts in continuous succession, taken as the essential core of the mind. All paths lead to the same track, and in the end there is no divergence."

Explanation: This was merely because I happened to encounter someone holding the eccentric views of Master Qingliang Guanding and questioned him; consequently, there arose this story of a divergent response.
Unable to do otherwise, I briefly invoked the teachings of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) to clarify Master Qingliang’s confusion.
However, Master Qingliang had originally studied the Tiantai tradition and had previously lectured on *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. (This was written by Pei Xiu regarding Master Qingliang.)
His *xingzhuang* (biography) contains this account). Having produced such eccentric interpretations, he was rebuked and excluded by Jingxi [Zhanran].
