"Three, yet not three"—this is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). One should also further state: "neither three nor not three"—this is the middle (*madhyama*).

Regarding "the absence of words": this is merely an abbreviation. It is the Middle Way that is neither conjoined nor dispersed, the double negation. Yet, conjunction is precisely emptiness; dispersion is precisely the provisional.

"Neither non-conjunction nor non-dispersion" refers to the aforementioned double negation; this very double negation is the double illumination. Having first clarified the double negation, one then clarifies the double illumination.
As for the discussion of the two truths within these two sections, it is because this perfect text precedes [the former].
Because there is no subsequent [existence]. One cannot say that identity and difference are themselves the Middle; yet, identity is Emptiness, and difference is the Provisional.

When these Three Truths—identity, emptiness, and the provisional—reside within the sense organs, objects, and the *tathāgatagarbha*, they are precisely the Provisional. How could the *tathāgatagarbha* lack Buddha-nature?

That those who hear this Perfect and Sudden teaching do not take it as their primary principle is truly due to the fact that those practicing the Mahāyāna in recent times have been mixed with [erroneous views].

This is because of excessive negligence. How much more so now, when the era is one of degenerate emotions and the faithful are few and thin; while the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuan-dun) overflow the treasuries and fill the cases, people do not reflect upon them for even a moment and instead fall into dark oblivion.
To die in vain and live in delusion—how painful this is! The Three Illuminations (San-ming) are established based on provisional names and meanings.
In the first section of the "Discrimination" (*Liao-jian*) of the *Zhi-guan*, it says: "To reach the text within the text—that which is not text, and that which is neither text nor..."

It is not the text; the text is its gateway. Because one attains the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) through the gateway, the text is its gateway. The gateway encompasses all dharmas; it is the gateway and yet not the gateway;

it is neither the gateway nor is it not the gateway. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "The text is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); that which is not the text is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
the double negation is the Middle Way, the primary truth (*prathama-artha-satya*). One may observe these three examples as a model for the gateways of contemplation.
When observing in this manner, how could the gates be distinct? Both are called "capable of passage" and both are "that which is reached.
It is by relying on these gate-names that the three contemplations are established; therefore, it is said they are "established by relying on names and meanings.

Furthermore, within the third [contemplation]—which encompasses the partial and the perfect, the provisional and the real—one clarifies the provisional, the real, and that which is neither provisional nor real; this can be understood by analogy. This concludes the section on the three contemplations within one mind.

Next is the specific explanation of the three contemplations within the single mind (*ekacitta*). This section is further divided into two parts. First is the formal explanation, which is itself divided into two:

first, distinguishing [the present] from what preceded; "it is entirely not the meaning of these three contemplations" means that it is not the meaning of the three types of contemplation—such as the formation of contemplation through the object (*ālambana*)—as elucidated in the preceding text.
Next, "it is merely... and so forth, is the formal explanation, which may be understood by reference to what precedes and need not be elaborated upon further.

Quotation again. "The *Zhiguan* [states] that the auxiliary practitioner does not see... and below. Next, the refutation of errors. This section consists of two parts. First, the refutation of those who arbitrarily add [elements] in contrast to the three contemplations.

Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, the text itself says... and below, second, the refutation of erroneous interpretations regarding the supernatural powers of walking and riding horses. This section also consists of two parts.

First, the main text of *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) is cited. Next, under the section beginning with "That Master," his erroneous interpretations are recounted. This section consists of two parts: first, the direct recounting of his views;

second, the refutation of those errors, beginning with "The horse and the rider are originally... This latter part is further divided into two: first, the refutation of his error in using emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*) to further negate emptiness and the provisional;

"originally" (*yuan*) means fundamentally. Regarding "single emptiness and single provisional": this refers to his horizontal differentiation of emptiness and the provisional, assigning each to a separate individual. First...

Therefore, in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*...

Section Twenty-Four: Distinguishing Errors. Regarding the error of [the Sudden Teaching] being divided into two—namely, the relative and the absolute—there are three parts to the text:

and [within this, there are three parts]: first, the direct counter-interrogation; second, the explanation of the reason, beginning with "What is it..."; and third, the refutation of your position, beginning with "If that were so... and ending with "...you."

He judges the *Avataṃsaka* to be "sudden-sudden" (*dun-dun*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to be "gradual-sudden" (*jian-dun*). Furthermore, he states that "sudden-sudden" is absolute (*juedai*), while "gradual-sudden" is relative (*xiangdai*).

Next, following the passage below, he directly refutes the error of such a classification.
Furthermore, there are three parts: first, a general refutation; second, a specific critique beginning with "Which ones..."; and third, [the conclusion].

Regarding "not gradual," this does not refer to the gradual teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*. Regarding "only sudden," this refers exclusively to the *Lotus Sūtra* alone, which uniquely reveals the suddenness of the opening and merging [of the teachings].
To judge it as "provisional" (*xiāngdài*) and also as "gradual" is a refutation of the erroneous judgment of Qingliang. Generally speaking, the term "provisional" appears in numerous texts.

Therefore, it is called "ordinary" (*fan*). When things manifest in relation to one another, they are called "characteristics" (*xiang*). To view another from the perspective of oneself is "conditionality" (*dai*).

Thus, if there were no coarse or gradual [teachings], how could there be the subtle or sudden? Consequently, the names "subtle" and "sudden" are established in dependence upon the "coarse" and "gradual.

Regarding the phrase "in dependence upon the preceding teachings," this correctly explains the subtlety of mutual dependence. As for the statement that the sudden teaching follows the gradual and includes what it refutes, etc.:

This is precisely the meaning of abandoning the provisional to clarify the real. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, below," it again rebukes those who do not understand the sense of the "absolute" (juedai).

The "relative" (xiangdai) is discussed in terms of destroying the provisional to clarify the real, as explained above. The "absolute" is discussed in terms of opening the provisional to reveal the real;
therefore, it is now said that being "absolute" because it transcends all that is relative is precisely what constitutes the wondrous sudden [teaching]. If it were not so, then the wondrous...
If there is coarseness externally, how can it be established as the wondrous and sudden?

Is it an immediate, immediate severance of all dependencies?
Twenty-fifth, [the section] on the "Two Subtleties" of the *Lotus Sūtra* addresses the error of erroneously dividing [the teachings]. This passage consists of three parts. First, the question:

regarding those who judge [the teachings] as belonging to two paths, this refers to the division between the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Lotus*. Second, the answer. Third, the three analogies. This section also consists of three parts; first, the refutation.
They do not grasp the intent of the "opening" (kai). When [the text] enters the phrase concerning the *Avataṃsaka*, one fears that the two characters "Huayan" (*Avataṃsaka*) may have been omitted;

That which is "absolute" in contrast to that *Avataṃsaka* opens up that *Avataṃsaka*, which includes both the distinct teaching (*bie*) and the broad dissemination (*xingbu*), as being coarse. Furthermore, those of the two vehicles were like the deaf and mute sitting in the assembly until the present day.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states that all shall attain Buddhahood; this is thus utterly distinct and even more luminous. Furthermore, it is not merely that it is "exclusive," but rather that it is "without dependence.

Although the *Avataṃsaka* possesses the single wondrousness of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), because it concurrently includes the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), its singular manifestation is incomplete.
Therefore, it cannot be uniquely designated as "wondrous. It is like a gentleman wearing the attire of a commoner; it causes the gentleman [to lose his distinction].
A son cannot be uniquely distinguished [from his father]. The *Lotus Sūtra* is not like that: "Setting aside expedient means with straightforwardness, it teaches only the unsurpassed Way.
Since it does not incorporate the coarse, its unique distinction is made manifest; therefore, the title of the sūtra calls it "Wondrous" (*miao*).

This is because it awaits the various preceding coarse teachings to manifest the pure and singular wondrousness of the present *Lotus Sūtra*. For this reason, the name of this sūtra is called "wondrous by way of mutual dependence" (*xiangdai miao*). "Flower" (*hua*)...

As for the statement, "Since the two types of *sū* (milk) are already explained, they are not even mutually dependent; how could there be anything upon which to rely?"—"to rely" (*ji*) means to depend upon or entrust oneself to.

Therefore, he now refutes this: if even the *Avataṃsaka* is neither mutually dependent nor absolutely independent, upon what could it rely? Since there is nothing upon which to rely, it follows that...
It is clear that the *Avataṃsaka* has not yet reached the ultimate cessation [of teaching]. If it were otherwise, why would it remain at the stage of distinct and sequential exposition?
Why would the followers of the Two Vehicles sit in the assembly as if deaf and blind? And why, after the conclusion of the three assemblies, would there be a subsequent refutation of contradictions?

The conclusion of the assemblies is precisely the revelation of the Dharma in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, it is said that [the *Avataṃsaka*] returns to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If this is so, then the absolute, sudden, and sudden [teaching] is indeed [the finality].
This belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Why, then, is it judged to be "not the sudden of the sudden"?

This section, which consists of twenty-six layers of critical inquiry regarding the error of judging the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as possessing only the "relative" [teaching], is divided into three parts. First, the question.

"How could there be a lack of convergence without the absence of 'absolute dependence'? Next, the answer is given through three metaphors.

Therefore, it is said that they ultimately fail to understand the names upon which [the categories] depend; this extends even to the statement that they "contradict their own tenets," where "to contradict" (fù) means to forget or to turn one's back on.

Regarding this contemplation (*guan*), since each and every contemplation is inherently without scriptural text, it is simply stated in general terms that "each contemplation is without text.

Distinguishing the error of establishing the characteristics of sudden-sudden contemplation. The text is divided into three parts: first, the question; second, the answer;

First, it cites Qingliang [Zhiyuan], who failed to recognize that the purification of the six sense faculties in the *Lotus Sūtra* implies that the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) have already fallen away. Consequently, he erroneously states only that they are "pure" without mentioning that they were "previously severed.
Second, as a metaphor, it should state that the mental faculty (*manas*) is purified according to the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and that this refers to the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

As previously analyzed, regarding the term "cause and effect," the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) merely states: "The beginning, the end, and the middle. Thus, the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is the causal practice;
the fruit of that practice is the middle; and being eternally separated from the ocean of suffering is the resultant fruit.

Consequently, both the initial and middle stages—which are the causal practice and the fruit of practice—are themselves resultant causes. Therefore, the cause and effect in the two sutras differ. Although the cause and effect...

Likewise, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*’s account of the purification of the six sense faculties does not mean there is no prior arousal of the bodhicitta.

Since Master Qingliang did not perceive that their underlying principles were identical, he proceeded to differentiate between the gradual and sudden teachings based on the textual passages of these two sūtras, thereby establishing the distinction between the "gradual-sudden" and the "sudden-sudden. This is profoundly untenable.
Furthermore, [the author] refutes the error of dividing one section of *Mohe Zhiguan* into two sudden teachings. The text is divided into two parts: first, the citation; second, the analogy.

The first part is further divided into four sections. First, the critique based on the contradiction between the extensive and the abbreviated versions. Then, from "Fifth" onwards, the critique based on understanding and practice.
This refutes the contradiction. How can one take "understanding" (*jie*) as being "sudden-sudden"? For now, I shall refute this based on the general meaning of a single chapter.

The eye’s ability to guide the feet serves as a metaphor for cessation-understanding (*zhijie*); the feet’ ability to reach the destination serves as a metaphor for cessation-practice (*zhixing*). "Gao" refers to grease;

the grease’s capacity to sustain light serves as a metaphor for contemplation-practice (*guangxing*); the light’s ability to burn the grease serves as a metaphor for contemplation-understanding (*guangjie*). Now, when the eyes look...

"To tread the West while facing East" and "to apply grease to the South while seeking light in the North" are criticisms of those who deviate from the union of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), as well as from the integration of understanding (*adhimokṣa*) and practice (*pratipatti*).
The third section, beginning with "Furthermore, if below," broadly cites various differing texts to criticize Qingliang [Zongmi] for his ignorance of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Although the subsequent text mentions the four teachings and eight teachings, the conceivable and inconceivable, the relative and the absolute, and so forth, all [of these distinctions]...
In order to manifest the single reality of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun yishishi), I have now broadly cited various differing texts to refute them. Following the phrase "The text already...
is the fourth section, the conclusion of the refutation.

This section, which analyzes the error of establishing two sudden approaches to the cultivation of contemplation and the resulting difficulty in distinguishing between them, consists of two parts: first, the citation; second, [the analysis].
The analogy consists of two parts. First, the explicit clarification of the present intent:

since entering the non-arising [of phenomena] must rely upon the teachings, and those teachings necessarily reveal the beginning and end of both principle and phenomenon, how can it be said that they are "difficult to distinguish"?

Furthermore, since the preceding five major chapters provide the arising of understanding to guide skillful means, how can the commencement of the five categories of practice be said to be "difficult to distinguish"? If they are not distinguished...
How else could understanding arise? If understanding does not arise, how can one proceed? Next, the text states "furthermore," refuting those erroneous explanations.

This section consists of two parts: first, restating the opponent's position and directly refuting it; second, showing that since there is no scriptural authority to distinguish between shallow and deep levels, they are like those who blindly realize and give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), failing to comprehend the Dharma of non-arising as true realization.
To erroneously explain the names [of the stages] is no different from a strange anomaly.
The rat makes a chirping sound; this chirping has no meaning. To indiscriminately equate birth-and-death with nirvana is like a strange bird making the sound "kūṅ-kūṅ.

How could it be appropriate to indiscriminately claim that this is identical to the *dveṣuṇya-śūnyatā-samādhi* (the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness)—wherein the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi* is signless (*animitta*), the signless is wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the wishless is empty, which is the noble dharma—and yet proclaim words of entry into realization? Such [claims] are merely self-proclamation.
Having already entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) and realized the wondrous Way, one causes others to conceive of one as a noble being and to take refuge in and revere one.

If one suddenly causes them to receive [teachings] while claiming to speak the truth, one falls into the offense of "exceeding human beings" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). "Falls" means to fall or to descend. To falsely claim to possess the qualities of one who has transcended the human realm (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) toward those in the human destiny (*manuṣya-gati*) constitutes this offense.

If the person before one understands and realizes this, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*); if the person does not know, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (or *ānantarya*, depending on the specific tradition). It is said:
If devas, nāgas, and others come to make offerings to me, it is a grave offense to speak of this person to that person and so forth while claiming, "I am a Buddha, a Teacher of Gods and Men.
To speak of superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) in the presence of an animal that cannot transform its shape constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

There is no offense in cases of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), or when the qualities are obtained as a result of karmic retribution; nor is there an offense if one speaks jokingly, speaks rapidly, or speaks in private.
This means that when one intends to speak of this but instead speaks of those, it is an error. "The person who understands" refers to causing them to receive and comprehend the truth.
"Committing a grave offense" means falling into a transgression beyond that of ordinary people. Regarding the phrase "even obtaining a true prediction incurs fault":
"fault" (*āpatti*) means a transgression. It means that although one has truly attained the Path, one speaks of superhuman states (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*) to laypeople, saying, "I have seen this."
"I know these [cases]: one commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) because it contradicts one's perception; 'sin' (*xìn*) refers to guilt or flaw.
That is, when one claims to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) in the presence of another human being, if that person understands and believes it, one commits a grave offense.

Even if one has actually attained the Noble Path, to speak of it to a layperson still incurs a *thullaccaya*, as it contradicts one's internal perception and involves falsely claiming superhuman qualities. This is what is meant by "a grave sin."

The great delusion regarding the realization of *tathatā* (True Suchness) is placed at the beginning for this very reason. Next, the phrase "Furthermore, if... is a concession used to refute the notion of actual attainment;

since others have not yet actually attained it, he provisionally grants it for the sake of argument, hence the words "Furthermore, if. This section is divided into two parts. First, he determines [the stages] by means of the five grades of provisional names.
"Provisional names" refers to the stage of names and words (*nāma-pada*). These names and words consist of empty understanding and do not yet possess reality.

Because they are attained [only through conceptualization], they are termed "provisional" (*prajñapti*). Thus, the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) states: "They exist within the stage of provisional names.
If one asks, "In what way do they differ from others?"—who is not subsumed under names? Therefore, they are no different from others.

If those in the five grades of practice were identical to the Great Master, then how could it be that the Great Master Tiantai personally received the transmission at Vulture Peak, attained the wondrous awakening at Great Sū Mountain, entered meditative absorption to subdue demons, and occupied the stage of the Perfect [Teaching]?
The teaching for ordinary people outside the gates consists of five grades. If you were to claim that you have attained these five grades, then you would be identical to the Great Master Tiantai.
However, in reality, you are not at all the same as the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai.

If you say you are the same, why then have you so erroneously misunderstood the method of *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation)? For this reason, it is truly not the same. The passage beginning with "Next, I truly... expresses self-humbling and admonition toward others. I...
"I truly cannot judge" means to humble oneself. "I pray that you do not deceive the Sage and do not contradict your own mind" is a warning to others.
"I" refers to the self; Jingxi refers to himself. "I truly cannot judge" means that he truly cannot decide upon or measure what you have said.
"Entering contemplation to know and realize it" means to understand it for oneself. This speaks of entering contemplation by oneself and attaining realization.
To claim knowledge and realization is to deceive the sages and contravene one's own mind. May you not deceive the sages nor contravene your own mind;
this is to admonish others not to speak falsely. One must enter contemplation for oneself before such knowledge and realization can be attained. "Realization" means self-comprehension.
Chapter Thirty-three: Distinguishing Errors Regarding Zhiyan’s Use of the Text on Contemplating the Mind in the Twelvefold Canon as a Deficiency of the "Sudden-of-the-Sudden.
This section consists of two parts. First, the citation of Master Ding’s text on contemplating the mind in the Twelvefold Canon:

In the *Miaoxuan*, within the section on the "Excellence of the Teaching," there is a deficiency regarding the category of contemplating the mind. The *Shiqian* states: "One should apply the twelvefold canon of contemplating the mind."

This refers to a separate small fascicle that has circulated, which points precisely to Zhiyan’s (Zhang’an) text on the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) within the twelvefold division of the scriptures.
Thus, Zhiyan said: "Sūtra means 'to proceed. The mind also proceeds; all phenomena are created by the mind proceeding.
To directly engage in the contemplation of the mind as empty, provisional, and middle is called *sūtra*. To contemplate it again and again is called *geya*.

At night, observing that within the emptiness, provisionality, and the middle of the mind, one can give rise to the mind that is itself empty, provisional, and middle—this is called *sūtra*. Observing it again and again is called *geya*.
Observing that within the emptiness, provisionality, and the middle of the mind, one can give rise to the three types of wisdom is called *vyākaraṇa*.

Observing that the mind is itself provisional, empty, and also empty is called *gāthā* (non-repetitive verse). Observing that the emptiness, provisionality, and the middle of the mind are neither prior thought nor subsequent realization is called *avaivartika* (unasked).
To speak of oneself: observing that the mind arises from conditions—like objects arising and ceasing—and is thus empty, provisional, and middle, is called the *avadāna* (parable).

Observing the beginning and end of the mind as being empty, provisional, and middle is called the *itivṛttaka* (past events). Observing the ten realms of the mind—from the hells up to the Buddhas—as being empty, provisional, and middle, including their original births, is called the *jātaka* (birth stories).
Observing the mind’s emptiness, provisionality, and middle nature to prevent error and cease evil is called the *nidāna* (causes and conditions). Observing...

The mind’s emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle pervade all directions and dimensions without exception; this is called Vaipulya (Extensive). Contemplating that the mind’s emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle do not exist within the mundane world is called Adbhuta-dharma (Marvelous).
As for why the mind is empty: it is because it arises from conditions. Why is it provisional? It is because it consists merely of names.
Why is it the Middle? Because it is free from the two extremes. This is called Upadeśa (Exegesis). The above is a brief summary of the general outline of the text.
[The section on] the Ear. Next is the analogy. The text is divided into two parts. First, a general presentation of the contemplative method (*guanfa*) of our own school.

This is further divided into two: first, a general indication; second, a detailed explanation. The text is divided into three sections. First, clarifying that the contemplation based on practice consists solely of contemplating the one mind within the myriad objects.

This is as explained in the preceding text; furthermore, one must first realize that the myriad phenomena are mind-only before one can contemplate the mind. Although the myriad objects differ, they are wondrously...

Regarding "contemplating the equality of principles" (*li deng*): although the myriad objects of contemplation differ, if the contemplating subject is such that its observation is nothing other than the one mind, then the principle revealed therein is nothing other than the three truths (*san di*).
This is precisely the meaning of "contemplating the aggregates" (*yin*) and so forth;

it demonstrates that although the myriad objects are distinct, the wondrous contemplation of their principles is equal. This contemplation is established based on practice (*xing*), not based on the [specific] dharmas.

It clarifies by examining the characteristics of phenomena; therefore, it is called "contemplation according to practice. Thus, this specifically refers to the ten objects and ten vehicles of the *Mohe zhiguan*.

Next, it clarifies the contemplation of the Four Truths and Five Practices according to the characteristics of the Dharma. These are originally the numerical categories of the doctrinal gate’s *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics).
However, fearing that practitioners might merely count another's treasures to their own detriment, it therefore employs these [categories] to lead them into [contemplation].

Taking the single thought-moment as the perfect contemplation (the *Wenju ji* states: "Generally, when constructing contemplations based on the text, they mostly pertain to the Perfect [Teaching]; this is precisely that meaning").

One does not abandon the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to have a separate practice of contemplation; therefore, it is called "contemplation according to the characteristics of phenomena. "According to" (*yue*) means to bind together or to grasp. It is also called "contemplation attached to the characteristics of phenomena.

Thus, this specifically refers to the four truths of the "Excellence of the Object" (*viṣayaparamatā*) and the five [truths] of the "Excellence of Practice" (*pratipattiparamatā*) within the *Xuanyi*.

This is the practice. One should know that the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) is not without its reliance on phenomena (*shì*). Thus, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states: "Relying on phenomena and attaching to the Dharma" (*yúncúnyún*).

Third, the mutual contemplation based on phenomena (*shìxiàng guān*). For example, when names such as Rājagṛha and Gṛdhrakūṭa are established based on phenomena, they are established from the characteristics of phenomenal objects;
they do not refer to phenomena characterized by the Dharma. By borrowing phenomena as objects of contemplation to guide deluded attachments, one... [text ends].

Fearing that students might become mired in objective phenomena and fail to attain awakening, he therefore borrowed these [phenomena] to serve as a sublime contemplation, in order to guide students away from their obstructed attachments.
Thus, this specifically refers to the *Fahua Wenju* (The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra). "To entrust" (*tuō*) means to rely upon or to lodge something therein.
Therefore, the *Wenju* (Text on Words and Phrases) states: "The 'King' is the mind-king; the 'house' refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The mind-king constructs this house.

If one dismantles the house of the five aggregates, emptiness becomes the city of nirvāṇa. If this contemplation is shallow—such as seeing the earth, wood, and tiles (as the *Xiangfa jueyi lun* says: "Or one sees the mountains, forests, ground, soil, sand, and stones of this place")—it is like that.
However, if one realizes that the house of the five aggregates is itself emptiness, and that emptiness is the city of nirvāṇa, this is the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching).
If one contemplates the five aggregates as empty, by the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so (and so forth).
If one contemplates the five aggregates as the dharma-nature, the dharma-nature is devoid of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

all sentient beings are themselves nirvana (and so forth). Regarding the contemplation of the mountain of the mind: if one contemplates the aggregate of form as being insentient like a mountain, [so too is] consciousness...

The *giri* (mountain) is like the *linga* (spiritual essence). The three *giri* (mountains) are like the *Gṛdhrakūṭa* (Vulture Peak). To contemplate this *Lingagṛdhrakūṭa* as impermanent is the contemplation of analytical discernment (*vibhajya-vipaśyanā*). It is the contemplation of the essence of emptiness (*śūnyatā-svabhāva-vipaśyanā*).

Contemplating the *linga* is the wisdom of the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (the cause of realization), which is the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā-alaṃkāra*). The *gṛdhra* (vulture) is the accumulation of the *paratantra-hetu* (the causal condition), which is the adornment of merit (*puṇya-alaṃkāra*).
The mountain is the *dharmatā-hetu* (the true cause), the immovable nature of the three dharmas; it is named the "Secret Treasury" (*Guhyakośa*). Thus says the text.

The *Jùjì* (Commentary on the Verses) states: "Regarding the initial statement in the section on the 'King's House' (*rājakula*) concerning the object of contemplation—'the mind-king constructs the house'—the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the king.
Since all minds that construct karma must be accompanied by mental factors (*caitta*), one now wishes to explain the 'king.

For the time being, the good and evil mind-kings are contrasted with the neutral 'house' (*avyākṛta-rājakula*), hence it is said 'the king constructs. This demonstrates that the method of contemplation differs from other sutras; this should be understood."
The ten vehicles and ten objects of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are all like this; they are fully detailed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mo-ho chih-kuan), which cannot be cited in full here.

Regarding the practice of contemplating the mountain as the object of contemplation, one first establishes the object of the contemplation (*vipaśyanā-viṣaya*). This precisely corresponds to the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*), as found in the text of the fifth chapter of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* onwards.

Since it is stated in the *Bieyuan guan* (Separate and Complete Contemplations) that "the mountain is the *dharmatā* of the true cause," the other two virtues may be inferred from various other texts. Therefore...

Know that this contemplation differs from other views. The reason for again taking the mountain as the object of contemplation is that although the mountain and the city differ, they are both *pariṇāmanirmita* (retributive environments).
Therefore, by means of them, one contemplates the *sambhogakāya* (the primary retribution). Furthermore, the objects of all contemplations do not go beyond the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Now, these mountains and so forth are taken because they are convenient for correlating with the aggregates. Since various texts simply speak of "object and wisdom" (*ālambana-jñāna*), one should also apply this principle here.

One must skillfully and correctly cultivate the characteristics of the similarities and differences between these two contemplations. This involves distinguishing the objects and the mind, as well as differentiating between the provisional and the real in contrast to the preceding two [contemplations], and so forth, up to the four contemplations, all of which must be revealed and clarified.
Since this is the case for the contemplation based on phenomena (*shikishō*), it is even more so for the contemplation attached to the Dharma (*fusshō*).

Thus, both the contemplation based on phenomena and the contemplation attached to the Dharma must be attained within the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) through skillful means and correct cultivation.

Only by practicing the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) and the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) can one, upon hearing a single phrase, encompass all phenomena to establish the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*).

This is what is meant by "not depending on the object of contemplation" before it is called the practice of contemplation. (Regarding the term "not depending": although the *Xuanyi* currently opens with a formal discussion of the characteristics of the Dharma, it merely provides a preliminary exposition of the meaning of the preparatory and formal practices of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Here, these are presented to decisively penetrate the path of contemplation, thereby enabling the practitioner to cultivate the contemplation that accords with the Dharma. It is not necessary to further wait for the lecture on those [specific] objects of contemplation within the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. For this reason, it is said that "only when one does not depend on the object of contemplation is it called the practice of contemplation.")

If it were not so, why would the *Commentary* (Ji) instruct one to rely on the skillful means of calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) to correctly cultivate the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*), given that the text [of the *Mohe zhiguan*] describes the contemplations of "relying on phenomena" (*fufa*) and "relying on events" (*toshi*) as being like the viewing of a mountain city?

Guishan did not understand this and claimed that these two types of contemplation—relying on phenomena and relying on events—lack the ten objects and the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*), and thus he prohibited people from practicing them. For this reason, Siming refuted him. I have no factional bias; I dare say that Siming’s refutation was most appropriate, as the meaning is explained in detail in the *Jinbi yuyan ji*.
This can be understood through examples such as those in the *Vaipulya* [sūtras] regarding Samantabhadra, or the "half-walking, half-sitting" samādhis in the *Zhi guan*.

The middle [period] involves the practice of contemplation by means of the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) teachings through the sequential engagement with phenomena (*vastu*), which serves as a precedent for this.

Therefore, by relying on phenomena to practice contemplation, one can come to understand it. Regarding the *Vaipulya*, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "By means of this wisdom of emptiness, one passes through all phenomena such that there is nothing that does not become an object of contemplation."
Regarding "Vaipulya" (fangděng): some say it means "broad and level. Here, "fang" (square) refers to the Dharma.
There are four methods within Prajñāpāramitā, namely the four gates for entering the pond of coolness; these are the "fang. The principle realized is equal great wisdom, which is the "děng.
Causing the seeker to dream of the King is the preliminary skillful means (*purva-yoga*) for the two contemplations. "Dharmacakra" (the site of enlightenment) refers to the realm of purity.

Furthermore, it treats the sugar of the five abodes to manifest the rice of the true mark (*dharmatā*). This, too, is the adornment of the *dharmakāya* through the functioning of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth.

Regarding Samantabhadra, the *Zhiguan* states: "Now, as one cultivates contemplation according to the text, the six-tusked white elephant represents the Bodhisattva’s six untainted supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The tusks possess utility, signifying the swiftness of these powers; the elephant possesses great strength, symbolizing the Dharma."
"Bearing it upon one's body; being untainted and undefiled, it is called 'white' (and so forth).

This indicates that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* clarify not only the contemplation derived from practice, but also the contemplation based on phenomena (*dharmapratisaraṇa*). Furthermore, among the four types of samādhi, only the "constant sitting" (*ekāsana*) is excluded from the recitation of sutras;
thus, the "constant walking" (*caṅkramaṇa*) and other practices are not without their basis in the Dharma. For instance, in the cultivation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...

When reciting the sutras in a state of mental dullness, one attains awakening regarding the characteristics and phenomena of the Dharma; is this not precisely the cultivation of the "contemplation based on the Dharma" (fufa guan)?

Therefore, following the twelve divisions [of the teachings], there next follows a specific refutation of the faults of erroneous application, which is further divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the ten [errors] of Zhang'an.
Regarding the fact that the contemplative methods (*guanfa*) in the two divisions of the sutras are concise and incomplete, and thus rely on phenomena to establish names for the contemplation:

this refers to what was previously mentioned—establishing the "contemplation of the mind" (*guanxin*) by taking phenomena as the basis for generating contemplation. Although the names of the "three contemplations" (*sanguan*) exist, this is because the texts concerning the contemplation of the mind within the twelve divisions of the scriptures speak only of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
As for the ten objects (*shijing*) and the ten vehicles (*shicheng*) not being listed, it is, for instance, as follows:
The *Miaoxuan* also clarifies the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*). The *Shiqian* even states that it merely distinguishes the ten contemplations by listing their names;

how much more so for the twelvefold division of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), where they are not listed at all? Under the title of each of the twelve divisions, only a single [phrase] is applied:

because under the name of each of the twelve divisions of the contemplation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*), only the single phrase "immediately empty, provisional, and middle" (*sahaiva śūnyatā-prajñapti-madhyamā*) is applied.

Therefore, if Qingliang were to correctly cultivate the ten objects and ten vehicles through the skillful means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, decisively penetrating and expanding upon the contemplations of the twelve divisions of the scriptures to clarify the characteristics of cultivation, what would be improper?

It is only because Qingliang followed his own arbitrary inclinations that he erroneously judged the ten objects and ten vehicles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as being gradual or sudden, and separately applied Zhanran’s ten... [text truncated]
To regard the two types of contemplation as "sudden-sudden" is precisely what Jingxi refuted.

Therefore, one must not cling to this [refutation] and conclude that the contemplations of "relying on phenomena" (*toshi*) and "attaching to phenomena" (*fuhō*) in the *Miaoxuan* and *Wenju* are inaccessible for human cultivation.

This is because the Master of the Records (Zhiyi) commanded that one employ the preparatory practices (*fangbian*) of *Zhiguan* to decisively open the path through formal cultivation (*zhengxiu*). How could it be that under this single phrase, the Great Master [Huisi] next... [elucidates]?
The "Comprehensive Sufficient Contemplation of Objects" (Jingguan Zhouzu) serves to refute erroneous applications [of the teachings]. The text is divided into two parts.

First, the refutation of the error of discarding the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) and the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) based on a single phrase; the character "fan" (煩) is correctly written as "fan" (繁). "Reng" (芿) means that grass has not been trimmed; it refers to being excessive or prolix.
Second, from "Therefore one knows" (*guzhi*) onwards, the conclusion which refutes the faults of relying on a single phrase or two phrases. One phrase, two...
Regarding the "phrases": this is a brief restatement of the application of the twelve divisions of the canon to the Contemplation of Coolness. The remainder is as previously analyzed.

Third, there is the analysis of the error in establishing a gradual and perfect contemplation that treats the "but-mid" (but-middle) as not being the true reality itself. The text is divided into three parts.
First, the question; second, the answer; third, the analogy. The text is divided into two parts. The first clarifies the primary intent of our own school (*jia*).

In all the texts of this school, it is taught that the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) is called "only-middle" (*danzhong*), whereas the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is the "not-only-middle" (*budanzhong*).

As for the term "only-middle": it is "only" (*dan*) because its teaching is provisional and does not encompass all phenomena; it is "middle" (*zhong*) because its principle is real and its essence is the nature of awakening (*juxing*). Now, the present text says "real" (*shi*)...

The "but-middling" (*danzhong*) of the provisional teaching is real; thus, both are real. When explaining the text according to the teachings, the "but-middling" resides in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). This is precisely because of this [distinction].
The "but-provisional" (*danquan*) refers to the fact that the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) possesses only the name of "middling," and thus it is called "but-middling.

Therefore, both this "but-middling" and the "real mark" (*shixiang*) are termed "provisional. As for the sequence of cultivating contemplation, it still occupies the subsequent mind. This is based on the ten stages of the path of the teachings (*jiaodao*).

The subsequent mind-observation pertains only to the Middle Way; it must not be conflated with the distinct teaching’s dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which involves the non-dual integration of the Perfect Teaching.
This is because the stage of dedication within the distinct teaching contains multiple meanings:

it may pertain to the provisional (*prajñapti*), or to the mere Middle Way, or to the reception and transition [of practitioners], or to the perfect cultivation. Therefore, one must carefully distinguish these four meanings (etc.). Others call this the gradual [teaching].

Yuan Guan’s [interpretation] of "only-middle" (but-madhyama) is an error; he mistakenly explains the "Perfect" (yuan) within the Four Teachings as the "Distinct" (bie) Teaching. Therefore, the present critique states:

regarding the textual explanation according to the teachings, "only-middle" resides in the Distinct Teaching, whereas the "Perfect" (yuan) among the Four Teachings—in all its texts—refers to the three perfect contemplations (san-guan) from the very first stage of the path.
How could it ever be said that one is contemplating "only-middle"? He proceeds below this contemplation to next refute [the opponent].

The error of misclassifying [the teachings] into two categories and the fault of lacking textual evidence for the "sudden" (dun) are further divided into two parts. First, the direct refutation of the misclassification:

when that [opponent] attributes this contemplation to the "sudden-of-the-sudden," they are refuted for their indiscriminate application of the "Perfect" (yuan) teaching from among the four teachings, taking the initial beginner’s practice of the three contemplations as the "sudden-of-the-sudden.
Therefore, the preceding analogy states: "According to this answer, one instead uses the 'gradual-perfect' (jian-yuan) as the 'sudden'."

"Immediate" (dùn) refers precisely to this. As for establishing the "mere Middle" (dànzhōng) specifically for those of the Perfect Teaching (yuán), it is intended to refute the error of taking the mind of the final stage of dedication in the Separate Teaching (biéjiào) as an observation of the mere Middle;
thus, the "mere Middle" is established specifically for those of the Perfect Teaching. The mutual inversion between the Perfect and the Separate is extreme;

moreover, since there is no authoritative basis [for such a claim], is it not merely a product of one's own imagination? Regarding the passage beginning with "Only afflictions," next, the *Shí* (The Collection/Selection) is refuted.

"Taking loss as gain" and "not abiding in discipline, etc. refers to what the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* says: Furthermore, there are practitioners who, upon hearing that one should not abide in discipline nor abide in non-discipline, become terrified of these two extremes.
They maintain themselves with great vigilance, wishing to cultivate middle-way wisdom to sever and destroy the two extremes.
Such people cannot realize that desire itself is the Way; they claim it is the Way only after desire has been severed. This...

This means that one abides in the mind of subduing; it is not that one does not abide [in it]. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "Furthermore, regarding the practitioner below," this is a re-examination of the person of the fourth phrase.
This is the same as the loss of the second phrase: failing to abide in both the subdued and the unsubdued while seeking the Middle Way.

Although one seeks the Middle Way, this merely results in abiding in the second phrase; therefore, it is called a "loss. (Regarding the four phrases, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "There is illness... )

A bodhisattva should discipline the mind in this way: neither dwelling within it, nor dwelling in an undisciplined mind. Why is this? To dwell in an undisciplined mind is the way of fools; to dwell in a disciplined mind is the way of the śrāvakas.

Therefore, a bodhisattva should not dwell in either a disciplined or an undisciplined mind. To be free from these two states is the practice of a bodhisattva. This is induced by *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. (The sequence of the phrasing is largely the same as in the sutra.)

Thirty-five: Distinguishing Errors and Establishing that "Mere Middle" (but-madhyama) is Not Identical to the True Nature (bhūtalakṣaṇa). This constitutes a fault within the "mere middle. The text is divided into three parts: first, the question;

second, the answer; third, the analogy. The [third] part consists of four sections: first, showing that the name applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; second, from the words "beginning practitioners" (*ādikarmika*)... [and so forth].
This correctly refutes errors and establishes the truth; that is, from the very beginning, one constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa*. This refers to what the *Śāstra* says:

"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the Bodhisattva constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa* while practicing the Path. Both the *Miaoxuan* and the *Wenju* cite this passage to authenticate the "Peaceful and Happy Practice" (*anle xing*).

Third, from the section below, it correctly distinguishes and judges according to the gates of teaching, stating that the "small *nirvāṇa*" is common to both the general and specific [Bodhisattva] paths.

The statement that "the *sat* (bodhisattva) is exclusively [this]" is a general, sweeping explanation; this is because, from the perspective of a specific beginner entering emptiness during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is no different from the universal *tathatā-satya* (true reality) and *nirvāṇa*.

However, if one discusses them specifically, this is not the case. Why? Because in the Universal Teaching (*pāryāyika-śāsana*), the seventh stage is already the stage of "accomplishment" (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*).
Fearing a fall into *nirvāṇa* refers precisely to the *nirvāṇa* of the biased emptiness of the *tathatā-satya*, which is like the three evil realms.
The Way. This refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*’s rebuke of Subhūti: "Those who give to you are not called fields of merit;

those who make offerings to you fall into the three evil realms. "Like" (*rú*) means similar or identical. This is because Bodhisattvas are identical to the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) in their stagnation within emptiness.

(This borrows the words of rebuke from the *Vimalakīrti*; that sutra refutes his [Subhūti’s] identification with the realm of compassion. Therefore, the meaning of the Śrāvaka as a "worthy recipient of offerings" (*arhat*) is partial. Thus, the *Zhi guan fu xing zhuan hong ming* cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, stating: "If one enters the seventh stage...")

Having already fallen into the two vehicles, they are therefore rebuked by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. For this reason, it is said here that when a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching reaches the seventh stage, there is a fear of falling into *nirvāṇa* as if into the three evil realms. Having reached the seventh stage, there is a fear of falling into *nirvāṇa*, becoming submerged in emptiness and stalled in quiescence.

Thus we know that emerging into the provisional [world] does not necessarily require the seventh stage or those of inferior capacity; rather, emerging into the provisional while still at the stage of an ordinary person is called "superior capacity," and having severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) and then emerging into the provisional is called "middle capacity.

As for the fact that in the Initial Mind of the Distinct Teaching it is merely termed the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) and the name "Nirvāṇa" cannot yet be established, this is based on the distinction between cause and fruit.

Discussing this: the entry into the true truth of emptiness during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) pertains to the cause; therefore, one cannot establish for it the designation of "Nirvana," which is the merit of cessation belonging to the fruit.
Fourth, "Thus we know" and below concludes by refuting [the opponent's position] as being without basis.

The thirty-sixth section distinguishes errors regarding the fallacy of establishing the existence of the "contemplation of the mere Middle" (butian zhong) as *nirvāṇa*. The text is divided into three parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the analogy. Regarding the phrase "not seeing even a slight judgment," etc.:
it means that not seeing even a slight judgment—that the initial mind’s contemplation of the mere Middle is named *nirvāṇa*—yet Qingliang [Wenbei] says it "exists," is clearly a false attribution.

In the thirty-seventh [section], "Discerning Delusion," the text establishes two errors regarding the sudden teaching. It consists of three parts: first, the question; second, the answer—in which the character "or" (或) should be read as "delusion" (惑);
and third, the analogies, which consist of two parts. First, the refutation of the erroneous application of passages such as the *Dà yì* (大意), which has already been refuted previously.
Second, the refutation of the false citation of Zhiyi’s (*Zhàngān*) commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which is itself divided into four sections. First, the cross-examination.
There is no such text. Next, it should be understood as a refutation of the reasons for pointing to the "lower" [teachings] as false. Third, from "Furthermore, the Great Master...
onwards, it cites that various texts by the Great Master do not record this, thereby refuting the separate citation of Zhanran’s (Zhang’an) text.

How could it be possible that while there is no mention of this in the Great Master’s various texts concerning the classification of teachings (*panjiao*), Zhanran would arbitrarily establish the distinction between two types of *dun* (sudden) teachings—those with and those without interruption? Therefore, one knows that...
The Master’s judgment regarding the classification of the teachings (*pianjiao*) contains no such textual evidence; there is no need to further cite the assertions of Zhangan.

As for the passage beginning "Furthermore," it concludes by rebuking the false attribution, as the established doctrine cannot be proven. If Zhangan had indeed possessed such a text, it would be acceptable; since he has none, how can he falsely attribute it?
Nevertheless, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Xuanming Jing* fully enumerate the four propositions within their applications. Although the fourth is indeed referred to as...

"Ton-ton. [The author] again points to the previous passage clarifying that within the school of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is yet another practice, namely the "Tathāgata-practice," which includes the Great Parinirvāṇa and the eternally abiding [nature], etc.
Qingliang did not understand this and falsely established a "Ton-ton" (Sudden-Sudden) as distinct from the "Yuan-ton" (Perfect-Sudden).

Therefore, [the author] now refutes him, saying: "Furthermore, since the 'non-sequential fifth practice' is precisely the Perfect [Teaching] among the Four Teachings, how can you erroneously judge it to be [Ton-ton]?"
Is it that [the teaching] is not interrupted, yet constitutes two "sudden" [teachings]?
Regarding the thirty-eighth section, which refutes the error of establishing two "sudden" teachings based on the eightfold classification of the Dharma, the text is divided into two parts:

first, the citation [of the opponent's position], and second, the analogy. Having already refuted the former in the preceding text regarding the establishment of two "sudden" teachings according to the eightfold classification, here we shall merely refute their numerical frequency and constancy.
It is said that since he has repeatedly and constantly spoken [thus] in the past, he now likewise frequently rebukes [us].
Section Thirty-nine: Distinguishing Errors Regarding the Confusion of the Two Sudden Approaches and Their Differences. This text is divided into two parts: first, the citation; second, the analogy.

The character *qiào* (pronounced *kǔdiào*) means a hole or an opening; this does not accord with the meaning of the text. It should instead be the character *pó* (meaning "to strike from the side"). Thus, it refers to striking from the flank.
Therefore, one must not use the difficulty of reconciling what is different yet the same, or what is the same yet different, as a pretext to launch lateral attacks against others.
Nor should one refuse to admit that gradual perfection is itself sudden enlightenment.

Section Forty: Distinguishing Errors in the Judgment of Form, Fragrance, and the Middle Way as Gradual or Sudden. This section consists of three parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the analogy.
Regarding this, *Zhi guan* quotes the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, saying: "The mind wanders through the dharma-realm like empty space," and further:

"That which is 'non-illumination' is illumination; this is ultimate emptiness. These passages cite emptiness as the starting point of the discourse. Emptiness is non-empty, and it is also not non-empty.
It is not non-empty. Furthermore, it is said that within a single atom there is a great thousand-fold world-system scripture, and that the mind contains all Buddha-dharmas;
this cites "existence" as the starting point of the discourse (students of Siming should reflect upon this passage). Existence is non-existence, and it is also neither existence nor non-existence.
Moreover, it is said that every form and every fragrance is none other than the Middle Way; this cites the "Middle" as the starting point of the discourse. This is precisely the Middle.

"Yet the 'edge' is neither an edge nor not an edge; it is complete and without deficiency. Do not cling to the words and thereby harm the perfection [of the teaching] by misrepresenting the Sage’s intent.

(Only one who speaks thus sees that raising one [aspect] immediately encompasses the three, being neither before nor after. Now, does the claim of the Four Ming [masters]—that each of the three truths of emptiness, conventionality, and the middle contains the ten realms and the three thousand worlds of the environment and its inhabitants—accord with the Great Master’s intent?

Alas! It is tragic; they cannot be saved. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "The text may be partial, but the meaning is perfect; one should not raise partial objections. Do not cling to the words."
"Et cetera" (*ādi*) refers to admonition and exhortation. Do not cling to partial words to the detriment of perfect integration. The *Yùpiān* states: "To add words is called *wú* (to slander);

it also means to conceal or to deceive. The meaning is largely the same as in the *Wǎngyì*. Regarding "words that may be exhaustive": as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies, the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-garbha*) may be [expressed] partially;
this is what is meant by "partial words with an exhaustive intent. Regarding "contradiction between one's own words," this is clarified in the Preface to the *Zhǐguān*.
In both the *Complete and Sudden Cessation and Contemplation* (*Yuandun zhiguan*) and the *Great Meaning* (*Dayi*), it is stated that every single form and scent is none other than the Middle Way.
Yet, while Qingliang previously classified the *Dayi* as "sudden-of-the-sudden," he now further classifies the Middle Way within forms and scents as "gradual-of-the-sudden.
Is this not a contradiction?

The forty-first section distinguishes the errors and establishes that the initial stage of contemplation is merely middling. The text is divided into three parts: first, the question; second, silence; and third, the analogy.
Regarding the statement that "silence is superior to speech": since speech that deviates from the Noble Path makes one's faults manifest, silence is therefore superior to speaking.
From the passage beginning with "In the general cultivation of contemplation" down to "the wordless," the text repeatedly refutes silence; this is evident in the text itself.

Section Forty-Two: Distinguishing Errors and Establishing the Two [Positions] Regarding the Faults of Suddenness—Having Parts versus Being Without Parts. This section consists of two parts: first, citing the scriptural texts; second, providing analogies.

Regarding the mention of "two texts," this refutes the reliance on those texts which insist that [the stages] must be distinguished. Regarding the mention of "observing one," this refutes the claim that [the stages] are actually difficult to differentiate.
Since the suffering of slandering the Dharma results in karmic retribution flowing through many kalpas, it is said that "vast accumulations are many. "Vast" means distant.
Since the mind is already deviant and perverse, it causes one not to encounter virtuous friends who can open up and clarify the Right Dharma in the future.

From this, one may know that learning the Dharma from a teacher must not follow mere human sentiment. Although human sentiments may provide temporary mutual comfort, who will bear the fault of the net of deception through long kalpas?
I respectfully entreat those of later virtue to reflect upon this and exercise great caution.
43. Distinguishing Errors: Judging the Failures of the Expedient Means of Neither-Simultaneous-Extinction-nor-Simultaneous-Illumination. The text is divided into three parts: first, the question;
second, the answer; third, the analogy. "Losing the thread" means losing its origin and cause. "Irregularity" means being disordered and inconsistent.

For details, as stated in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation): "The contemplation of the primary meaning of the Middle Way refers to the previous contemplations of the provisional and the empty."

One contemplates that birth and death are empty; subsequently, one contemplates that the emptiness of emptiness is itself the emptiness of nirvāṇa. To simultaneously negate both extremes is called the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).
As a means to realize the Middle Way, it is said that "mind after mind is quiescent and enters the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.

Furthermore, the initial contemplation employs emptiness, while the subsequent contemplation employs the provisional (*prajñapti*); this constitutes the skillful means of maintaining both. Upon entering the Middle Way, one is able to maintain both.
This illuminates the two truths. Thus, a sutra states: "If the mind is in meditative concentration, one can know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena.
The meaning here is that the preceding two contemplations serve as the two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says:

"In the *Yingluo jing*, after the explanation of the preceding two contemplations is finished, it immediately states: 'By means of these two emptiness-contemplations as the path of skillful means, one attains entry into the Middle Way and the simultaneous illumination [of both truths].'"
Regarding the two truths: when the mind and mental factors are stilled, one naturally enters the first stage (*bhūmi*). First, in explaining the skillful means (*upāya*), there are two types:

first, the simultaneous negation of both; second, the simultaneous illumination of both. Regarding the initial mention of the "two emptinesses": these are the emptiness of the conventional and the emptiness of emptiness.

Emptiness is precisely negation (*pratiṣedha*); negation is precisely negation. Through the aforementioned skillful means of simultaneous negation at different times, one now enters the Middle Way spontaneously.

Both are extinguished. Extinction is itself the Middle. Therefore it is said that "mind after mind is quiescent. Furthermore, from "first observing the lower" onwards, the text next explains the simultaneous illumination (*shuangzhao*).

During the first two observations, one employs emptiness and the provisional (*jia*). Because of the previous simultaneous employment of these two expedients (*fangbian*) at different times, this "employment" is itself "illumination."

Illumination is itself the Middle Way. Therefore, a sutra is cited stating that "the mind abides in meditative concentration," and so forth. Arising is the conventional, while cessation is the ultimate.
Thus, by abiding in the Middle Way, one is able to know arising and cessation; this knowing is itself illumination. This is the intended meaning, for all [three] are the Middle Way.

Therefore, one attains spontaneity (*anābhoga*). This spontaneity arises because the preceding mental attention (*manasikāra*) functions as a skillful means through the mutual disappearance of subject and object;
thus, when entering [the middle way], one is able to act in such a manner.
44. Distinguishing Errors: Refuting the Faults of General and Specific Cultivation. This section consists of three parts. First, the question:

*The First [Fascicle] of the *Zhi Guan* states: "The four samādhis are general cultivation; the Buddha-recollection (*nianfo*) is specific cultivation. This refers merely to the distinction between the general and the specific. Second, the answer:
Master Qingliang’s intention was that there was an error in Zhiyi’s compilation; thus he said, "This is merely the mistake of Master Ding. Third, the analogy.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Because the four samādhis encompass all practices, they are termed 'universal' (*tong*). Since the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*nienfo sanmei*) is but one among these various practices, it is termed 'particular' (*bie*).

Although the universal and particular differ, both are none other than sublime practices. Furthermore, because all four samādhis universally involve the remembrance of the Buddha, they are termed 'universal';
yet, when speaking specifically of the remembrance of the Buddha, one is singling out a single practice, and thus it is termed 'particular. Therefore...

The *Sishennianchu* (Four Foundations of Mindfulness) states: "In all four, one contemplates the Buddha; however, they are termed 'distinct' because the objects of contemplation differ according to the specific teachings.

In the first three teachings, one contemplates each of the bodies individually—namely, the birth-body, the response-body, and the retribution-body. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), one contemplates the Dharma-body, wherein all bodies are fully present."

Furthermore, the four samādhis apply across all four teachings; therefore, they are also called "universal" (*tong*). Some have altered this to say that while the four samādhis are specific to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, the latter is universal.

This does not lose the general meaning. Why needlessly contravene the text? (According to Zhiyi’s compilation of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, it states: "The four samādhis are universal cultivation; mindfulness of the Buddha is specific cultivation.

This has never lost the Master’s intent, nor has it lost the general meaning of the universal and the specific, nor the general meaning of the first ten chapters of the *Zhiguan*. As for the phrase "why needlessly" (*he jia*): *jia* means "to reach" or "to arrive at. Why needlessly [contravene]?

As for the "Text," it refutes Qingliang’s [Zhiyi]—why should one even trouble oneself with this? It contradicts the text of the *Mohe Zhiguan* and arbitrarily alters it by claiming: "The four samādhis are distinct practices; the recollection of the Buddha (nienfo) is a universal practice. Is this not erroneous?
45. Distinguishing Errors: Judging the Faults of the Three Worthies and Ten Sages. The text is divided into two parts: first, the citation; second, the analogy.

Regarding "the four stages of the Perfect Teaching," this refers to the forty stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering. The phrase "this master only sees below" introduces his erroneous division of the two teachings.
The statement that "the titles 'Worthy' and 'Sage' borrow names from the Distinct [Teaching] to clarify the Perfect" explains the true intent of our own school.
Therefore, the present school’s commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* states: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in the fruit-retribution.
This is a case of borrowing the names of the three worthies and ten sages from the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) to designate the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

It reveals that the forty stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering abide in the stage of the unobstructed land of true retribution; thus, while borrowing the names of the Distinct Teaching, it correctly elucidates the stages of the Perfect Teaching. — Qingliang.
I do not understand. To arbitrarily divide the ranks of sages and saints between the two teachings—how laughable this is!

If you say that the ranks of sages and saints in the Separate Teaching (biejiao) cannot be born there, then since the three stages of worthiness (sanhuan) in the Separate Teaching merely suppress afflictions without severing them, how could they be born in that land of true retribution?

As for those in the ten stages (shidi) who have broken through ignorance and are born in the land of true retribution, if their realization of the Way were identical to that of the Perfect Teaching, then [the distinction] would not hold.

[The previous argument] already pertains to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*); how much more so when considering that, in the actual teaching of the Path of Reality, there is no distinct person who attains birth [in that realm].

Therefore, it is illogical for the sages and saints of the Distinct Teaching to be born there. As for the judgment that the Ten Stages belong to the Distinct Teaching, this refers back to Qingliang’s erroneous judgment that the ten stages of sainthood constitute the Distinct Teaching.
Regarding the statement that all forty positions of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) equally destroy ignorance (*avidyā*): since all forty positions equally destroy ignorance, for what reason...

Is it that the three stages of the ordinary sages (*pṛthagjana*) are assigned to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), while the ten stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) are assigned to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*)?
Furthermore, if one considers them identical to the Perfect Teaching in terms of the path of realization (*zhengdao*), then the first stage (*bhūmi*) is precisely the first dwelling (*vihāra*).

Why, then, must the ten stages be divided and assigned to the Separate Teaching? Even if one maintains the provisional explanation regarding the path of teaching (*jiaodao*), the ten stages already encompass both teachings. Why? Because the path of realization is identical.
The Perfect [Teaching] and the Teachings of the Path are distinct. Therefore, there is no separate division of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) belonging to a distinct meaning.
Thus, the tenth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* states: "If the Distinct and the Perfect can destroy ignorance, they directly open up the reality of the path of suffering.

From this real dharma, one attains the retribution of reality. Directly within conditioned existence, one fulfills all practices and brings forth the primary and secondary environments without any obstruction."

With sharp faculties and profound merit, they differ from those of middling or inferior capacity. If the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sages abide in their karmic fruition, they all fully accomplish the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

For the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samantabhadra-bhūmi*), there remains one final birth as a link of dependent origination. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "If [the practitioner is] at the lower level of the Separate or Perfect Teachings..."

This further clarifies that the merit of the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Bodhisattva) stages surpasses that of the preceding teaching. This refers to the stage of the Sages (*ārya*), which is not identical to what preceded it;

however, because their realization of the Path (*mārga*) is identical to that of the Perfect [Vehicle], they are treated together. Nevertheless, the original distinct names are established according to the path of the teachings. From the three levels of Worthies (*śaikṣa*) downward, the causal stage of realizing sainthood is superior from beginning to end;

therefore, the previous passage explained the stages of the Separate Teaching only in terms of the practices of the *prayoga-mārga* (path of preparation) and *darśana-mārga* (path of seeing), whereas from the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward...

These are subsumed within this [classification]. Within the stage of the Three Worthies (trividya), because they are identical to the Perfect [Teaching] in terms of the path of realization, the first ground (*bhūmi*) is precisely the first dwelling (*vihāra*).

Therefore, they are subsumed within the fruit-retribution dwellings of the Three Worthies; for this reason, in terms of realization, one does not differentiate between the distinct levels of the Perfect [Teaching], but merely speaks of the stages of the Three Worthies and the Ten Sages (*daśārya*).
46. Distinguishing Errors: Refuting the Fault of Contradiction with the Lotus Sūtra’s Own Words. This section has two parts. First, the question;
this further has two parts: first, citing the opponent's question; second, presenting their answer. Next, the analogy. All of these texts are easily understood.
Third, from this point downward is the conclusion, which consists of two parts. First, the formal conclusion of the preceding text:

although the faults of the teaching were also discussed, they were mentioned only incidentally because they stem from the faults of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, the present conclusion states: "The faults of contemplation have been briefly explained;

the faults of the teaching are not discussed. Second, from "I take refuge" (*namo*) downward, it clarifies the intent of refutation and establishment. Thus, a metaphor is now established to enlighten the reader.
I have doubts. If he is not [as you say], then this [criticism] is likewise lost. It is like speaking of "emptiness within emptiness" to one facing a flower; there are no names for it.
Therefore, I take refuge in the various worthies and sages, praying that they will abandon the mind of right and wrong.

However, my previous [intent] was merely to establish the sublime practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as transmitted to us as the cause for unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. It was not that I intended to disparage it according to my own fixed views.
To suppress and thwart others may be considered a failure. May all those of future virtue embody this intention.
*Zhi guan yi li zuan yao*, Volume Six (End).
